articles.title: Winter rains threaten 1,000 Gaza shelter sites, councils warn
articles.excerpt: Gaza’s municipalities have warned that winter rains could flood about 1,000 camps and other sites hosting displaced Palestinians in the war-torn enclave, adding that damage to drains and sewers, and a...
articles.body_text:
Gaza’s municipalities have warned that winter rains could flood about 1,000 camps and other sites hosting displaced Palestinians in the war-torn enclave, adding that damage to drains and sewers, and a shortage of pumps, have left their crews with little means to clear the water.

After a meeting in Gaza City on Wednesday, the Union of Gaza Strip Municipalities singled out al-Mughraqa and al-Zahra in central Gaza, where water levels in Wadi Gaza could rise suddenly. Across the territory, about 200,000 tents need replacing, and more than 2,000 damaged buildings are at risk of collapse, the union said. Gaza’s Government Media Office had warned on Tuesday that it expected another storm within days.

This is Gaza’s fourth winter since Israel launched its war in October 2023. The union said storms in early November flooded about 70,000 tents and affected more than 350,000 displaced people. During a winter storm this November, families piled sand at tent entrances to keep out the rain. Others carried their children out and salvaged what belongings they could.

One displaced mother said she had cut up the burial shroud she had bought for her son and used it to patch her tent. She wanted to keep the family’s bedding and clothes dry. “I couldn’t get a tarpaulin,” she said.

When the first rains hit, Gaza’s civil defence crews reached only a minority of those who called for help. Most of the other callers received advice by phone, Al Jazeera reported.

In Brussels on Wednesday, the European Commission called on Israel to reopen all Gaza crossings to humanitarian aid. Commission spokesperson Eva Hrncirova said tents were waiting on trucks outside Gaza because Israel had not allowed them or the equipment needed to put them up to enter.

The UN said earlier this month that more than 150,000 tents were awaiting entry into Gaza.

Al Jazeera’s open-source unit (Ar.) measured a queue of trucks stretching about 1.1km (0.7 miles) along the Egyptian road to the Rafah crossing in a November 17 satellite image, up from about 460 metres (1,510 feet) on October 6. The images do not establish what the trucks carried. Freight from Egypt is routed through the Karem Abu Salem crossing, known as Kerem Shalom in Israel, for inspection rather than entering Gaza through Rafah.

COGAT, the Israeli military body that coordinates aid, said that nearly 100,000 tents had entered Gaza since the start of a winter aid programme. It said Israel would allow reconstruction equipment into Gaza only after Hamas had fully disarmed.

Inside Gaza, aid workers have cleared drains, installed flood barriers and reinforced shelters. The UN’s humanitarian affairs office reported on November 20 that teams had recorded such work at 162 of the 356 flood-prone locations they had identified. Gaza’s municipalities are asking for pumps, backup generators and fuel before the next storm, as well as 10,000 tonnes of cement for emergency repairs and mobile homes that can withstand wind and rain.

articles.title: Charlie Sheen swung bat, threatened to ‘break’ Emilio Estevez’s head open before cops swarmed teen brawl
articles.excerpt:
Charlie Sheen and Emilio Estevez reflected on their tumultuous relationship growing up. (Getty Images)

Charlie Sheen and Emilio Estevez may have eventually shared the screen in films like "Young Guns...
articles.body_text:
Charlie Sheen and Emilio Estevez reflected on their tumultuous relationship growing up. (Getty Images)

Charlie Sheen and Emilio Estevez may have eventually shared the screen in films like "Young Guns" and "Men at Work," but growing up, their off-camera dynamic was rocky at times.

During a recent appearance on Sheen’s "Mostly Sheenius" podcast, the brothers reminisced about their "toxic" and "dangerous" teenage rivalry.

"We didn't always get along. And we fought a lot as siblings do," Estevez said, admitting that even filming Super 8 movies together in their youth turned into an "insane" battle over creative control.

DENISE RICHARDS SAYS SAMI 'STANDS UP' TO DAD CHARLIE SHEEN AND THAT HE NEEDS IT

Sheen has previously opened up about the complicated dynamic between the two, including feeling excluded during Estevez’s rise in the 1980s "Brat Pack" era.

Long before they were competing for Hollywood roles, however, they were clashing at home — including one explosive high school fight that ended with Sheen swinging a baseball bat and sheriff’s deputies arriving at their front door.

Sheen recalled gearing up for his first high school date at 16 and didn't want to show up in his "piece of s--- Ford Escort," so he turned to his brother, who turned him down.

"I said, ‘OK, but like, you don’t mean "no" no, because this really matters to me, this is important, man. This girl's really pretty, I think she likes me, and if I had your car I think everything would work out,'" Sheen recalled pleading, while Estevez admitted he was "just being a douche" by refusing.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Emilio Estevez and Charlie Sheen once got into an argument so bad the police were called. (Ron Galella, Ltd./Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)

Sheen snapped in what he described as a "blackout" rage and hurled a sandwich toward Estevez. Realizing he was "in trouble," Sheen bolted down the hallway and locked himself in his bedroom.

"I was like, 'All right, he's going to die tonight,'" Estevez said, remembering how he stalked down the hall yelling, "'You clean it up right now!'"

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

When Estevez kicked the bedroom door open, Sheen was frantically swinging a baseball bat to keep some distance between them. Estevez remembered him yelling, "Don't come near me. I'll break your head open."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Sheen said he and his brother learned the art of acting the night the police were called on them.  (Dominik Bindl/Getty Images)

"I was saying, ‘I’ll kill you! I'll kill you!'" Estevez remembered, adding that the windows were open. Sheen said that he egged him on, with Estevez saying, "Then you said, ‘Do me a f---ing favor, kill me, kill me!’"

Around 10 minutes later, the brothers shared, there was a knock at the door, and when they opened it, four sheriff's deputies were there, ready to intervene.

Facing law enforcement, the future Hollywood stars immediately pivoted to damage control.

"We both became brilliant actors in that moment," Estevez said, recalling how he draped an arm around Sheen with a forced laugh and told the deputies, "'Why would I want to kill my brother? We were just kidding ... rehearsal.'"

Christina Dugan Ramirez is an entertainment journalist with more than 15 years of experience, including a decade at PEOPLE writing high-profile cover stories, covering Hollywood's biggest events, and interviewing many of the industry's most influential stars before joining Fox News Digital in 2024.

articles.title: US Education Department probes Virginia schools after sexual abuse scandal
articles.excerpt: The United States Department of Education says it is launching an investigation and withholding funding from a district in the state of Virginia after local officials shut down all of its schools in t...
articles.body_text:
The United States Department of Education says it is launching an investigation and withholding funding from a district in the state of Virginia after local officials shut down all of its schools in the wake of a child sexual abuse scandal involving its employees.

“Parents should never have to question whether their child’s school is aiding and abetting child predators,” US Secretary of Education Linda McMahon said in a statement on Tuesday. “The Trump Administration is taking decisive enforcement action to hold those responsible accountable and ensure Virginia schools are safe places for children to learn.”

Officials in Albemarle County, Virginia, announced they were closing all 29 schools in the district last week, after learning that more than 500 staff had not been subjected to a routine background screening for a history of child sexual abuse. The school system has about 2,800 employees, and only a fraction of its $284m budget comes from the federal government.

Local officials emphasised that none of the 524 employees is suspected of abuse.

Approximately 14,000 students attend the schools, and parents have scrambled to find childcare, while many who depend on free school meals for their children have had to look for other sources of food.

Bob Beard, a member of the Albemarle school board, told Al Jazeera that families were struggling to deal with the shutdown, but schools would reopen on Monday.

The child abuse allegations have shaken the county and caught the attention of the Trump administration.

A former elementary school teacher was arrested for possession of child sexual abuse material earlier this year, while a counsellor at another school was put on leave and later indicted on 20 counts of sexual crimes involving seven different children, according to the Albemarle County Police Department.

Two county school officials and a school principal were later charged with failure to report child abuse, and the county’s superintendent of schools resigned.

Jason Grant, a spokesman for Albemarle County Public Schools, told Al Jazeera that none of the individuals implicated in those cases was among the 524 employees who were hired without the proper screening required to check for a history of child sexual abuse.

“This was not about having the policies in place, this was about processes that were not followed,” Grant said. He said officials were working with the state to “make sure the processes are in place to make sure this doesn’t happen again.”

Grant said all employees in the district undergo several stages of vetting, including a criminal background check and an attestation that they have no history of child abuse or neglect. Then the school system submits their information to the Virginia Department of Social Services to verify that they are not part of the agency’s abuse and neglect database.

For three years, it appears that vetting procedures were not consistently applied. Putting employees hired over that period on leave to carry out background checks meant schools would not be able to run, so officials decided to close them until next week.

“Those were for every range of employee, from teachers to bus drivers to substitutes and across the division, so we couldn’t get coverage for that amount of people,” Grant said.

All but three of the 524 employees have now been properly vetted, and none had background issues, Grant said, adding that the county will reopen schools on Monday.

The Trump administration has long called for the dismantling of the Department of Education. The US president  signed an executive order last year that tried to set that in motion.

The department, which distributes federal funding to states for use in schools, also traditionally investigates whether local officials are complying with civil rights laws banning discrimination against minorities and marginalised groups.

Since returning to office in 2025, the Trump administration has cut more than half of the department’s staff and subjected it to wider changes it says are aimed at rooting out “diversity, equity, and inclusion” (DEI) policies.

articles.title: Maddow says Democrats can abolish Electoral College if they 'swing for the fences'
articles.excerpt:
MS NOW host said getting rid of the Electoral College was "doable" for the Democrats if they swing for the fences during an interview on Saturday.

MS NOW host Rachel Maddow said during an interview o...
articles.body_text:
MS NOW host said getting rid of the Electoral College was "doable" for the Democrats if they swing for the fences during an interview on Saturday.

MS NOW host Rachel Maddow said during an interview on Saturday that getting rid of the Electoral College was "doable" for Democrats if they "swing for the fences."

MS NOW's Jacob Soboroff asked Maddow about her thoughts on Democrats getting rid of the system, which has received criticism after the last two Republican presidents won their first elections despite losing the national popular vote.

"My whole life, it has been this kind of theoretical, you know, this hypothetical math problem. You know, if ever enough states to speak for 270 electoral votes all got into this agreement, then it would go into effect, and it always just seems so pie in the sky," she said.

GOP WIPEOUT GOES FROM BAD TO WORSE AS DEMS QUIETLY SCORE ANOTHER MAJOR WIN WITH BIG RAMIFICATIONS

Maddow said she felt it was doable for the Democrats after speaking with Ben Wikler, a Democratic advocate for eliminating the Electoral College.

Rachel Maddow appears in an interview with host Seth Meyers on Sept. 29, 2026. (Lloyd Bishop/NBC via Getty Images)

Soboroff and Maddow said that Democrats could use the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, an agreement that makes it so a state will award all of their electoral votes to whichever presidential candidate wins the overall national popular vote — regardless of who actually won the vote inside that individual state.

GAVIN NEWSOM EXPRESSES 'OPENNESS' TO PACKING SCOTUS, CALLS ELECTORAL COLLEGE SYSTEM 'PERVERTED'

Eighteen states have signed the compact, in addition to Washington, D.C., which means the compact has 222 electoral votes pledged to it — 48 short of the 270 needed to take effect. However, Democrats now control the governor’s office and both chambers of the state legislatures in the swing states of Michigan, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and Nevada.

Those legislatures' combined 50 electoral votes would push the compact to 272 and activate it should they vote to sign the compact.

PROGRESSIVES UNVEIL $25 MINIMUM WAGE PUSH TO SOLVE AFFORDABILITY CRISIS DESPITE ECONOMIST INFLATION WARNING

MS NOW host Rachel Maddow is seen in conversation with David Remnick during the 2024 New Yorker Festival at Webster Hall on Oct. 27, 2024, in New York City. (Craig Barritt/Getty Images for The New Yorker)

"There are enough Democratic states right now who have a Democratic trifecta — governor and the full legislature — that puts you way over 270 if they all decided to do it, and you don't need very many states to act right now for that to be operative," Maddow said. "It's doable. I mean, raising the minimum wage is doable. Getting rid of the Electoral College is doable, age limits for Supreme Court justices might be doable. I mean, the Democrats have big majorities and if they decide to swing for the fences, they could do a lot right now."

KAMALA HARRIS CALLS TO EXPAND SUPREME COURT, ADD STATES IF DEMS TAKE CONGRESS

Former Vice President and 2024 Democratic nominee Kamala Harris called for major institutional changes in October during an interview, which included "changing" the Electoral College.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

"I believe that we need to expand the Supreme Court. We need more justices on the Supreme Court so that we can have a court that actually reinforces the spirit and principles behind the Constitution of the United States," Harris told podcast host Keke Palmer.

"I believe that we should be pushing for what is possible around changing the Electoral College. Right?" she added.

Harris also lost the popular vote in 2024, making her the first Democratic White House candidate to do so in 20 years.

The system allocates 538 electors to the 50 states and Washington, D.C. A majority of 270 is needed to win the presidency.

Proponents argue, among other benefits, that the Electoral College ensures that all parts of the country play a part in choosing the president, rather than just major population centers.

Hanna Panreck is an associate editor at Fox News.

articles.title: Czech jet engine maker eyes growing role as US supplier in drones, missiles
articles.excerpt: WARSAW, Poland — Czech jet engine producer PBS Aerospace aims to expand its manufacturing capacity in the United States, targeting at least a twofold increase in its production capacity there, accordi...
articles.body_text:
WARSAW, Poland — Czech jet engine producer PBS Aerospace aims to expand its manufacturing capacity in the United States, targeting at least a twofold increase in its production capacity there, according to senior company representatives.

Jan Havránek, PBS Aerospace’s chief government relations and strategy officer, told Defense News that is because the business is booming due to a rising demand for compact propulsion systems used in drones and cruise missiles.

“Everybody wants to build drones and missiles that are fast, fly far, and they want to have them now. That puts scale and quality at the center of the conversation,” Havránek said. “Global conflicts, including the war in Ukraine, have made clear how important it is for the United States to have a reliable domestic supply of these engines, and the market is moving quickly.”

While continuing to produce engines at its factory in Velká Bíteš, in the Czech Republic, PBS Aerospace expanded its American presence in September 2025 with the launch of a plant in Roswell, Georgia. The manufacturing facility was opened as part of a $20 million investment.

“We’re building engines in America, for America,” Havránek said. “Our Georgia facility serves the U.S. market first and foremost, with the U.S. government as our end customer. We supply engines to prime contractors that deliver systems to the Department of War, and we’re proud to help strengthen the U.S. defense industrial base and bring critical manufacturing back onshore.”

In the U.S., the group’s partners include Lockheed Martin and Pratt & Whitney.

To meet rising demand, PBS Aerospace plans to increase its Roswell facility’s annual output to between 10,000 and 20,000 engines over the next three years.

“For next year, we’re looking at up to 5,000 engines to be produced in America,” he said.

With the manufacturing ramp-up in mind, PBS Aerospace is planning to allocate around $100 million to boost its capacity in Roswell, according to Havránek.

Some of the company’s most sought-after products include the TJ40-G1, a compact jet engine that weighs 3.4 kg (7.5 pounds) and delivers up to 425 N of thrust, as indicated by data from the manufacturer.

Jaroslaw Adamowski is the Poland correspondent for Defense News.

articles.title: Overnight RSF drone attacks kill 19 in Sudan
articles.excerpt:
At least 19 people have been killed in drone attacks in Sudan’s Blue Nile state, according to a rights group.

A Sudanese military source told Al Jazeera that the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) targeted t...
articles.body_text:
At least 19 people have been killed in drone attacks in Sudan’s Blue Nile state, according to a rights group.

A Sudanese military source told Al Jazeera that the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) targeted the city of Damazin in a series of attacks late on Tuesday that also injured at least 20 people.

The attacks targeted multiple sites across Damazin, the capital of Blue Nile, and the neighbouring town of Roseires.

Three families were killed in the bombing of a residential area in Damazin, the military source said.

According to Emergency Lawyers, a rights group based in the Sudanese capital, Khartoum, drone attacks also targeted electricity facilities in Damazin and a big dam in Roseires.

Emergency Lawyers said six women were among the dead.

Sudan is currently in the grip of a large-scale civil war between the Khartoum-based Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary group RSF.

The southeastern Blue Nile state is strategically significant because it neighbours some of Sudan’s most unstable regions and is home to some of the SAF’s most experienced fighters, Al Jazeera correspondent Almigdad Alruhaid explained.

Reporting from Omdurman in Sudan, Alruhaid said, “The attacks come amid a sharp escalation in the use of drone attacks between the RSF and the SAF in the last days.”

On November 22, drone attacks in Sudan’s capital area around Khartoum and Omdurman killed at least four people and damaged a United Nations building while staff were inside.

Between January and June this year, at least 1,390 civilians were killed in Sudan – 80 percent of them by drones. In the following four months, another 840 civilians were killed, including about 520 in drone attacks.

“Civilians right now are paying the price. There is no safe zone for civilians, whether in Damazin or in Khartoum,” Alruhaid said.

Civil war broke out in Sudan in 2023 after a power-sharing agreement between two rival camps fell apart following the protest-led ousting of then-President Omar al-Bashir in 2019.

Two rival military leaders emerged in al-Bashir’s wake: Sudan’s de facto ruler Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, who now heads the SAF, and his deputy-turned-rival Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, also known as “Hemedti”, who heads the RSF.

Each accuses the other of attacking first and starting the war that is now in its fourth year.

Reports say the war in Sudan has killed at least 59,000 people, displaced about 13 million and pushed parts of the country into famine.

articles.title: Israeli strike kills Hamas official, his wife and children
articles.excerpt:
An Israeli air attack on Gaza has killed a senior Palestinian security official and his wife and daughters, according to a statement from the enclave’s Ministry of Interior.

In a statement posted on ...
articles.body_text:
An Israeli air attack on Gaza has killed a senior Palestinian security official and his wife and daughters, according to a statement from the enclave’s Ministry of Interior.

In a statement posted on its Telegram channel on Wednesday, the ministry identified the official as Muhammad Majid Abu al-Awf, 47, director of the Internal Security Service in northern Gaza.

Noura Ezzat Abual-Awf, his wife, aged 41, and his children, Yusra Mohammed Abu al-Awf, 15, and Jana Mohammed Abu al-Awf, 13, were also killed in the strike, the statement added.

The ministry described the killings as a “horrific massacre perpetrated by the Israeli occupation forces when they bombed [the family’s] residence in the Shati refugee camp, west of Gaza City, at dawn today”.

The attack is part of “ongoing attempts to undermine the security apparatus in the Gaza Strip in an effort to spread chaos within Palestinian society”, it added.

The strike comes less than 24 hours after the killing of the Internal Security Service’s director general, Brigadier-General Naim Abu Nahal.

Israeli strikes reported overnight killed several people, according to medical sources.

A source at al-Shifa Hospital confirmed to Al Jazeera that four people from the same family were killed and several others were wounded in an Israeli attack on a residential apartment in the Shati refugee camp.

Separately, medical sources at the Nasser Medical Complex reported that a Palestinian girl was shot by Israeli forces in areas outside their control in Khan Younis, in the southern Gaza Strip.

Daily violations of the so-called “ceasefire” in Gaza have been recorded since October 2025, with Israeli air attacks regularly targeting the enclave and at least 1,680 people killed and more than 6,000 injured as Israel’s genocidal war continues.

Hamas called on the guarantor states of the “ceasefire” deal to intervene immediately “to rein in the occupation, impose a halt to its crimes, and obligate it to adhere to the agreement’s path”.

articles.title: Saudi-led coalition intercepts Houthi attacks after Hodeidah strike
articles.excerpt: Saudi Arabia says its air defences have intercepted several drones launched by Yemen’s Houthi rebels, a day after the Saudi-led coalition supporting the Yemeni government carried out an air strike on ...
articles.body_text:
Saudi Arabia says its air defences have intercepted several drones launched by Yemen’s Houthi rebels, a day after the Saudi-led coalition supporting the Yemeni government carried out an air strike on the rebel-held port city of Hodeidah.

The coalition’s spokesman Turki Al-Maliki said that Saudi air defence systems destroyed four drones in Ras Tanura in Saudi Arabia’s east on Wednesday morning, adding that fragments fell due to the interception, with no casualties reported in the initial assessment.

Al-Maliki said earlier that three drones were also shot down in the Eastern province.

The interceptions came after the Saudi-led coalition, which backs Yemen’s internationally recognised government, said it had struck Yemen’s Hodeidah.

The Houthi armed group earlier threatened to retaliate against the kingdom’s Red Sea ports, including Jeddah in the event of an attack.

In a statement issued by Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree, the Iran-aligned rebel group urged employees and workers at the ports, as well as people nearby, to evacuate immediately and called on shipping companies to withdraw their vessels.

The attacks are the latest further escalation in the confrontation between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, with attacks increasingly targeting strategic infrastructure on both sides.

On Tuesday, a Houthi drone struck the tallest tower in Riyadh, injuring at least 11 people, according to Saudi authorities.

Qatar and Pakistan, which have been mediating efforts to end the wider war in the region between Iran and the United States, both “strongly” condemned the attack on the tower, which houses the Saudi sovereign wealth fund.

The building had already been attacked last Thursday and is one of several high-profile targets hit since fighting with the Iran-backed Yemeni group reignited in July.

The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis promised a firm response to the attack.

The Saudi-led coalition targeted operational capabilities at Hodeidah and destroyed several targets in the Yemeni governorates of Saada and Amran, al-Maliki said.

Hodeidah, on Yemen’s Red Sea coast, is the main port through which food and other essential supplies enter Houthi-controlled northern Yemen.

It has long served as a key entry point for humanitarian aid and commercial imports, making it a lifeline for millions of Yemenis in a country heavily dependent on imported food.

Renewed fighting between the two sides has intensified since the Houthis announced a blockade on Saudi ports in July. In September, the Iran-aligned group launched a lightning offensive, seizing territory from Yemeni government forces near the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a strategic shipping chokepoint at the southern entrance to the Red Sea.

Yemeni government forces launched a counteroffensive last month, reclaiming some territory as fighting continues to rage on several fronts.

The Houthis have also stepped up strikes on Saudi airports, ports and oil facilities, while Saudi Arabia has ramped up air strikes on Houthi targets in Yemen in response.

articles.title: Comedian Alfred Robles wears many hats: Cowboy, Catholic and crowd therapist
articles.excerpt: Stand-up comedian Alfred Robles opened up about getting kicked out of the police academy, the career-changing advice Gabriel "Fluffy" Iglesias gave him at a local bar show, and why he’s using comedy t...
articles.body_text:
Stand-up comedian Alfred Robles opened up about getting kicked out of the police academy, the career-changing advice Gabriel "Fluffy" Iglesias gave him at a local bar show, and why he’s using comedy to break cultural stigmas around men's health.

After Alfred Robles’ career took off, he started noticing something funny on the comedy circuit: other comics adopted cowboy hats of their own, hoping for a piece of the magic that turned him into a headliner.

"Everybody thought that I started blowing up because of the hat. After that, I saw a bunch of comedians wearing hats waiting to blow up," Robles told Fox News Digital in a sit-down interview following the release of his new YouTube stand-up special, "El Cowboy."

The irony is that Robles’ signature tejana didn't start as a branding play at all, and according to the older guys in his community, he’s not even wearing it right.

Comedian Alfred Robles discusses his first hour-long stand-up special, "El Cowboy," with Fox News Digital in New York City on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. (Julia Bonavita/Fox News Digital)

"The crazy part is there's a wrong way to wear a hat, and I wear it the wrong way," the East L.A.-raised comic said, explaining that the hat is "supposed" to be worn low so it covers your eyes.

"I get a lot of older Mexicans [who] come up to me [saying], 'I love it, but you wear it wrong.' I go, 'I know, I get it, bro. But the reason why I do it is because I'm being filmed, and I want them to see my eyes and my face and all that.'"

"'You're still wearing it wrong!'" the cowboy hat purists say.

For Robles, the hat isn’t a calculated gimmick. It’s just a piece of his background adjusted to fit the stage, much like the rest of his unconventional path to headlining.

COMEDIAN DES BISHOP ON HOW AMERICA MADE HIM FUNNIER AND HIS 'HEALTHY COLLABORATION' WITH WIFE HANNAH BERNER

Before he was headlining theaters and dropping back-to-back comedy specials, the East L.A. native tried on plenty of other roles: police academy cadet, retail security guard, shaky-handed tour photographer and reluctant caretaker — all before becoming a tequila-pouring comedy therapist for hundreds of strangers a night, with a little help from renowned stand-up comedian Gabriel "Fluffy" Iglesias along the way.

Comedy wasn't part of the neighborhood curriculum growing up in East L.A. (and don't confuse it with neighboring Boyle Heights, a distinction Robles still guards with hometown pride). Nobody around Robles was talking about open mics, aside from his childhood friend Jay Hernandez, who the comedian said treated acting like an inevitable business plan long before landing his starring role in the "Magnum P.I." reboot and other Hollywood credits.

For Robles, stand-up only came into focus after his first career choice fell apart.

He first enrolled in the police academy before being disqualified due to a restraining order filed by an ex-girlfriend in his early 20s.

"It was a long time ago. I was innocent, guys."

"And then, right after I got kicked out from the police academy, I went straight into comedy," he said, recalling that he used to write jokes and poems in high school.

DAVID CROSS DOESN’T 'GIVE A F---’: THE ACTOR-COMEDIAN ON HIS NEW SPECIAL, SOCIAL MEDIA AND ‘TERRIFYING’ AI

"I said to myself, maybe that was my calling — is to become a comedian."

At the time, Robles was living with his mother and working a loss prevention job at Old Navy.

"In the early 2000s I was making $17 an hour. So that was a lot of money," he said. "So I went from $17 an hour, 40 hours a week, to getting paid drink tickets."

Alfred Robles recalled watching a show called "¡Qué Locos!" and seeing young comedians like Gabriel Iglesias, Willie Barcena, Jeff Garcia and Felipe Esparza featured early in his life. (Julia Bonavita/Fox News Digital)

He said his mother was skeptical at first, but that he was glad she was still around to see his success, even if she doesn't understand enough English to really get his jokes.

"The only positive thing she said was, 'You know what? I didn't understand you, but the people were laughing, and I was proud,'" he said.

His big break arrived a few years into his open-mic grind in the early 2000s at a bar show in Montebello, California, when Iglesias pulled him aside with a blunt piece of advice: cut the profanity.

"He goes, 'You cuss a lot. I know you don't need your cussing because you don't say it in your punchlines. You'll just clean that up, and you'll go far,'" Robles recalled.

He was resistant at first, but cleaned up his set anyway. Iglesias saw the difference and invited Robles on the road in 2010, though not as an opener.

"He told me, 'You know what, I'm going to give you a spot, but you're not going to go up on stage, you're going to take pictures for me,'" Robles said.

JEFF ARCURI REVEALS HOW 'BACHELORETTE' WIFE’S CANCER FIGHT TRANSFORMED HIS COMEDY — AND THEIR MARRIAGE

"I'm not even a photographer, bro. I don't even know a camera... The messed-up part is my hands shake, so every picture was messed up."

"Anything to get your foot in," Robles maintained. "That's the way I saw it."

Those blurry photos eventually turned into five-minute sets, then 10-minute spots, and eventually led to Robles performing at arenas like Madison Square Garden and Dodger Stadium alongside Iglesias. Still, Robles knew he couldn't build a legacy as someone else's opener.

Stand-up comic Alfred Robles said the work ethics of his friends Jay Hernandez and Gabriel Iglesias inspired him to be disciplined in his pursuit of comedy, saying "I would be dumb if I didn't try." (Julia Bonavita for Fox News Digital)

"I didn't do comedy to become someone's friend. I said, 'You know, I got to start my own life. I got to start my career.' I don't want to go thinking, 'Oh, I never tried it, to go on my own.'"

He hired a videographer friend of his, with whom he has now been working for nearly four years.

"We grew together. And now I'm here headlining across the country. And it was because I took a risk on myself, and I bet on myself. And I started posting clips up, and the clips blew up."

The momentum snowballed into a massive recent run, capped by releasing two specials within two months of each other. The first was a Kevin Hart-produced half-hour on Hulu in September, and the second was his new hour, "El Cowboy," which dropped in November.

Robles' comedy routine begins with around 45–50 minutes of traditional stand-up before he starts to "mess around" and bring people up on stage.

It all started because he likes crowd work, and he used to enjoy playing matchmaker by bringing single people in his audience on stage. Then, one onlooker raised his hand and, instead of looking for a hook-up, wanted an outlet to share a problem.

"So he came up onstage, and he just told me a sad story. And I go, 'Bro, do you want a shot?'"

COMEDIAN MATT RIFE SAYS HE DITCHED HOLLYWOOD'S OLD PLAYBOOK FOR SUCCESS AFTER HITTING 'ROCK BOTTOM'

"So I give him a shot and just, that took me to another level ... So now, at the end of the show, I just ask them, 'Hey, whoever's going through a problem or just has a story they want to share with me, we'll take a shot together.'"

Robles speculated that speaking openly about his own experiences set the stage for everybody else to open up.

Alfred Robles said he doesn't build his act with social media clips in mind. "If it happens, it happens. There's a lot of times where we go and we don't get any clips. But I feel like if you force it ... people could tell." (Julia Bonavita/Fox News Digital)

"And then the alcohol helps. Now we're all crying, bro," he laughed.

The unfiltered nature of the audience-interaction portion of Robles' show occasionally leads to unexpected places, Robles told Fox News Digital. One woman's story about sleeping with an ex during a two-day breakup with her baby's father and what followed prompted Robles to blur her face in his clips, even though she never asked him to.

But it has also led him to shoot eight episodes of a series "kind of like 'The Jerry Springer Show'" focused on the audience participation piece of his act that he now wants to pitch.

"My stuff is just all real, bro. They're real problems, real people, man. So people love that. People love problems, as long as it's not your problem."

The candor of the crowd is cultivated by Robles' own honest discussion of topics that could be considered taboo in Mexican-American culture, like men's health and aging.

"El Cowboy" features a bit about Robles' first time having enough money to afford a visit to the doctor's office and the unexpected prostate exam that followed.

"The reason why I say it a lot, too — and I love that joke — is because, in my culture, Mexican men don't want to go have your prostate checked," Robles said, adding that nowadays you can get a blood test instead of a digital rectal exam.

"They still don't even want to do that because a lot of them don't want to know. For whatever reason, that's big in our culture. They do not want to know, and I'm over here trying to tell them, 'Hey bro, you got to know, man! You could save your life,'" he said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

"We just feel like, if we know, and we tell someone else, now we put, like, a burden on them. Now they're going to feel sorry for us, and I don't want that to happen. And that's something I want to break."

One friend of his lost a toe to diabetes, to which Robles said, "If you would have went to the doctor, bro, a year before, you would've had a toe."

Comedian Alfred Robles told Fox News Digital that he doesn't necessarily set out to make a statement in his act; he just talks about what he is experiencing in his life, saying his act practically writes itself. (Julia Bonavita/Fox News Digital)

Another friend had a stroke while working at Disneyland, and instead of seeking help for his symptoms, he left the park to have the stroke in his car because he didn't want to bother anyone.

"Well, you could have died, fool," Robles said. "You would have died in the happiest place in the world."

Beneath the on-stage bravado, the cowboy hat and the late-night tequila shots sits one more role that anchors everything else: a grounded Catholic kid from East L.A. who still relies on quiet faith.

Robles admitted he hasn't been to church in a while, but prayer remains a constant rhythm in his day.

"I pray when I wake up, and I pray at night ... I mean I forget here and there, but I always catch myself praying. You know, when I jump on a flight, when I jump on the freeway ... When I'm sitting down just having my own thoughts, that's when I pray," he said.

Asked whether he attributes his success to his faith or hard work, comic Alfred Robles told Fox News Digital that "a little bit of everything helped," calling his faith "key." (Julia Bonavita/Fox News Digital)

"I never lost faith, bro. I just grinded and grinded and prayed and prayed, and here I am."

Even with a new special in the works and an unscripted TV project ready to pitch, Robles doesn't measure his career by what’s still on the horizon. After years of wearing many hats, he’s content with where things stand.

"My dream? I'm already living my dream, man. Whatever happens, happens, bro. I'm cool if it does, and I'm cool if it doesn't," he said.

"Like I said earlier, bro, I didn't do this to be someone's friend. I didn't do this to blow up. I did it because I love comedy. The rest is just extra, bro, and I am cool with that."

Max Bacall is an associate editor for Fox News Digital covering media, culture and comedy.

articles.title: DANNY DANON: From Auschwitz to the UN, Israel must never retreat
articles.excerpt:
Israel's UN ambassador responds to world leaders' accusations over Gaza and the West Bank as Trump defends his administration's efforts to bring peace to the region.

Earlier this month, at a time whe...
articles.body_text:
Israel's UN ambassador responds to world leaders' accusations over Gaza and the West Bank as Trump defends his administration's efforts to bring peace to the region.

Earlier this month, at a time when antisemitism is surging around the world, I walked with dozens of United Nations ambassadors through the haunted gates of Auschwitz.

No matter how many times I return to that hallowed ground, the experience never becomes easier. Each visit reminds me of the devastating cost of antisemitism and the catastrophic consequences of a world that remains silent in the face of hatred.

This diplomatic mission came at a critical moment. The race to elect the next U.N. Secretary-General is advancing quickly. Whoever assumes this position must confront the institutional antisemitism that has taken root within the U.N.

AMBASSADOR JEFF BARTOS: UN MUST ABANDON ANTI-AMERICAN, ANTI-WESTERN LEGACY OF DURBAN CONFERENCE

Israel's U.N. Ambassador Danny Danon with a group of ambassadors on a visit to Auschwitz.  (Israel's Mission to the United Nations.)

This institutional antisemitism is prevalent throughout the U.N. Headquarters. We hear it from U.N. officials, read it in U.N. reports, and even encounter it in the Secretary-General’s own rhetoric. An institution founded in the aftermath of the Holocaust can't claim to fight antisemitism while providing a platform for the demonization of Israel.

As representatives of the Jewish state, we have a responsibility to address this issue. But we cannot do it alone. We must leverage our diplomatic relationships to build coalitions with other nations and ensure that combating antisemitism becomes a collective international priority.

That is why, in September, we established a task force of U.N. member states to combat antisemitism within the organization and around the world. At our inaugural meeting, we focused on translating declarations against Jew-hatred into concrete action. The next Secretary-General must build on these efforts, not allow them to fade into another round of empty promises.

Our mission to Poland was a natural extension of that work. We must ensure that the memory of the Holocaust remains permanently etched in the international community’s consciousness. Never again means nothing if the world forgets what happened before.

THE ANTISEMITISM HORSESHOE IS PLAYING OUT IN REAL TIME — FROM NEW YORK TO PARIS AND BEYOND

A woman reacts as the community of Kibbutz Kfar Aza commemorates their members who were killed, taken hostage and who died in captivity, following the deadly Oct. 7, 2023 attack by Hamas terrorists, in Kibbutz Kfar Aza, southern Israel, Oct. 16, 2025. (Hannah McKay/Reuters)

For many of the ambassadors accompanying me, this was their first encounter with the remnants of the Holocaust. They had studied it, heard about it and read about it. But nothing compares to standing on the very ground where the Nazis committed their atrocities.

Witnessing history is only the beginning. My colleagues must return to their countries determined to confront antisemitism not just at the U.N., but in their own countries as well.

Around the world, 2025 was the deadliest year for antisemitic violence in three decades, with more than twenty people killed in at least four attacks.

In the United States, FBI data shows that antisemitism remains the most prevalent form of religiously motivated hate crime. Although Jews account for less than three percent of the population, they were targeted in 63% of religiously motivated hate crimes in 2025.

And this wave of hatred has not yet broken. Earlier this month, the eve of Kristallnacht, an anti-Israel bike rally targeted Jewish and Israeli-owned restaurants in Philadelphia, accusing them of supporting "genocide." The rhetoric echoed familiar antisemitic patterns of prewar Europe: demonize Jews, assign collective guilt and turn hatred into a campaign of intimidation.

Being in Poland allowed me to confront these realities alongside my colleagues against the backdrop of history. But the most important part of this mission came when I brought the delegation to Israel.

SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER

Israel's ambassador to the United Nations, Danny Danon, took fellow ambassadors on a visit to the Gaza Strip. A tunnel opening is visible in the background. (Israel's Mission to the United Nations)

There, I showed my colleagues the beauty of our country, the strength of our people, and the challenges we continue to face. They visited the sites of the Oct. 7 massacre and received informative briefings on the realities Israel confronts.

The visit underscored why a strong, independent Jewish state is indispensable. Israel is not merely a refuge from antisemitism. It is the eternal homeland of the Jewish people; a country capable of defending its people, preserving its history, and shaping its own future.

At a time when many question whether Israel should continue engaging with the U.N., this mission reinforces exactly why we must.

Despite the relentless hostility Israel faces within the organization, we cannot afford to abandon the battlefield. We must remain, confront the lies, challenge the bias and find creative ways to achieve meaningful diplomatic victories.

Fighting antisemitism requires education, firsthand encounters with history and conversations that challenge entrenched misconceptions about Israel and the Jewish people.

Most importantly, fighting antisemitism requires leadership. The next Secretary-General will inherit an institution facing a profound credibility crisis. Combating antisemitism must be more than another campaign promise. It must become a defining test of leadership for every candidate.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian (L) shakes hands with the United Nations (UN) Secretary General Antonio Guterres during the UN's General Assembly on Sept.r 25, 2025, in New York City. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)

The diplomats who joined this mission learned a powerful lesson that no meeting or lecture could convey: we must confront hatred before it becomes catastrophe. Speeches alone are not sufficient to combat antisemitism. It requires concrete action, institutional accountability, and a willingness to confront those who spread hatred.

We will take that lesson back to the United Nations. We will continue building coalitions, challenging antisemitism and demanding that the institution live up to the principles on which it was founded.

The next Secretary-General will have a choice: confront antisemitism or allow it to continue poisoning the United Nations. We intend to make sure that choice cannot be ignored.

Ambassador Danny Danon is Israel’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations.

articles.title: 400-year-old shipwreck lock finally opened after researchers crack secret code: 'Incredibly satisfying'
articles.excerpt: Researchers in Wales used non-destructive CT scanning to peer inside a 400-year-old brass combination lock from the 1583 shipwreck of the Ann Francis, lining up internal notches to crack its four-lett...
articles.body_text:
Researchers in Wales used non-destructive CT scanning to peer inside a 400-year-old brass combination lock from the 1583 shipwreck of the Ann Francis, lining up internal notches to crack its four-letter code — ANCE — without damaging the artifact.

A 400-year-old brass lock recovered from a 16th-century shipwreck off the coast of Wales has finally been opened — and researchers didn't need a key to crack it.

The discovery, conducted as a joint effort between Amgueddfa Cymru (Museum Wales) and Cardiff University, was announced earlier this month.

Museum officials said in a statement that the brass lock had "remained firmly locked" since its vessel was destroyed off the coast of Wales in the 16th century.

DIVERS UNCOVER HUNDREDS OF ANCIENT RELICS NEAR SHIPWRECK UNTOUCHED FOR 2,100 YEARS

The Ann Francis was overtaken by a storm on Dec. 28, 1583, while returning from Spain.

It was blown off course before wrecking on Margam Beach, near Port Talbot.

A centuries-old brass padlock from the wreck of the Ann Francis remained sealed for more than 400 years before experts identified its four-letter combination without damaging the artifact. (Amgueddfa Cymru/Museum Wales)

More than 400 years later, metal detectorist Peter Hughes began unearthing parts of the ship's hoard on Margam Beach in 1996.

He continued recovering artifacts from the site through 2017 — including the brass lock — after dredging and storms stripped away layers of sand.

Speaking to officials, Hughes said he was "immediately astonished" when he uncovered the lock.

TREASURE HUNTER STRIKES GOLD WITH 1,000-YEAR-OLD DISCOVERY LINKED TO 'HAND OF GOD'

"When I moved the ring dials of the combination, they turned with ease after over 400 years beneath the sands, and I was left in disbelief," he said, as Cardiff University reported.

"I also remember being left excited at the prospect of finding wonderful things [in] the treasure chest it once locked."

The Ann Francis was overtaken by a storm on Dec. 28, 1583, while returning from Spain and blown off course before wrecking on Margam Beach, near Port Talbot in Wales. Port Talbot is pictured above. (iStock)

Researchers revealed the four-letter combination that kept it sealed for more than four centuries: ANCE.

To crack the code without damaging the artifact, museum experts partnered with specialists at Cardiff University to examine the lock's internal mechanism using CT scanning technology.

'SPECTACULAR' SHIPWRECK FOUND WITH UNDERWATER TIME CAPSULE OF UNTOUCHED CARGO: 'AMAZING FIND'

David Williams, a research associate at Cardiff University's School of Engineering, said micro-CT scanning allowed him to inspect the interior of the lock without harming it.

"By creating a detailed 3D image of the internal mechanism, I could see how the notches lined up with the letters and identify the exact combination," said Williams, according to Cardiff University.

Found near Spanish silver coins and two coin weights, the 16th-century padlock from the Ann Francis wreck is now on display at the National Waterfront Museum in Swansea, Wales. (Amgueddfa Cymru/Museum Wales)

"We normally use this technology to study bones and other biological structures, so investigating a 400-year-old padlock was certainly a first for us," he said.

After waiting until later that evening for museum officials to test the code, Williams got the news that it worked.

"Getting the message that we'd cracked it was incredibly satisfying," he said.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Alastair Willis, a senior curator at Amgueddfa Cymru, said the meaning behind the lock's code remains unknown.

"Elizabethan combination locks are known in Britain, but this one is in exceptionally good condition and is associated with a dated wreck, making it a unique find and the code a tantalizing mystery to solve," said Willis, the release noted.

"Now [that] we've solved it, we are left wondering if the code meant something to its owner."

He added, "Of course, now [that] we've solved it, we are left wondering if the code meant something to its owner."

Officials said the lock is believed to have once secured a small chest holding valuables.

Because it was found near Spanish silver coins and two coin weights, researchers think it may have protected those items or a chest containing organic materials that did not survive, such as documents or textiles.

The hoard also included rare gold coins dating to the reign of Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain, as well as a boatswain's whistle.

Rare gold coins dating to the reign of Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain were also recovered from the Ann Francis treasure hoard. (Amgueddfa Cymru/Museum Wales)

The combination lock and other artifacts from the Ann Francis hoard are now on display at the National Waterfront Museum in Swansea.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Recent archaeological and historical finds across Wales have drawn similar attention.

Earlier this year, archaeologists revealed new findings from a remote Roman fort in Wales — including fourth-century coins and artifacts — that may link the site to a centuries-old legend about Emperor Magnus Maximus.

Last winter, volunteers cleaning a South Wales beach uncovered roughly 200 mysterious old-fashioned shoes that may have washed ashore from a 19th-century shipwreck.

Andrea Margolis is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital and Fox Business. Readers can follow her on X at @andreamargs or send story tips to andrea.margolis@fox.com.

articles.title: Virginia school district defends Thanksgiving 'Day of Mourning' resources for kids as young as third grade
articles.excerpt:
The exterior of Loudoun County Public Schools in Virginia. (Google Earth)

A Virginia school district at the center of past education controversies is defending Thanksgiving "resources" for children a...
articles.body_text:
The exterior of Loudoun County Public Schools in Virginia. (Google Earth)

A Virginia school district at the center of past education controversies is defending Thanksgiving "resources" for children as young as third grade that describes the holiday as a "Day of Mourning" for some Native Americans, according to documents obtained by the watchdog group Protect the Public's Trust.

"The Loudoun County Public Schools (LCPS) Resources for Recognition Days & Months guide does not label Thanksgiving a ‘Day of Mourning,’" LCPS Communications told Fox News Digital in a statement Wednesday. "Rather, it includes multiple suggested resources that explore Thanksgiving traditions and historical perspectives, including Native American perspectives."

Loudoun County Public Schools, located outside Washington, D.C., includes the "resources" in a district resource guide for teachers, according to a Washington Free Beacon report. The materials also reportedly featured a Columbus Day lesson described as a "Debated Celebration," while Christmas does not appear in the guide's listed holiday resources.

LOUDOUN SCHOOL BOARD URGES STUDENTS TO ‘CELEBRATE’ LGBTQ+ HISTORY IN NEW PROCLAMATION

A modern recreation of the first Thanksgiving in the autumn of 1621 at Plimoth Patuxet Museums (formerly Plimoth Plantation) in Plymouth, Mass. Only half the Mayflower passengers, about 50, survived the first winter in Plymouth; while at least 90 Wampanoags attended the feast, according to Pilgrim Edward Winslow, who offered the only contemporary account of the first Thanksgiving. (Courtesy of Kathy Tarantola/Plimoth Patuxet Museums)

A slide for grades 3–5 labeled "The Real Story of Thanksgiving," shared by The Washington Free Beacon, reads, "Some Native American groups protest Thanksgiving as a Day of Mourning. They claim that the arrival of European explorers and settlers is not a cause for celebration, because it began the ill-treatment and deaths of millions of Native Americans. For them, Thanksgiving marks the beginning of a long period of violence and discrimination."

LCPS Communications went on to say that the guide contains optional teaching materials rather than mandatory curriculum, noting that educators are not required to use any specific lessons or activities. The district said the resources include materials from the Virginia Department of Education as well as supplementary content, and that teachers are encouraged to determine which materials are appropriate for their individual classrooms.

VIRGINIA SCHOOL DISTRICT FACES PROBE OVER 9/11 TEACHING GUIDE TELLING TEACHERS NOT TO ‘CENTER THE EXTREMISTS’

"Loudoun County seems determined to filter American history and traditions through a DEI lens," Alexa Moutevelis, Protect the Public's Trust communications director, told Fox News Digital. "There’s nothing wrong with teaching the complicated parts of American history, but these materials seem to emphasize grievance, oppression, and critical interpretations." (iStock)

"Thanksgiving is included in the LCPS curriculum and is taught in accordance with Virginia’s History and Social Science Standards of Learning," LCPS Communications continued. "In second grade, students learn about Thanksgiving traditions and the origins of the holiday. Instruction also includes opportunities to learn about Native American history and perspectives, including the Wampanoag tribe."

LCPS added that it is "intentional about ensuring students have opportunities to learn history through multiple perspectives and develop a more complete understanding of historical events. Instruction is designed to be age-appropriate and aligned with students’ developmental levels."

HOW VIRGINIA SCHOOL DISTRICT SHAMES KIDS TO MARK THANKSGIVING

The Washington Free Beacon also reported that a district-approved Thanksgiving lesson for middle and high school students, titled "Thanksgiving: A Day of Mixed Blessings," features a HuffPost-produced video examining why some Native Americans observe a National Day of Mourning on Thanksgiving. The video opens with a man invoking Malcolm X's famous remarks about Plymouth Rock to describe the arrival of European settlers from a Native American perspective.

Loudoun County Public Schools said its resource guide includes materials addressing both Columbus Day and Indigenous Peoples’ Day, consistent with Virginia’s educational standards. The district added that the guide does not include dedicated resources for religious holidays such as Christmas, Hanukkah, Eid and Diwali, but said those holidays are covered in the elementary curriculum under state standards.

CPS said their "resources" have materials addressing both Columbus Day and Indigenous Peoples’ Day, "consistent with Virginia’s educational standards." (Fine Art Images/Heritage Images/Getty Images)

"LCPS remains committed to providing a high-quality education that meets the needs of all students and prepares them for future success," LCPS Communications added.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Alexa Moutevelis, Protect the Public's Trust communications director, said, "From introducing elementary school students to LGBTQ pride to teaching children that Thanksgiving is a ‘Day of Mourning,’ Loudoun County seems determined to filter American history and traditions through a DEI lens. There’s nothing wrong with teaching the complicated parts of American history, but these materials seem to emphasize grievance, oppression, and critical interpretations."

Moutevelis added, "It’s a good reminder for parents to pay attention to messages their children are receiving in the classroom and how public schools are choosing to frame important holidays and historical events."

Rachel del Guidice is a culture reporter for Fox News covering the intersection of politics, faith, family, and American culture.

articles.title: Slain student’s family faces first Thanksgiving without her, blames missed chances to stop illegal alien
articles.excerpt: Sheridan Gorman's parents speak with Fox News Digital about their daughter's beloved holiday traditions, the empty seat at their Thanksgiving table and the memories they cherish as they face their fir...
articles.body_text:
Sheridan Gorman's parents speak with Fox News Digital about their daughter's beloved holiday traditions, the empty seat at their Thanksgiving table and the memories they cherish as they face their first holiday without her.

EXCLUSIVE: The parents of an 18-year-old college student allegedly killed by an illegal immigrant in Chicago are preparing for their first Thanksgiving without their daughter, as they grapple with an empty seat at the table and what they believe to be missed opportunities to prevent her death.

In an emotional Zoom interview with Fox News Digital, Sheridan Gorman's parents, Thomas and Jessica Gorman, remembered their daughter's love for the holidays while saying they're frustrated over what they believe were several missed opportunities by Chicago authorities to arrest the illegal immigrant accused of killing her.

Jose Medina-Medina, 25, was arrested after he allegedly killed Gorman, an 18-year-old Loyola University Chicago student, on March 19. According to the Department of Homeland Security, he illegally entered the U.S. from Venezuela in 2023, when he was apprehended but released into the country by the Biden administration. He has pleaded not guilty to murder, attempted murder, aggravated assault, aggravated discharge of a firearm, and illegal possession of a weapon.

ANGEL FAMILIES PLEAD WITH LEADERS TO 'CHOOSE' AMERICAN CHILDREN OVER PROTECTING ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS

Sheridan Gorman, 18, whose parents are preparing for their first Thanksgiving without her, was accepted into a Vanderbilt University internship program just two days before her death. (Thomas Gorman)

"Our dogs actually still sit in her bedroom window every day waiting for her to come home. It's been over seven months and that's where they are all day, just waiting." - Jessica Gorman

The Gormans said Sheridan's favorite Thanksgiving tradition was making apple pie. This year, her parents will continue that tradition without her, and said they plan to leave an empty seat at the dinner table.

"We're going to share an apple pie together and try to start, I guess, some new memories," Sheridan's father said. "As hard as it is without her, it's definitely going to be an empty seat at the table."

Sheridan's mother said the family usually gathers around the Thanksgiving table to share what they're thankful for, but this year will be different.

"I guess this year for us, it's going to be gratitude and grief at the same time," she said. "I think we're thankful that we had 18 years with her. The grief part is I wish we had so many more."

SHERIDAN GORMAN'S PARENTS SAY PROTECTING CHILDREN FROM FAILED IMMIGRATION POLICIES ISN'T A ONE-PARTY FIGHT

Close up of Sheridan Gorman, an 18-year-old Loyola University Chicago student who was fatally shot near campus. (Sheridan G. Gorman via Instagram)

More than seven months after Gorman's death, her dogs still sit by her bedroom window, waiting for her to come home.

"Our dogs actually still sit in her bedroom window every day waiting for her to come home. It's been over seven months and that's where they are all day, just waiting," Jessica Gorman said.

BIDEN BORDER OFFICIALS RELEASED ALLEGED KILLER OF CHICAGO STUDENT 'DUE TO LACK OF SPACE,' DOCUMENTS SHOW

Prosecutors said during an earlier detention hearing for Medina-Medina on April 3 that Gorman was with her friends at a Rogers Park pier when she looked around a lighthouse and saw Medina-Medina was there. Gorman then walked back toward her friends and mouthed, "There's a man behind the lighthouse," at which point Medina-Medina began chasing them.

Court documents earlier obtained by Fox News Digital show that Medina-Medina told officials he was living at Leone Beach Park fieldhouse in Rogers Park in 2023, which was being used as a city-sponsored shelter for migrants.

WATCH: ANGEL MOM TURNS TABLES ON SANCTUARY POLITICIANS WITH BASIC QUESTION ABOUT THEIR PRIORITIES

Sheridan Gorman, a New York native, was reportedly only a few months away from completing her freshman year at Loyola University Chicago in Illinois. (Sheridan G. Gorman via Instagram)

"We made one mistake. We made a mistake sending our daughter to a school in Chicago. Sending our daughter to a sanctuary city. We had no idea." - Jessica Gorman

Medina-Medina was arrested in 2023 and charged with shoplifting after he allegedly stole just over $130 in merchandise from a Macy's in downtown Chicago. He failed to appear for court hearings related to that case, and an arrest warrant remained active until the alleged murder.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Medina-Medina's attorney also said he suffers from epilepsy and still has bullet fragments lodged in his brain. The murder suspect turned himself in at the Texas border in 2023, where he was held in detention before being released. His attorney said that Medina-Medina had requested to be sent back to Colombia, where his mother had moved, but he was transported by bus to Chicago.

FATHER OF SLAIN STUDENT SHERIDAN GORMAN CALLS DEATH A 'FAILURE' AFTER ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT'S NOT GUILTY PLEA

Despite failing to appear for court hearings and living in city-funded housing, Medina-Medina wasn't arrested until after he was accused of fatally shooting Gorman. Thomas Gorman said "multiple" opportunities were missed to stop the murder suspect.

Jose Medina-Medina, a Venezuelan national, was also arrested for shoplifting and released before the alleged murder, DHS confirmed. (DHS)

"We made one mistake. We made a mistake sending our daughter to a school in Chicago. Sending our daughter to a sanctuary city. We had no idea," Jessica Gorman said.

WATCH: Slain college student's parents blast missed chances to stop illegal immigrant accused of murder

The Gormans said neither Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson nor Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker called them after Sheridan died. They have one pointed question for both officials:

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"What if Sheridan were your daughter? Again, would these policies, would these decisions, would these ridiculous explanations you give be enough for you?" they asked.

Fox News Digital reached out to Johnson and Pritzker for comment.

Sheridan Gorman smiles alongside the Chicago skyline in Illinois. (Sheridan G. Gorman via Instagram)

Just two days before she died, Gorman found out she was accepted into an internship program at Vanderbilt University in Nashville, Tennessee. Her mother said the college student was "really thrilled to spend that time in cowboy boots with her sister," which she never got to do.

As Gorman's family prepares for their first Thanksgiving without her, her mother said she'll miss the simple moments with her daughter the most.

Adam Sabes is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to Adam.Sabes@fox.com and on Twitter @asabes10.

articles.title: Ex England star Sterling given suspended sentence for dangerous driving
articles.excerpt: Former England winger Raheem Sterling has been ⁠spared ⁠an immediate jail sentence after he admitted dangerous driving by inhaling “laughing ⁠gas” while behind the wheel before crashing his Lamborghin...
articles.body_text:
Former England winger Raheem Sterling has been ⁠spared ⁠an immediate jail sentence after he admitted dangerous driving by inhaling “laughing ⁠gas” while behind the wheel before crashing his Lamborghini.

Sterling, 31, was reported ⁠driving erratically on the M25 and M3 motorways in southern England during the morning rush hour on May 28, with witnesses saying ‌he was inhaling from a balloon and weaving between lanes.

Police later found Sterling sitting in the passenger seat of his crashed car holding two canisters of nitrous oxide. No other vehicles were ⁠involved and no injuries were ⁠reported.

Sterling, who most recently played for Dutch side Feyenoord, pleaded guilty in September to dangerous driving, possession ⁠of nitrous oxide and failing to provide a blood specimen.

He ⁠appeared for sentencing on Wednesday at ⁠Basingstoke Magistrates’ Court where Judge Kirsty Allman said Sterling had acted with “conscious disregard for the safety of other ‌road users”.

She sentenced Sterling to 12 months’ imprisonment, suspended for 18 months, and ‌ordered ‌him to carry out 100 hours of unpaid work.

articles.title: DR MARC SIEGEL: Why angels remind us to give thanks and never lose hope on Thanksgiving
articles.excerpt: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel discusses his new book, ‘The Angels Among Us,’ featuring gunshot survivor Chris Smith’s powerful story of recovery and the role of faith and hope in ove...
articles.body_text:
Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel discusses his new book, ‘The Angels Among Us,’ featuring gunshot survivor Chris Smith’s powerful story of recovery and the role of faith and hope in overcoming tragedy and more, on 'Outnumbered.'

In the Hebrew Bible, the prophet Isaiah describes God sitting on an exalted throne, with seraphim angels attending to him and proclaiming his glory. This is an act of Thanksgiving (Isaiah 6:1–3). In the New Testament, specifically in the Book of Revelation, there are several scenes of heavenly worship and Thanksgiving, with living creatures falling down before God’s throne and giving thanks, worshiping his glory, honor and power over all things. They offer a collective Thanksgiving (Revelation 4:8–11; Revelation 7:11–12).

In my new book, "The Angels Among Us," there are many stories of survivors who have received messengers from God and survived near-death experiences, giving back to the Lord by doing good deeds for others. This is in the spirit of Thanksgiving. Spiritual leader Basye Holland-Shuey survives three cancers thanks to the intervention of angels, and becomes a spiritual leader and teacher. Suicidal alcoholic Bill Wilson sees God’s angels in a bright light on a mountaintop and gives thanks for this lifesaving vision by forming Alcoholics Anonymous, sharing his suffering and gratitude to God to help cure alcoholics everywhere.

DR. MARC SIEGEL: 'THE ANGELS AMONG US'--A DYING WOMAN, THE SHOFAR AND THE MIRACLE THAT FOLLOWED

On Thanksgiving Eve in 2021, as described in "The Angels Among Us," Chris Smith goes on a first date with Leslie Reeves. They return to his place and warm a pizza in the oven, but Reeves’s former boyfriend, who has been stalking her, breaks in through the back door and shoots them both in the head. She is killed, but he manages to survive thanks to a visitation from heaven by his father, who died when Chris was 8 years old.

Chris remains on the floor bleeding as his dog scratches his chest and tries to revive him. He experiences being in a dark room, sitting at a long wooden table. He can see light over to his left side. It is an otherworldly, heavenly light. There are three beings there with him: Roy, Dave and John. John says, "Chris, we are three angels here to care for you. We are here to save you."

Chris says that after that, he is in a doorway where everything is lush and green. His father appears and says he is here to get Chris to a hospital. The next thing Chris knows, he is floating down the road in a vehicle, riding in the air above the pavement.

In the waking world, when Chris doesn’t show up for Thanksgiving dinner, a young girl named Brijon is sent over to his house, where she finds blood everywhere and calls 911.

But in the world inside Chris’s coma, his father proves his existence by telling Chris that his best friend Brad put two marijuana joints in his coat pocket while he was in the casket. Only Brad and Chris’s mother know about this, and when Chris wakes up from his coma two months later, his mother, Sharon, breaks into tears, verifying the story, as does Brad. Sharon relays this to me in an interview. Chris’s doctors are amazed that with a bullet in the right frontal lobe of his brain, his thoughts and speech are still clear. And then, with the help of much rehab and mesenchymal stem cell treatments, he goes on to regain the strength and function on the left side of his body.

In a great message for Thanksgiving, he dedicates his life to "helping young people understand the dangers of internet dating and domestic violence, and restoring faith in God to as many as I can around the world."

CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM DR MARC SIEGEL

Marc Siegel, M.D. is a professor of medicine and medical director of Doctor Radio at NYU Langone Medical Center. He is Fox News Channel's senior medical analyst. His latest book is "The Angels Among Us: How God's Messengers Play a Role in Healing." (Fox Books, November 17, 2026). His previous book "The Miracles Among Us: How God's Grace Plays a Role in Healing" (Fox Books, November 18, 2025) debuted at #1 on both the New York Times and Publisher’s Weekly bestseller lists. He is also the author of "COVID: The Politics of Fear and the Power of Science." Follow him on X @drmarcsiegel.

articles.title: Colombian police storm supermarket to free 20 held hostage for 17 hours
articles.excerpt:
Relatives of those being held hostage spent anxious hours as the situation unfolded

Colombian security forces have freed around 20 shoppers and employees who had been held hostage for about 17 hours ...
articles.body_text:
Relatives of those being held hostage spent anxious hours as the situation unfolded

Colombian security forces have freed around 20 shoppers and employees who had been held hostage for about 17 hours at a supermarket in the city of Cartagena.

Gunmen had stormed into the building at 08:00 (13:00 GMT) on Tuesday after what Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella said was a failed attempt at robbing an armoured car carrying money.

They held those inside at gunpoint while trying to negotiate their getaway.

With the situation becoming ever more intense as the day progressed, De la Espriella gave the green light for special forces and police to launch a daring operation to free the hostages, in which one gunman was killed.

Around 20 people were still being held hostage when the security forces moved in

Residents living near the supermarket reported hearing explosions as the security forces moved into the building.

Police later confirmed that officers had used stun grenades to overpower the hostage takers.

One was killed in the operation and four have been arrested.

De la Espriella described it as "an extraordinary joint operation", which he said had been carried out "flawlessly".

He flew into the northern city to oversee the operation.

In footage released since then, he can be seen, with a handgun strapped to his belt, flanked by the commanders of the operation.

Speaking after the successful rescue of the hostages, he said that the gunmen had been given the chance to hand themselves in, which they had refused.

Earlier in the day, the assailants had freed 10 of their hostages, among them elderly women.

But they continued to hold around 20, even as a police helicopter hovered above and special forces teams prepared to enter the building, which is located in a popular shopping mall.

Local media said that as well as asking for safe passage out of the supermarket, the gunmen also demanded nearly $2m (£1.5m) and armoured vehicles.

According to President De la Espriella, they had no political affiliations but had taken the hostages once their plan to rob an armoured car carrying money had been foiled.

"It's not that a terrorist group carried out a kidnapping - no, these are criminals who were caught off guard, had no way out, and then kidnapped a group of people," he said.

Photos taken during the rescue operation show armed soldiers inside the building as people are kneeling with their hands behind their heads.

It is not clear from the photos whether those kneeling are hostages or the hostage-takers.

Local media are reporting that the authorities feared that some of the gunmen may have tried to pass themselves off as hostages as the rescue mission unfolded.

The identities of the four arrested have not yet been released.

The hostages are being reunited with their families after being checked over by medical teams, according to the mayor of Cartagena.

Many anxious relatives had spent hours waiting for news outside the perimeter place around the supermarket by security forces.

A woman called Sandra told news site Caracol that her 76-year-old mother was one of those being held hostage.

Sandra's mother - among a group of elderly people released after six hours - was reunited with her daughters and grandchildren.

Footage recorded by local media showed bystanders cheering as some of those freed were escorted to ambulances waiting nearby.

But with around 20 people still inside the building, tension outside rose and police said they had to stop some of the relatives from breaching the perimeter.

Relatives and bystanders congregated outside the entrance to the supermarket

At one point, flights into the city were halted, with planes diverted to Barranquilla.

Special forces, including units specialised in dealing with kidnappings, were deployed to Cartagena, a popular destination with foreign and Colombian tourists.

Cartagena's mayor, Dumek Turbay called for calm but the granddaughter of one of the hostages told Colombian newspaper El Tiempo that "this shows we're not safe anywhere".

President De la Espriella was elected earlier this year on a promise to crack down on Colombia's criminal groups.

On Tuesday, he had travelled to the central city of Villavicencio to inspect the damage caused by a car bomb which detonated outside the regional government's offices.

While De la Espriella blamed the leader of a dissident rebel group for that attack, he was adamant that the hostage takers were "simple bandits" without political affiliations.

articles.title: Sinner uncertain for Australian Open after undergoing knee surgery
articles.excerpt:
Jannik Sinner risks missing the Australian Open in January after confirming that he has undergone surgery on his troublesome right knee.

The five-time Grand Slam champion has not played a match since...
articles.body_text:
Jannik Sinner risks missing the Australian Open in January after confirming that he has undergone surgery on his troublesome right knee.

The five-time Grand Slam champion has not played a match since winning Wimbledon for the second time in July, with less than two months until the start of the first major tournament of the season in Melbourne.

“Over the past few months, together with my team we’ve tried everything to treat my injury without surgery,” Sinner said in a statement on Tuesday.

“After some very encouraging progress early on, my knee unfortunately didn’t respond as we had all hoped, that’s why today I underwent a minor surgery to improve the condition of my iliotibial band.”

The procedure, which had been reported earlier in the day by broadcasters RAI and Sky Sport, and sports daily La Gazzetta dello Sport, was performed by knee injury specialist Lasse Lempainen at a clinic in Finland.

Another knee specialist, Fabrizio Terrone at the Isokinetic centre in Turin, told Sky Sport that Sinner’s absence could last “at least three to four months”.

That means the earliest Sinner might be back on court with a racket in hand would be during the American hard-court swing, at Indian Wells and Miami Masters.

The 25-year-old admitted recently that the worst injury of his career left him barely able to move.

“The worst part for me about this injury is that I cannot compete, I cannot play tennis,” said Sinner in a recent video.

“Also, my life outside of tennis is a bit more limited because of a simple fact that I cannot do things that I really like, because I want to protect my knee.”

Sinner, a two-time champion at the Australian Open which begins on January 17, recently said that he will make his comeback at the “Six Kings Slam” tournament in Saudi Arabia, which has been rescheduled for late December due to the conflict with Yemen’s Houthis.

But that now looks impossible and a difficult start to 2027 seems in store for the man who has in recent years risen to be, alongside Spanish star Carlos Alcaraz, the pre-eminent force in men’s tennis.

Sinner was having a brilliant campaign before being stopped by his knee problem, with five Masters 1000 titles going alongside his triumph at Wimbledon.

The Italian’s 94 percent winning record in 2026 is the best of his career, even beating his figures from the previous two seasons in each of which he won two Grand Slams and the ATP Finals.

He suffered a major disappointment at the French Open when, leading Argentina’s Juan Manuel Cerundolo by two sets and 5-1 ahead in the third, he succumbed to heatstroke and was eliminated in the second round.

Sinner recently lost top spot in the men’s world rankings to losing Wimbledon finalist Alexander Zverev, who has taken advantage of injury problems for both Sinner and Alcaraz to win Roland Garros and the US Open.
