articles.title: Mexico to try ‘El Chapo Isidro’ despite US extradition request
articles.excerpt: Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, an alleged cartel leader known as “El Chapo Isidro”, will be tried in Mexico despite an extradition request by the US, in a move that could worsen already-strained relations...
articles.body_text:
Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, an alleged cartel leader known as “El Chapo Isidro”, will be tried in Mexico despite an extradition request by the US, in a move that could worsen already-strained relations between the two countries.

Attorney General Ernestina Godoy told reporters on Monday that Mexican authorities “are going to put him on trial in this country”.

Meza Flores, one of the FBI’s 10 most wanted fugitives, was captured after an hours-long firefight between Mexican forces and cartel gunmen on Friday at a compound in Guasave, in the northwestern state of Sinaloa. He was flown to Mexico City the following day.

He faces local charges for weapons offences and methamphetamine possession with intent to sell.

Earlier on Monday, Security Minister Omar Garcia Harfuch said Washington had requested Meza Flores’s extradition after his capture in the northern state of Sinaloa.

President Claudia Sheinbaum said US authorities provided intelligence support but did not participate directly on the ground.

US surveillance drones were authorised to help track Meza Flores before ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠the raid, authorities added, despite sensitivities over US anti-drug operations in the country in recent months.

Four Mexican soldiers and 16 alleged cartel gunmen were killed in the overnight operation, according to the Mexican Secretariat of National Defence.

Meza Flores is accused by US authorities of leading a major trafficking network that moved heroin, cocaine, methamphetamine, marijuana and fentanyl across the border.

The US Department of Justice said he faces six charges in the US that include running a continuing criminal enterprise, narcoterrorism, money laundering conspiracy and weapons offences.

His arrest is the latest in a series of high-profile anti-cartel operations by Mexico, including the February killing of Nemesio “El Mencho” Oseguera, as US President Donald ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌Trump presses ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌the Sheinbaum government to crack down on organised crime.

articles.title: Coast Guard boards 2 foreign ships bound for US amid reports of Iranian hacking probe
articles.excerpt: U.S. Central Command said U.S. Marines in the Gulf of Oman "boarded M/T Celestial Sea, an Iranian-flagged commercial oil tanker suspected of attempting to violate the U.S. blockade by transiting towar...
articles.body_text:
U.S. Central Command said U.S. Marines in the Gulf of Oman "boarded M/T Celestial Sea, an Iranian-flagged commercial oil tanker suspected of attempting to violate the U.S. blockade by transiting toward an Iranian port." (Credit: CENTCOM)

The U.S. Coast Guard deployed specialized cyber teams to board two foreign-flagged commercial ships bound for U.S. ports in August after indications that their networks had been compromised by "foreign cyber actors," a Coast Guard spokesperson told Fox News Digital on Monday.

The offshore operations took place Aug. 21 and 24 in the Gulf of America, with teams mitigating the threats before the vessels reached U.S. ports.

The confirmation came as The Wall Street Journal also reported Monday that U.S. authorities are investigating whether Iran was involved in dozens of cyberattacks targeting energy tankers.

FEARS OF CHINA SPYING ON US MILITARY PROMPT GOP HAWKS TO DEMAND RETALIATION AGAINST THE SHIPPING GIANT

The U.S. Coast Guard and Homeland Security Investigations conducted a joint boarding operation aboard the tanker in the Port of Los Angeles. (Department of Homeland Security)

"The U.S. Coast Guard (USCG), in close coordination with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and federal cybersecurity experts, recently conducted joint offshore security boardings of two inbound foreign-flagged commercial vessels in the Gulf of America," a Coast Guard spokesperson said.

"The measures were designed to ensure the integrity of the vessel’s operational and information technology systems following indications that the networks of both vessels were compromised by foreign cyber actors."

The Coast Guard said a specialized team of law enforcement personnel, Coast Guard Cyber Protection Team members, a vessel inspector and FBI Cyber Action Team operators boarded the first vessel Aug. 21 to investigate the suspected cybersecurity breach.

"The captain, crew, and shore-side corporate staff were critical partners in helping to ensure the threats were mitigated," the spokesperson added.

A similar multiagency boarding and safety verification operation was conducted Aug. 24 aboard the second vessel, also in the Gulf of America, the Coast Guard said.

FRENCH SUPERMARKETS FACE MILLIONS IN LOSSES AFTER CYBERATTACK HITS REFRIGERATORS NATIONWIDE

The Coast Guard (pictured here in Miami) has complete authority to make sure ships comply with US law and international law. (iStock)

No operational disruptions, vessel instability, threats to crew safety or environmental impacts have been reported.

The Coast Guard said it is coordinating with port operators, vessel owners and local maritime stakeholders to ensure port operations continue safely and without interruption.

According to The Wall Street Journal, attackers exploited vulnerabilities in Fortinet networking equipment, prompting Coast Guard boardings after crews received bomb threats warning that "traitor ships will burn in hell."

STRAIT OF HORMUZ CRISIS TRAPS 6,000 SAILORS AS ATTACKS ON SHIPS MOUNT, UN MARITIME CHIEF SAYS

A Coast Guard MH-65 Dolphin helicopter crew. (U.S. Coast Guard photo by Chief Petty Officer David Mosley)

As many as 50 vessels carrying oil, liquefied petroleum, chemicals and other potentially explosive cargo are believed to have been targeted, the outlet reported, citing U.S. officials.

A European shipping executive also said officers received threats on their cellphones.

A ransom letter addressed to the captain of the Liberian-flagged supertanker Prosperity, which was carrying about 2.3 million barrels of oil, described the operation as a "planned execution."

Hackers reportedly breached one vessel's propulsion and navigation systems, disrupting communications for about 30 hours and forcing the crew to switch to manual procedures, potentially delaying energy shipments to Asia and Europe.

AMERICA MUST DEFEND OUR DIGITAL INFRASTRUCTURE, HERE AND OVERSEAS, TO WIN THE NEXT WAR

The U.S. Coast Guard will be ending admissions for college students wanting to commission as officers that take race into consideration as part of the Trump administration’s continued anti-diversity, equity and inclusion initiative, Fox News Digital has learned. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

"The Marine Transportation System is vital to America's economic prosperity and national security, and safeguarding it against potential cyber risks is a standard part of the United States Coast Guard's safety and security mission," the Coast Guard spokesperson said.

"Just as we monitor for mechanical or weather-related hazards, we incorporate cyber risk management into our routine, professional approach to facilitating commerce and ensuring safe vessel transits into and from our ports and waterways.

"While confirmed cyber disruptions in the maritime domain remain uncommon, even isolated technical issues can cause avoidable commercial delays.

"We encourage all maritime stakeholders to leverage Coast Guard Cyber Command’s free, non-regulatory technical resources to maintain strong digital hygiene and report any suspected anomalies to the National Response Center," the spokesperson added.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

articles.title: Newly elected Florida commissioner's son shot dead inside tent during camping trip
articles.excerpt:
Carey Washington Vinson was fatally shot inside his tent along Florida's Blackwater River on Sunday night.

A newly elected Florida politician is mourning the death of his son after the young man was ...
articles.body_text:
Carey Washington Vinson was fatally shot inside his tent along Florida's Blackwater River on Sunday night.

A newly elected Florida politician is mourning the death of his son after the young man was fatally shot inside his tent during a weekend camping trip, his father confirmed Monday.

Joe Vinson, who made history earlier this year as the first non-party-affiliated county commissioner elected in Escambia County, announced the tragedy on Instagram, revealing that his son, Carey Washington Vinson, was killed while camping with friends near the Blackwater River in the Florida Panhandle.

"I don’t know how to say this," Joe Vinson wrote. "Our son Carey Washington Vinson is dead. He was camping with friends on the Blackwater River last night when a gunshot from outside their campsite struck him in his tent."

CALIFORNIA NURSING STUDENT AND MOM ARRESTED MONTHS AFTER MAN’S BODY TURNS UP IN RAVINE: POLICE

Carey Washington Vinson was killed while camping with friends near the Blackwater River in the Florida Panhandle, his father confirmed Monday. (@joepensacola / Instagram)

He added, "It’s an ongoing investigation, and I don’t have any more details at this time. We are shocked and heartbroken about our sweet boy."

According to the Santa Rosa County Sheriff's Office, officers were dispatched to the Blackwater River area on Sunday following a 911 call about a shooting.

First responders arrived to find a male victim with a gunshot wound to the head and pronounced him dead at the scene.

RUSH HOUR ROAD RAGE SUSPECT’S BAIL REVOKED AS SLAIN UTILITY WORKER’S SUPPORTERS SHOUT AT ACCUSED MURDERER

Joe Vinson was elected this year as the first non-party-affiliated county commissioner in Escambia County history. (Escambia County)

Carey, 19, and his friends had been camping on sandbars along the river since Friday, Santa Rosa County Sheriff's Office Chief Deputy Randy Tifft told People Magazine.

Law enforcement has not yet said whether they believe the shooting was intentional or accidental.

Escambia County Sheriff Chip Simmons offered condolences to the commissioner's family on Facebook.

"There are simply no words that can ease the pain of losing a child," Simmons said. "I ask that you join me in keeping Joe and his entire family in your thoughts and prayers during this incredibly difficult time. May God grant them strength, comfort, and peace in the days ahead."

LOUISIANA MAN ACCUSED OF RANDOM NATURE TRAIL MURDER, KILLING COWORKER WITH CROSSBOW DAYS LATER

Law enforcement has not yet said whether they believe the shooting was intentional or accidental. (iStock)

Detectives are urging anyone who was in the area or witnessed suspicious activity to come forward.

"This incident remains under active investigation," a spokesperson for the Santa Rosa County Sheriff's Office told Fox News Digital in an email. "We will provide updates as additional information becomes available for release."

Fox News Digital reached out to Joe Vinson for comment.

Sophia Compton is a Writer at Fox News Digital. Sophia was previously a business reporter covering finance, energy and tourism and has experience as a TV news producer. She graduated with a journalism degree in 2021 from the University of Hawaii at Manoa. Story tips can be sent to sophia.compton@fox.com.

articles.title: Army sergeant pleads guilty to cashing in on US military secrets in China-linked plot, DOJ says
articles.excerpt: U.S. Attorney Scott Bradford announces charges against Army Sgt. Jian Zhao, accused of passing sensitive U.S. military information to individuals linked to China. (Credit: Scott Bradford, U.S. Attorne...
articles.body_text:
U.S. Attorney Scott Bradford announces charges against Army Sgt. Jian Zhao, accused of passing sensitive U.S. military information to individuals linked to China. (Credit: Scott Bradford, U.S. Attorney for the District of Oregon)

An active-duty U.S. Army sergeant pleaded guilty Monday in a yearslong plot that turned his access to sensitive military information into a payday from buyers in China.

Jian Zhao, 37, used his personal cellphone to photograph restricted Army documents, handed over excerpts from technical manuals for the High Mobility Artillery Rocket System, or HIMARS, and put military computers and government hard drives up for sale, federal prosecutors said.

"Protecting our national security depends on holding accountable those who compromise their oath and endanger the security of our armed forces," U.S. Attorney Scott E. Bradford wrote on X.

CHINA COULD EXPLOIT US TECHNOLOGY TO THREATEN AMERICAN FORCES, CONGRESSIONAL WATCHDOG LEADERS WARN

"Jian Zhao violated that trust by exploiting his access to military information and equipment for personal profit while knowingly providing materials to individuals linked to China."

Zhao pleaded guilty to conspiring to gather, transmit and transfer national defense information. Prosecutors said he enlisted in 2017 and served as a battery supply sergeant at Joint Base Lewis-McChord in Washington, where his duties and security clearance gave him access to sensitive Army information and equipment.

CHINA-LINKED HACKERS INFILTRATED US GOVERNMENT NETWORKS BEFORE FBI TAKEDOWN

A redacted image released by the Justice Department shows a person holding a cellphone at a desk. According to court records, Army Sgt. Jian Zhao admitted using his personal cellphone to photograph controlled military documents. (U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Oregon)

The documents Zhao photographed covered Army operations, communications networks, military exercises and rocket and missile systems, prosecutors said.

He also took military storage devices without permission and collected thousands of dollars for materials he described as sensitive, secret or top secret.

SENIOR US ARMY SOLDIER ARRESTED IN UK ON SUSPICION OF SPYING FOR RUSSIA

A U.S. Air Force C-17 sits on the flight line at Joint Base Lewis-McChord in Washington, where Army Sgt. Jian Zhao was stationed. (Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images)

"This guilty plea reflects a deliberate betrayal of the oath every Soldier takes to defend our nation and safeguard our fellow service members," said Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, who leads Army Counterintelligence Command.

Stinchon said the scheme put soldiers at risk and urged troops to report suspicious activity or outreach.

CALIFORNIA REALTOR NABBED AT LAX IN ALLEGED CHINA SPY CASE TARGETING TAIWAN PRESIDENT’S RELATIVE

Prosecutors traced the plot back to late 2021. Ruoyu Duan, a former Army soldier living in Hillsboro, Oregon, recruited Zhao and other active-duty troops to provide defense information and helped arrange payments from buyers in China, prosecutors said. Duan previously pleaded guilty to conspiring to transmit national defense information.

Federal agents arrested Zhao at his home in Lacey, Washington, on March 6, 2025, and recovered about $30,000 in cash, electronic devices and multiple Army hard drives.

FORMER CALIFORNIA MAYOR ADMITS TO SECRETLY WORKING FOR CHINA, SPREADING BEIJING PROPAGANDA IN US

Two soldiers in camouflage stand in front of a tan military truck. (Christopher Chen/U.S. Air Force)

Under his plea agreement, Zhao agreed to forfeit $17,500 in proceeds from the scheme and give up his claim to the seized cash.

"By pleading guilty, Jian Zhao has admitted to betraying that trust and abusing the responsibilities that came with his position and security clearance," said Doug Olson, the FBI’s special agent in charge in Portland.

"Those who choose to compromise sensitive military information for personal gain put our nation's interests at risk, and the FBI, alongside our law enforcement and military partners, remains committed to holding them accountable," he continued.

Zhao faces up to 10 years in federal prison, a $250,000 fine and up to three years of supervised release. His sentencing is set for March 1, 2027.

Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

articles.title: Russia warns of 'preventive nuclear attack' as Medvedev claims Ukraine, NATO crossed line
articles.excerpt:
Fox News chief national security correspondent Jennifer Griffin reports on Russian President Vladimir Putin's warning to NATO regarding the use of long-range weapons in Ukraine on ‘America Reports.’

...
articles.body_text:
Fox News chief national security correspondent Jennifer Griffin reports on Russian President Vladimir Putin's warning to NATO regarding the use of long-range weapons in Ukraine on ‘America Reports.’

Russia warned Monday that it could carry out a "preventive nuclear attack" under certain circumstances, with former President Dmitry Medvedev claiming Ukraine and NATO allies have already crossed certain thresholds that could push Moscow to consider using nuclear weapons.

"The massive use of non-nuclear means that cause catastrophes makes a preventive nuclear attack by the Russian Federation possible," Medvedev, deputy chairman of Russia's Security Council, wrote in an article published Monday in the Moscow Journal of International Law and excerpted by the state news agency TASS.

Medvedev also warned that "secret or hidden supplies of nuclear weapons from the West to Kyiv will provoke a legitimate preventive nuclear attack by Russia."

MOSCOW THREATENS NUCLEAR RESPONSE OVER TINY FORTRESS WEDGED BETWEEN US ALLIES AS CLASH FEARS GROW

Dmitry Medvedev takes part in a wreath-laying ceremony marking Defender of the Fatherland Day at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier by the Kremlin Wall in Moscow, Russia, Feb. 23, 2024. (Yekaterina Shtukina/Sputnik/Pool via Reuters.)

"Kyiv and its allies must remember that the Russian Federation not only has the right, but in various situations has the obligation to use nuclear weapons," he wrote.

Medvedev's warning came amid continuing tensions between Moscow and the West over the nearly five-year war in Ukraine and NATO's military support for Kyiv.

He argued that Ukraine and its Western allies have already created circumstances under which Russia could consider a nuclear strike, though he said Russian President Vladimir Putin carefully weighs the consequences before making such a decision.

"Formally, in a number of cases, the parties collectively opposing us (Ukraine, NATO countries, and several Western countries outside the alliance) have already created situations in which Russia considers the possibility of launching a nuclear strike," Medvedev wrote in the article, titled "State Sovereignty and Nuclear Weapons: International Legal Aspects of Ensuring National Security".

TRUMP HOLDS THE NUCLEAR CARDS TO PLAY AGAINST CHINA AND RUSSIA ON ARMS CONTROL

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin (Genya Savilov/AFP via Getty Images; Contributor/Getty Images)

Despite those warnings, Medvedev wrote that Putin "is always guided by a comprehensive analysis of all factors and the proportionality between the actual damage inflicted and the retaliatory measures."

Medvedev also said Russia has not used nuclear weapons during the war with Ukraine because it has not considered them necessary, though he warned that calculation could change.

"Obviously, so far the course of events in the Ukrainian crisis has not created a state of direct necessity to use nuclear weapons," he wrote.

"The decision on Russia's use of nuclear weapons during the special military operation was not taken due to the lack of a direct necessity to do so," he added, using the Kremlin's preferred term for the war in Ukraine.

Medvedev argued that while Russia's nuclear doctrine does not explicitly authorize preventive nuclear strikes, certain scenarios — including catastrophic attacks using conventional weapons or the transfer of nuclear arms to Ukraine — could justify preemptive action.

He said any final decision rests solely with Putin.

TRUMP'S HISTORIC SUMMIT WITH XI, PUTIN MARKS DIPLOMATIC MILESTONE, BUT BREAKTHROUGHS REMAIN ELUSIVE

Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump meet during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Leaders' Summit in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 19, 2026. (Reuters)

"In making such decisions, the Russian president is always guided by a complete analysis of all factors and the proportionality between the actual damage caused and the retaliatory measures," Medvedev wrote.

"The Kyiv regime and its sponsors must not harbor dangerous illusions," he warned.

"If the scenarios mentioned above were to occur, the head of state not only has the right, but also the obligation to use nuclear weapons. All those who are currently fanning the flames must fully realize this".

Medvedev's remarks came within days of President Donald Trump meeting with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Nov. 19 in Shenzhen, China, where the leaders of the three nuclear powers agreed to pursue talks aimed at reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation.

While the summit produced no major breakthrough on arms reductions, the leaders reaffirmed in a declaration that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.

TRUMP WILL FACE REPORTERS AFTER HISTORIC XI-PUTIN TALKS AS WAR QUESTIONS LINGER

Dmitry Medvedev, Russian Security Council deputy chairman, speaks at a meeting of the United Russia party programme commission in Moscow, Oct. 1, 2025. (Ekaterina Shtukina, Sputnik Pool Photo via AP)

To support his argument, Medvedev cited a 1996 International Court of Justice advisory opinion, contending that international law does not categorically prohibit the use of nuclear weapons when a state's survival is at stake.

The court concluded that the threat or use of nuclear weapons would generally violate international humanitarian law, but it did not definitively resolve whether such use would be lawful in extreme circumstances of self-defense.

Medvedev, who served as Russia's president from 2008 to 2012 and later as prime minister under Putin, has become one of Moscow's most outspoken voices on nuclear escalation since Russia invaded Ukraine.

Medvedev accused NATO members of undermining nonproliferation efforts, criticizing Germany's participation in nuclear deterrence arrangements and arguing that NATO's nuclear-sharing policies do not represent a universally accepted interpretation of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT)

On Monday, he also accused the U.S. of applying double standards toward Iran and said Washington used nonproliferation fears to justify military action against Tehran while following its own objectives.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

articles.title: What strike on Russian ship in Libya says about spread of Ukraine war
articles.excerpt:
Anchored in a Mediterranean harbour nearly 2,000 miles from Moscow, the Captain of Russia's corvette Merkury might well have thought his ship was safe from attack. It wasn't.

The audacious and succes...
articles.body_text:
Anchored in a Mediterranean harbour nearly 2,000 miles from Moscow, the Captain of Russia's corvette Merkury might well have thought his ship was safe from attack. It wasn't.

The audacious and successful night-time attack in Benghazi, co-ordinated by Ukraine's SBU intelligence agency and its armed forces, has raised the obvious question: is the Ukraine war spreading well beyond its borders?

The answer is yes, in fact, it was already spreading. But this attack, which Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky called "an exemplary operation" will inevitably raise the stakes another notch.

Russia, which is currently engaged in a non-stop campaign to batter Ukraine's civilian population into submission with daily missile and drone strikes, has called it "a dangerous escalation".

It follows the suspected Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian dry-cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland at the weekend, which the Kremlin described as an act of terrorism.

Ukraine's long-range drones have also previously struck Russia's Baltic oil terminal at Ust-Luga.

Some of Ukraine's more audacious long-range drone attacks – what Zelensky likes to call "long-range sanctions" – have also struck targets thousands of kilometres beyond Ukraine's borders with Russia, deep inside Siberia.

The most notable of these was last year's Operation Spider's Web, which involved a specially adapted lorry that drove close to a Russian strategic nuclear bomber airbase and released a "swarm" of explosive drones that damaged or destroyed several expensive bombers.

And Ukraine has also been active further south in Africa where its forces have targeted Russian mercenaries from the Africa Corps, the successor to the infamous Wagner Group that was accused of carrying out numerous human rights abuses.

It's not just Russia that will be alarmed by this latest Ukrainian operation in Benghazi harbour. The United Nations mission in Libya has already expressed its "deep concern".

Libyan officials point out that their country is not a party to the Russia-Ukraine war, although the Merkury and an accompanying cargo ship that was also hit were berthed in the eastern part of Libya controlled by the pro-Moscow warlord and self-styled "Field Marshal" Khalifa Haftar.

How Ukraine drone attacks on Russian ships unfolded

Throughout this year the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) has condemned all attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and today the global shipping community will be wondering whether this attack does indeed set a dangerous precedent.

If Ukraine can plan and execute such a bold attack on Russian ships in a nominally neutral harbour so far from home, where does this stop?

As the fifth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine approaches, this war has already been spreading, notably in other parts of Europe.

On Friday, several Russian projectiles landed well inside Poland's borders, just 60 miles from an Anglo-French exercise of forces intended to be deployed following an eventual ceasefire in Ukraine.

This, said Poland's PM Donald Tusk, was "a deliberate provocation" by Moscow.

It's not the first time Russian munitions have landed inside Poland, and therefore inside Nato territory, but observers have pointed out that Russia's probing of Nato's borders is becoming ever more brazen and some are calling for a firmer response.

But Russia is already heavily sanctioned by the West, with Europe having reduced much – but not all – of its energy imports from Russia, so the options for retaliation are limited, short of military confrontation, which no one wants.

Watch: CCTV shows explosion after Poland says airspace violated by Russian missile

Both Romania and Moldova have found themselves frequently struck by overflying Russian drones targeting Ukraine's Black Sea ports, while Bulgaria and Romania have suffered maritime drone attacks on commercial shipping just offshore in the Black Sea.

In the case of Romania, a Nato member, fast jets have had to be scrambled to intercept incoming Russian drones and there is a profound suspicion that these incursions are not all accidental.

The three Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania – all have borders with Russia and all consider themselves right on the front lines in this war.

There have been a number of anonymous attacks on military industrial facilities in these countries, blamed on agents acting on Moscow's behalf.

Russia, for its part, suspects Estonia of being complicit in Ukrainian drone attacks on the Baltic involving overflights through Estonian airspace.

Hybrid warfare isn't new but it is on the rise.

It refers to the practice, by either side, of carrying out largely anonymous and unattributable operations using methods like cyber attacks, the burning down of warehouses supplying military equipment and the dispatching of drones, both for surveillance and loaded with explosives.

This autumn, Germany's Leipzig-Halle airport, which is used as a resupply hub by Ukraine's cargo aircraft, was targeted by three explosive drones that were discovered before anyone was hurt.

There have been other incidents involving explosive packages sent across Europe targeting Germany, Poland and the UK. Moscow denies any involvement.

articles.title: Russia could launch nuclear-capable satellite within weeks, Western intelligence warns: report
articles.excerpt: Chief national security correspondent Jennifer Griffin joins ‘The Faulkner Focus’ to discuss the growing threat of orbital warfare after the U.S. confirmed it has deployed weapons in orbit. She examin...
articles.body_text:
Chief national security correspondent Jennifer Griffin joins ‘The Faulkner Focus’ to discuss the growing threat of orbital warfare after the U.S. confirmed it has deployed weapons in orbit. She examines the security implications as concerns over China and Russia’s space capabilities continue to mount.

Russia could launch a nuclear-armed satellite into orbit within less than 60 days according to new Western intelligence assessments reported Monday, raising fears that Moscow is preparing to deploy a weapon capable of crippling thousands of satellites used by the United States and its allies.

The intelligence reports emerged just four days after President Donald Trump met with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping at a high-profile summit in Shenzhen, China, where nuclear arms control was a central topic.

The three leaders issued a joint declaration affirming that nuclear war should never be fought, but stopped short of announcing binding arms-control commitments.

NEXT GENERATION OPIR GEO: BUILDING AMERICA’S GATEWAY TO THE FUTURE OF SPACE-BASED MISSILE WARNING AND TRACKING

On Monday, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz publicly addressed the reports, while the Kremlin dismissed the allegations.

According to a joint investigation published Nov. 23 by German broadcasters WDR and NDR and the newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung, Western intelligence agencies believe Russia has assembled a satellite known as "Sputnik-S," which has reportedly been stored in the Moscow region for several years.

Intelligence warnings shared among several NATO countries in early November indicated that the satellite, reportedly designed to carry a nuclear warhead, could be launched within 60 days. Germany's military Space Command reportedly assessed that a December launch was possible.

The German investigation also reported that military officials had briefed senior government figures, including German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius, about the threat.

The reports prompted an immediate response from European leaders.

Speaking alongside Rutte in Berlin on Monday, Merz described the allegations as "shocking," while noting that concerns about Russia's nuclear space ambitions were not entirely new.

PUTIN LAUNCHES UKRAINE BARRAGE HOURS AFTER TRUMP MEETING AMID ALLEGED RUSSIAN MISSILE BREACH OF NATO AIRSPACE

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz sparked backlash while remarking about the country's migration policies. (Thomas Traasdahl/Ritzau Scanpix via AP)

Rutte, meanwhile, stressed that NATO was continually assessing its defensive capabilities.

"I can assure you, we will always make sure that we defend every inch of NATO territory," Rutte said, according to Reuters.

He added that the alliance's defense planning included threats in space and said NATO had response options that were not always visible to the public.

The Kremlin rejected the allegations. Russian presidential spokesperson Dmitry Peskov questioned the credibility of the intelligence reports, saying they contained numerous unsubstantiated claims that were "hardly worth taking seriously," according to The Moscow Times.

"We haven’t seen the report. But there are so many ‘alleged’ and ‘possible’ claims in it, attributed to who knows whom, that it’s certainly hardly worth taking them seriously," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters during a daily briefing.

Russia's Embassy in Berlin separately dismissed the reporting as part of a propaganda campaign and maintained that Moscow's space activities were peaceful and consistent with international obligations.

The latest warnings follow an earlier assessment by the U.S. Defense Intelligence Agency , which publicly identified Russia's development of a nuclear-capable satellite in October. "Russia is developing a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon," the DIA stated in its 2026 Challenges to Security in Space assessment.

NATO WARNS RUSSIA: 'WE WILL BREAK' FORCES, DESTROY 'ANYTHING AND EVERYTHING' IF YOU ATTACK

FILE - Russian President Vladimir Putin chairs a meeting aboard the missile cruiser Varyag in Russia's far eastern Sakhalin region on Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. Putin previously said Russia is not waging a sabotage campaign against Europe. (Reuters)

As Fox News Digital reported on October 29, the agency warned that such a weapon could cause the rapid loss or degradation of thousands of satellites operated by governments and private companies.

Unlike a conventional anti-satellite weapon targeting an individual spacecraft, a nuclear detonation in orbit could potentially disable large numbers of satellites through radiation and electromagnetic effects.

The consequences could extend far beyond the military. Satellites support GPS navigation, international communications, financial transactions, weather forecasting and critical infrastructure.

The threat also has implications for Ukraine, whose military relies heavily on satellite communications, including SpaceX's Starlink network, during its war with Russia.

The concern was initially addressed on February 2024 when the Biden administration publicly acknowledged that Russia was developing a troubling anti-satellite capability, although officials said at the time that no such weapon had been deployed.

Placing a nuclear weapon in orbit would violate the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which prohibits stationing nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in space.

The latest German reporting suggests the threat could be approaching a more immediate stage, but critical questions remain unanswered, including whether the satellite already carries a nuclear warhead and whether Western intelligence has independently verified the reported launch preparations.

A Defense Intelligence Agency graphic shows the number of satellites operating at different orbital altitudes around Earth, including more than 15,000 in low-Earth orbit. (Defense Intelligence Agency)

Fox News Digital has reached out to the White House, Pentagon, U.S. Space Command and German Embassy for comment.

Efrat (Effie) Lachter is a reporter for Fox News Digital with more than 15 years of experience covering conflict, global affairs, human rights and political accountability. She has directed and produced more than 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries, documenting conflicts, humanitarian crises, corruption, human trafficking, gender-based violence and the human stories behind major world events.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. Lachter is the recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award and was a 2023–2024 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

articles.title: US urges Americans in historic region to stay alert after 'dangerous' airspace incident
articles.excerpt: Travelers share sharply different plans following the FAA ground stop, with several fliers telling Fox News Digital they're opting to drive instead to Florida and Boston. Others say they are nervously...
articles.body_text:
Travelers share sharply different plans following the FAA ground stop, with several fliers telling Fox News Digital they're opting to drive instead to Florida and Boston. Others say they are nervously sticking with their booked flights.

Americans in Poland are being warned to stay extra cautious following reported "dangerous" airspace violations near the Ukrainian border.

U.S. Mission Poland said there were airspace violations reported in southeastern Poland on Friday, according to a statement.

Two suspected Russian missiles and a drone crashed in the region that day — including two within 30 miles of the Polish-Ukrainian border, according to The Associated Press (AP).

AMERICANS WARNED OF VIOLENT PROTESTS AS MAJOR TOURIST DESTINATION FACES SHUTDOWN THREAT

In an X post, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte called the airspace violations "grave."

He added, "This incident is clearly dangerous — a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine.... We continue to stand united as Allies and will continue to support Ukraine."

Two suspected Russian missiles and a drone crashed in southeastern Poland on Friday, including two within 30 miles of the Polish-Ukrainian border, according to The Associated Press. Seen above are Polish soldiers on Friday. (Wojtek Radwanski/AFP via Getty Images)

U.S. officials said they were "closely monitoring the situation."

"U.S. citizens in Poland should follow guidance from Polish authorities and monitor local media and official government announcements for the most up-to-date information on this event and other events of this nature," officials said.

AMERICANS WARNED AGAIN TO RETHINK TRAVEL AS MISSILE ATTACK RATTLES HISTORIC REGION

Though major Polish cities like Warsaw and Kraków are popular with tourists, southeastern Poland is home to a number of attractions, including the Bieszczady Mountains and Łańcut Castle.

The region also includes Zamość, a 16th-century Renaissance town that's listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Americans in Poland are being urged to exercise extra caution following reported airspace violations in southeastern Poland near the Ukrainian border. Polish soldiers are seen above. (Wojtek Radwanski/AFP via Getty Images)

Poland is ranked as Level 1, labeled "Exercise Normal Precautions," under the State Department's travel advisory system.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

The State Department's travel advisory on Poland notes the country "has a low crime rate overall, but the risk of crime is higher in major cities."

Zamość, seen above, is listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site and is located near the region where airspace violations were reported. (iStock)

The State Department urges travelers to keep a close eye on their belongings at tourist attractions, train stations and on public transit.

Officials also advise avoiding adult entertainment clubs, where foreign visitors have reportedly been overcharged.

Travelers should keep a close eye on belongings at tourist attractions, train stations and on public transit, officials said.

Fox News Digital reached out to the State Department for additional information.

The warning comes amid a wave of recent security alerts for Americans across Europe.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Earlier this month, the U.S. Consulate in Kraków warned American tourists to avoid the city's historic center and remain vigilant after a 24-year-old gunman opened fire in Main Market Square on Nov. 7, killing six people and wounding 15 others.

Visitors to southeastern Poland often tour Zamość, a historic 16th-century Renaissance town pictured above. (iStock)

Also this month, U.S. embassies across Europe — including in London, Berlin, Madrid and Rome — urged Americans to "keep a low profile" and stay alert in crowded holiday spots amid terrorism and protest concerns.

The Associated Press contributed reporting.

Andrea Margolis is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital and Fox Business. Readers can follow her on X at @andreamargs or send story tips to andrea.margolis@fox.com.

articles.title: Israeli strikes kill at least three, including UNRWA worker, in Gaza
articles.excerpt:
Israeli air strikes have killed at least three people in Gaza, including a worker for the UN Palestinian refugee agency, according to the relief agency and local health officials.

The United Nations ...
articles.body_text:
Israeli air strikes have killed at least three people in Gaza, including a worker for the UN Palestinian refugee agency, according to the relief agency and local health officials.

The United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA) on Monday named the worker killed as Adel al-Helo.

He was working near a well in the Jabalia refugee camp in the enclave’s north when hit, the agency and medics said. Three others were wounded in the strike.

Later on Monday, another Israeli air strike ⁠targeted a vehicle in western Gaza City, killing two people and wounding others, medics said, according to the Reuters news agency. The Israeli military did not immediately comment.

Israel continues to launch attacks across the enclave, despite an October 2025 “ceasefire” deal with Hamas, which formally halted around two years of fighting but has failed to bring Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza to an end.

“The initial reports indicate that the strike hit a target on the street near the water well, which was manned by UNRWA staff and a guard. The staff were engaged in their regular duties associated with water well operations,” an UNRWA spokesperson told Reuters.

Israel has yet to respond to the incident. But since the October ceasefire, at least 1,679 Palestinian people and five Israeli soldiers have been killed.

Israeli forces have also continued to destroy residential buildings in Gaza, beyond the “Yellow Line”  to which they were required to withdraw under the ceasefire.

Al Jazeera journalist Moath al-Kahlout, reporting from Deir el-Balah, said displaced Palestinians who live in the area near the line gathered on Saturday to demonstrate against Israel’s intensifying air strikes.

“More than 500 housing units have been destroyed in less than a month,” Mohammed Musleh, mayor of Deir el-Balah’s Maghazi municipality, told Al Jazeera.

“This is part of what appears to be a systematic policy of gradual creeping displacement aimed at forcing residents out of their camp and destroying as many homes as possible,” he added.

articles.title: China’s fourth aircraft carrier, bigger than others and nuclear-powered, nears completion
articles.excerpt: NEW TAIPEI CITY, Taiwan — China’s fourth aircraft carrier, a gigantic vessel known so far as just Type 004, will come out as early as next year bigger than its predecessors and with nuclear power that...
articles.body_text:
NEW TAIPEI CITY, Taiwan — China’s fourth aircraft carrier, a gigantic vessel known so far as just Type 004, will come out as early as next year bigger than its predecessors and with nuclear power that can launch planes faster than usual in case of any conflict, analysts say.

And it’s tipped to add pressure on countries, such as Japan and the United States, that already keep a high alert for the Chinese military.

The carrier being built now in the northern port city Dalian could accommodate 75 to 90 planes once deployed, the Asia program director at the think tank Defence Priorities has said.

As of October, the vessel’s hull measured about 322 meters in length from the unfinished bow to stern with a width of approximately 46 meters, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), also a think tank.

CSIS called Type 004 “far larger than any other class of surface combatant” in China’s navy.

Aerial photos of the carrier show the “basic hull form” already built, auguring well for a 2027 launch, said Collin Koh, a senior fellow at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore. Deployment would take five to 10 years, he said.

The specs would make Type 004 “slightly larger” than China’s Fujian aircraft carrier, currently the biggest one in its fleet, Koh said.

Information available today about the Type 004 – likely to be renamed after a Chinese province like the existing three – classify the vessel as a “supercarrier” in terms of electronics, tonnage and aircraft carrying capacity, said Alexander Huang, chairman of the Council of Strategic and Wargaming Studies in Taipei.

Nuclear power on board would offer the aircraft more propulsion than China’s existing electromagnetic aircraft launch system, Koh said. He said that would eliminate the need for power generators on board the carrier while allowing faster takeoffs – without payload compromises – and quick combat turnarounds for refueling.

“It seems to signal a certain strategic objective,” Koh said of the nuclear capability. “It’s not just going to move along your coast. It seems to signal a certain global ambition.”

Nuclear power will give the carrier “essentially unlimited endurance” and allow for global deployment without the kind of tanker support a conventionally powered carrier needs, said David Silbey, a Cornell University professor specializing in military history and defense policy.

The fourth carrier may get posted to northern China because the other three are in the south, Huang said. In that scenario, he said, China could “use one of the four to always operate somewhere.”

Type 004 may be used for training and maintenance as well as operations, Huang added.

China’s fourth carrier gets it closer to rivaling the U.S. navy, analysts said.

It will compare in size to the Nimitz and Ford class U.S. carriers, which means it can carry as many as 100 aircraft, Silbey said. “That gives it much more striking power than previous carriers, which could only carry around 50,” he said.

The U.S. navy has 11 carriers, all nuclear powered.

Even if smaller than the U.S. fleet, a Chinese navy with nuclear-powered carriers can mount a challenge to the United States, Koh said.

The U.S. navy maintains bases in Guam, Hawaii and Japan plus treaty alliances with Japan and the Philippines. The U.S. and China have long seen each other as rival superpowers.

Experts have said China sent an especially large number of its naval deployments near Japan’s southernmost islands and nearby waters since a political rift that erupted in November 2025 over a remark by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.

The Philippines is embroiled in a maritime sovereignty dispute with China.

China plans to build more carriers over the next decade for a “blue water capability that they’ve never really had before,” Silbey said. “In the Pacific, it means that they can go after American assets that are out of range of their other assets.”

articles.title: Flights cancelled in Belgium due to cost-of-living strike
articles.excerpt:
A few people have turned up at Brussels airport where no flights are leaving

Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and public transport severely disrupted across Belgium as a result of a strike aga...
articles.body_text:
A few people have turned up at Brussels airport where no flights are leaving

Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and public transport severely disrupted across Belgium as a result of a strike against planned austerity measures.

All air traffic has been halted at Brussels Airport in Zaventem as well as at Charleroi, home to low-cost airlines such as Ryanair.

Underground services have also been halted in capital Brussels, where large numbers of people joined a protest march.

The protest comes as Prime Minister Bart De Wever continues talks with his coalition allies over a budget to cut borrowing costs. King Philippe declined his resignation earlier this month, giving De Wever more time to negotiate.

No flights are taking off or landing at Brussels Airport between 07:00 and 21:00 local time (06:00-20:00 GMT) as a result of the strike by air traffic controllers.

"In total, 404 flights today cannot be operated, which has an impact on more than 50,000 passengers," Brussels Airport spokesperson Jeffrey Franssens said.

Reuters news agency spoke to Florence Faure, a French passenger who had arrived in Brussels from China's capital, Beijing, only to find that her flight to Paris Charles de Gaulle airport had been cancelled.

"Since our luggage was supposed to go on to Paris Charles de Gaulle, we didn't even collect it," she said.

A similar situation has affected Charleroi, where all flights were shown as "scheduled", regardless of the time of departure or arrival.

One passenger told Belgian broadcaster RTBF that she had received no warning and only discovered there were no flights when she arrived at the airport.

Philippe Naime, a teacher, was one of the tens of thousands taking part in the protest march in Brussels.

"Quite simply, no more money is being invested in education, and people are left to fend for themselves. But people do not have the means to do that," he told Reuters.

Public transport, schools and other public services are also facing disruptions.

Large numbers of people have descended on Brussels for a protest march

The Belgian prime minister leads a five-party coalition.

One of its members, the socialist Vooruit, has been refusing to endorse plans agreed by the other four. It wants to raise taxes on the rich and for there to be fewer cuts to pensions and the health sector.

De Wever met King Philippe on Monday for the third update since the impasse.

"While expressing regret over the lack of significant progress, the king encouraged the prime minister to persevere in order to reach an agreement as soon as possible," the royal palace said in a statement.

The leader of one of the country's main unions, FGTB, said the government had alternatives to "dismantling the social protection system".

Bert Engelaar, head of the union, called for "a genuine wealth tax, fair taxation, and the elimination of tax loopholes".

"Political responsibility is not about keeping a government afloat at all costs. It's about knowing when to stop," he added, praising the Vooruit party.

Another union leader, Ann Vermorgen of the CSC, criticised government plans to cut bank holidays when they fall on weekends.

articles.title: Ukraine shares video of strikes on Russian ships off Libya
articles.excerpt:
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky has shared footage on social media which he says shows strikes on Russian vessels off the coast of Libya on Sunday.

A Russian warship was sunk by Ukrainian drones...
articles.body_text:
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky has shared footage on social media which he says shows strikes on Russian vessels off the coast of Libya on Sunday.

A Russian warship was sunk by Ukrainian drones and the attack also targeted a second vessel, a cargo ship which was being used to transport weapons, Zelensky said.

Footage verified by the BBC shows a ship ablaze at Benghazi's port.

The local health ministry said it had received injured people from a commercial ship that was targeted off the coast. It is not clear whether this is the same vessel as the one Ukraine has claimed responsibility for.

Following the strikes, the Kremlin warned of an "escalation of tensions in the region", but declined to comment directly on the attacks in Libya.

articles.title: US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal

The US has said it intends to ban a Singaporean artificial intelligence (AI) company allegedly tied to the Nvidia scandal from doing business in America.

The US Department of Commerce announced on Mo...
articles.body_text:
The US has said it intends to ban a Singaporean artificial intelligence (AI) company allegedly tied to the Nvidia scandal from doing business in America.

The US Department of Commerce announced on Monday that it planned to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are blacklisted from buying or selling goods in the US.

The company is mainly a developer of data centres, but in recent weeks, a former executive of Megaspeed was accused of working as spy for China while having a romantic relationship with Nvidia head Jensen Huang.

The relationship led to additional scrutiny by US officials and heightened concern that Megaspeed was funneling Nvidia's advanced AI computer chips to China.

articles.title: Former Navy SEAL says New Jersey’s Islamophobia bill puts protected speech in the crosshairs
articles.excerpt: Bill Brown, a Parlatore Law Group partner and former Navy SEAL, tells Fox News Digital why he believes New Jersey’s Islamophobia bill could make people think twice before criticizing religious and pol...
articles.body_text:
Bill Brown, a Parlatore Law Group partner and former Navy SEAL, tells Fox News Digital why he believes New Jersey’s Islamophobia bill could make people think twice before criticizing religious and political ideas.

A New Jersey proposal aimed at combating anti-Muslim discrimination could make Americans think twice before criticizing religious and political ideas, a lawyer and former Navy SEAL warned.

Bill Brown, a partner at Parlatore Law Group, told Fox News Digital that Assembly Bill 1146 contains language broad enough to discourage public debate, even though the legislation expressly preserves First Amendment rights.

"The mere threat of state scrutiny is a direct assault on public debate," Brown said.

TRUMP DOJ EXPANDS RELIGIOUS LIBERTY PROTECTIONS AFTER MAJOR SUPREME COURT RULINGS

A New Jersey bill would create a state definition of Islamophobia for officials to consider in certain civil and criminal matters. An unrelated photo shows Muslim men praying in Marseille, France.

The proposal would establish a state definition of Islamophobia and require public officials and law enforcement officers to consider it when determining whether alleged discriminatory acts were motivated by anti-Muslim bias.

Brown argued that requiring officials to use a definition that includes harsh criticism and other speech could make people afraid to speak openly.

CHRISTIAN GROUPS AND PASTORS SAY NEW CALIFORNIA LGBT HATE SPEECH LAW IS DISGUISED AS INDOCTRINATION

Shiite Muslims stand over a representation of an American flag during a rally to condemn Israeli strikes on Iran, in Karachi, Pakistan, Sunday, June 22, 2025. (Fareed Khan/AP Photo)

"The First Amendment guarantees that no religion or theology is immune to criticism," he said.

Democratic Assemblyman Joe Danielsen sponsors the bill, which is co-sponsored by fellow Democrats Assemblywomen Verlina Reynolds-Jackson and Mitchelle Drulis and Assemblyman Roy Freiman. The legislation describes a uniform definition as a tool to help officials identify and investigate anti-Muslim crime, harassment and discrimination."

Fox News Digital made multiple attempts to contact Danielsen and all three co-sponsors for comment but did not receive a response.

Its definition includes "hatred or severe disparagement towards Muslim persons or their culture," as well as "rhetorical, violent, or physical anti-Muslim manifestations."

Other examples include pulling hijabs from Muslim women, discriminatory treatment and blaming Muslims collectively for wrongdoing committed by an individual or group.

CONNECTICUT BARS NATIVITY DISPLAY IN STATE CAPITOL BECAUSE IT'S 'RELIGIOUS,' LAWSUIT THREAT SAYS

The bill would create no standalone criminal offense for criticizing Islam. It directs officials to consider the definition when reviewing an alleged violation of an existing policy, law or regulation prohibiting discriminatory acts.

It also explicitly says nothing in the legislation should diminish or infringe on rights protected by the First Amendment or New Jersey’s Constitution.

AMERICA'S FIRST MUSLIM SENATOR EXPOSES A POLITICAL BLIND SPOT

Asked about that safeguard, Brown maintained that the prospect of scrutiny itself could discourage people from speaking, regardless of whether a case ultimately succeeds.

He also singled out a provision in the bill’s legislative findings that lists "anti-Islamism" among terms that may describe the same characteristics as Islamophobia. Brown argued that the wording risks blurring the distinction between prejudice against Muslim people and criticism of a political movement.

JONATHAN TURLEY: FRANCE'S FREE SPEECH CRACKDOWN SHOWS WHAT HAPPENS WHEN POLITICIANS DEFINE TRUTH

Former Navy SEAL and attorney Bill Brown warns that New Jersey’s proposed Islamophobia bill could discourage Americans from criticizing religious and political ideas. (Jahi Chikwendiu/The Washington Post via Getty Images)

"Islamism is a distinct geopolitical movement," he said. "It’s not just a religious faith."

Brown described the proposal as a "backdoor blasphemy law," arguing that government should protect people’s rights while allowing their religious beliefs to face public scrutiny.

PASTOR UNLEASHES ON DEARBORN AS RELIGIOUS TENSIONS ERUPT AT CITY COUNCIL MEETING: 'ENOUGH IS ENOUGH'

The measure would require officials to consider its definition when reviewing alleged violations of existing anti-discrimination laws, while also preserving First Amendment protections. (Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images)

The legislation excludes criticism of Muslim-majority countries comparable to criticism directed at other countries. Brown argued that criticism of religious and political ideology also needs protection.

Brown said his concerns are informed in part by his military service. He recalled responding to two suicide bombings in Iraq and said he remains committed to speaking out against jihadist ideology.

He also recalled studying Arabic at Rutgers after leaving the military, where Muslim American classmates helped him when he struggled with the language.

For Brown, the broader concern is whether Americans will feel free to challenge ideas they oppose.

"True diversity is diversity of thought," he said.

Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

articles.title: With Skubal signing, the New York Mets should have bought themselves the 2027 World Series title | Ian Miller
articles.excerpt:
Tomi thinks Mets fans are more loyal than Yankees fans and KFC agrees.

Cancel the 2027 Major League Baseball season. Why even bother playing the games? We don't need a World Series, just hand the tro...
articles.body_text:
Tomi thinks Mets fans are more loyal than Yankees fans and KFC agrees.

Cancel the 2027 Major League Baseball season. Why even bother playing the games? We don't need a World Series, just hand the trophy to the New York Mets right now.

Sounds a bit ridiculous, doesn't it? Except those exact phrases were repeatedly used ahead of the 2026 MLB season to describe the Los Angeles Dodgers. Because they signed Kyle Tucker and Edwin Diaz after winning the 2025 World Series over the Toronto Blue Jays.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Now though? The Dodgers are on the outside looking in, thanks to the Mets' stunning, 9-year, $450 million deal with superstar starting pitcher Tarik Skubal. Who we were told just a few months ago was going to bring about the end of baseball after being traded to those same Dodgers at the deadline.

METS, TARIK SKUBAL AGREE TO RECORD CONTRACT AS MLB LOCKOUT LOOMS OVER OFFSEASON

Los Angeles Dodgers starting pitcher Tarik Skubal works against an Atlanta Braves batter during the first inning of Game 1 of a National League Division Series baseball game Saturday, Oct. 3, 2026, in Los Angeles. (AP Photo/Mark J. Terrill)

First, some background on Skubal. He just turned 30, meaning he'll play all of 2027 in his age-30 season. He's been one of the best handful of pitchers in baseball for the past four seasons, with ERAs under 2.80 in each. His command and consistency is second to none, with walk rates from 2023–2026 of 1.57 per nine innings, 1.64, 1.52, and 1.53. Hard to be more consistent than that.

He's been worth, per Fangraphs WAR calculations, 3.3 wins above replacement in 2023 in just 15 starts, 6.0 in 2024, 6.7 in 2025, and 5.2 in 2026, despite making only 26 starts. Skubal is a two-time Cy Young Award winner, and if you made a list of pitchers you'd want taking the ball in a postseason game, he'd be at or near the top, along with Jacob Misiorowski, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Chris Sale or Paul Skenes.

NEW STATEMENTS FROM ROB MANFRED, MLBPA, GUARANTEE BASEBALL IS SHUT DOWN INDEFINITELY IN TWO WEEKS

He was widely expected to get the largest free agency contract for a pitcher ever handed out, and that's exactly what he got from Mets owner Steve Cohen and a beleaguered front office. At least three other teams, the Dodgers, Blue Jays and San Diego Padres, met with Skubal. But only New York was willing to get to a whopping $50 million per year for the remainder of his career.

Now though, it's worth evaluating what this actually means, the fan reaction, and how this impacts New York's chances of winning their first World Series since 1986.

The short version? Fans don't seem to be bothered by the fact that the Mets have now guaranteed over $1.2 billion to just two players: Skubal and Juan Soto. Yes, there's been some complaining about big markets, but there's little of the wailing and gnashing of teeth that explode when the Dodgers make an acquisition or signing. The implication here is that fans don't care when bad teams try to improve, only good teams. An interesting sentiment.

What does it actually mean for baseball, for free agency, and for the Mets? Well, there's plenty to dig into. For baseball, it once again means that money is flowing into the sport at a record pace. The Mets do not have the Dodgers' television deal that's caused such misplaced consternation among fans. They are conclusively the second team in their media market, although New York obviously is not your average market, and they ranked No. 12 out of 30 teams in attendance in 2025.

In fact, they sold 1.3 million fewer tickets than the Dodgers and 600,000 fewer than the Padres.

So how are they raking in enough money to afford $1.2 billion on two players? On top of that, they have to pay the rest of the roster while also paying tens of millions for the luxury tax, scouting, research and development and so on.

Maybe, just maybe, there's more money coming into baseball teams than they're willing to let on. That might have raised some interesting possibilities, wouldn't it?

As for what it means for free agency, again, this is why the players don't want a salary cap. Clearly, teams can afford these types of contracts. Clearly, the interest is there for a pitcher with a lengthy and recent injury history to make $50 million per year. It's not the players' problem that some owners are cheap, or some are more concerned with increasing their franchise valuations or raking in another $50 million in profits, than they are with fielding a competitive baseball team. That's on the owners to figure out. So why should players take a massive cut in both total income and potential peak income, just to make ownership richer?

But what about competitive balance? Doesn't this, as the headline suggests, guarantee the Mets a championship? Shouldn't we just cancel the season now?

MILWAUKEE BREWERS BROKE BASEBALL ON THEIR WAY TO REMARKABLY DOMINANT WORLD SERIES RUN

Tarik Skubal No. 29 of the Los Angeles Dodgers celebrates a call at home plate by Tommy Edman No. 25, not pictured, during the sixth inning against the Chicago Cubs at Wrigley Field on Aug. 4, 2026, in Chicago, Ill. (Getty Images)

Of course not. It's ridiculous to even suggest that it guarantees anything. Just as it was ridiculous to suggest that the Dodgers bought their title, or would ruin baseball by trading for Skubal in the first place. We just saw, with the Milwaukee Brewers, how postseason baseball actually works.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

The Dodgers entered October with arguably the greatest playoff rotation in modern memory. Skubal, Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow. It was better than their rotation in 2024 or 2025, and significantly better than any that the competition brought to the postseason. How'd it work out for them?

Well, all four of those pitchers started the four games of the NLCS. And the Dodgers lost all four. Brewers' Robert Gasser (who is not a Cy Young contender), was one of the best pitchers in the postseason. Despite a woeful strikeout rate and thanks to incredible luck on balls put in play, Gasser had a 0.60 ERA in the playoffs. He gave up one run in over 15 innings. Skubal gave up three in 11 innings.

Aaron Ashby was the most valuable pitcher of the playoffs, with just five hits allowed in 18 innings, only three walks, literally zero runs, and 20 strikeouts. He was making $5.5 million, compared to Skubal's upcoming $50 million salary. Drew Rasmussen also earned $5.5 million and was brilliant over 28 playoff innings, with just a 2.20 ERA. Gavin Williams was dominant too, making $822,000. Should Skubal make 30 starts in 2027, he will take home $1.67 million per start. More than double Williams' yearly salary. And Williams outpitched him in October.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

This is the problem with fans trying to say you can "buy" a title. You cannot. Because the small sample sizes of playoff baseball mean that players like Williams, Rasmussen, Ashby and Gasser can outpitch Skubal, Yamamoto or Chris Sale over a few weeks' span. It's not even remotely surprising that it happens! In fact, it happens all the time during the regular season, though nobody notices, or cares.

Gasser, who nobody outside of Brewers fans or hardcore baseball diehards had even heard of, threw the best start by a left-handed pitcher in a World Series since Sandy Koufax. Skubal's never made the World Series. That's how baseball works.

For the Mets in particular, they're still not very good! They were 74-88 in 2026, and assuming Skubal puts up another Cy Young-caliber six WAR season, and all other things remain equal, they'd be an 80-win team in 2027. That's still bad. They were bad at everything in 2026. Here's how they ranked in some important statistical categories last season:

Skubal will help some, but one player ain't fixing that mess. Even with spending as much or more than any team in baseball over the past five seasons. And over $400 million in commitments for next year. Lindor had the worst season of his career and is now 33 years old. Bichette made over $40 million to be a below-average hitter. Former top prospect Brett Baty has looked awful. A.J. Ewing was a below average hitter. Juan Soto missed time and while still outstanding, was far below his 2024 peaks. Carson Benge was the lone bright spot, but used some BABIP luck to boost his numbers.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

New York Mets third baseman Bo Bichette (19) stands on the field during a game against the Atlanta Braves during the fifth inning at Truist Park in Cumberland, Ga., on Aug. 10, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

Their rotation looks solid, but the back half is still shaky at best. And as usual, there's no depth. Devin Williams was mediocre, and Freddy Peralta and Clay Holmes are now free agents.

This is the problem fans ignore when talking about free agency; teams paying for players in their 30s are paying for the declining phase of their careers. Especially with pitchers, there's added injury risk, and the valuation of these contracts makes it, so there's little margin for error.

Even if the Mets were good, signing Skubal wouldn't guarantee anything. And that's what makes baseball so beautiful. It's unpredictable, always. New York might win 100 games, or it would be equally unsurprising if they lost 100. Skubal might win a Cy Young, or get booed off the mound in August.
