The Ohio State Buckeyes have one of the most expensive rosters in colle...
articles.body_text:
Anthony Colandrea found Quinn Clark for a 26-yard TD that extended the Nebraska Cornhuskers' lead over the Ohio State Buckeyes.

The Ohio State Buckeyes have one of the most expensive rosters in college football, but on Saturday, that didn't matter a lick.

Nebraska rode a little home cooking and some fourth quarter magic to secure one of its biggest wins in the last decade, taking down the Buckeyes 31-28.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Despite the heroics of wide receiver Jeremiah Smith, who hauled in six catches for 165 yards and two scores, Ohio State was not able to overcome the loss of quarterback Julian Sayin, losing for the third time in four games since his injury.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Jeremiah Smith No. 4 of the Ohio State Buckeyes scores against the Nebraska Cornhuskers during the first half at Memorial Stadium in Lincoln, Neb., on Nov. 21, 2026. (Getty Images)

Though it could be argued the Buckeye offense did enough to grab the W, since the Cornhuskers controlled the game to the tune of 31 points and 176 yards rushing.

Despite the relatively identical numbers in the yardage department, the Huskers ran nearly twice as many plays as the Buckeyes and had the ball for almost a full quarter longer.

Couple that with relatively mistake-free football (Nebraska was plus-two in the turnover battle), and you get what is perhaps head coach Matt Rhule's signature win in his fourth year in Lincoln.

If the Huskers can win next week in Iowa City, they will have completed the most successful season since Mike Riley won nine games in 2016.

Isaiah Mozee #22 of the Nebraska Cornhuskers celebrates a first down against the Ohio State Buckeyes during the first half at Memorial Stadium on Nov. 21, 2026, in Lincoln, Neb. (Getty Images)

For the Buckeyes, this almost certainly drives the final nail in the coffin for their CFP chances, and punctuates a season that started with so much promise before falling off the rails.

The Buckeyes were 6-1 heading into their Halloween showdown with USC, but the aforementioned injury to Sayin proved to be too much to overcome.

Ohio State can salvage what's left of their season by defeating bitter rival Michigan in next week's edition of "The Game" in Columbus.

The Maize and Blue haven't exactly been a free win for the Buckeyes since the turn of the decade, though, as the Wolverines are 4-1 in the rivalry post-COVID.

FILE - Ohio State head coach Ryan Day looks on before the College Football Playoff national championship game against Notre Dame, Jan. 20, 2025, in Atlanta. (AP Photo/Jacob Kupferman, File)

Regardless, it's sure to be a long, cold offseason in central Ohio, while a Nebraska program in purgatory has suddenly found new life.

articles.excerpt:

Bahrain’s Defence Force said its air defences interc...
articles.body_text:
Bahrain says an Iranian attack has struck a civilian industrial facility, starting a fire, in the latest escalation of the war in the Middle East.

Bahrain’s Defence Force said its air defences intercepted a number of Iranian aerial attacks late on Saturday.

In a post on X, Bahrain’s Ministry of Interior said the attack was part of “Iranian aggression”.

It said preliminary reports pointed to material damage but no injuries, and that civil defence teams were working to bring the fire under control.

The Interior Ministry did not name the facility or say where it was. Earlier, air raid sirens sounded in Bahrain, and the ministry urged residents to move to the nearest safe place without saying what the threat was.

In a statement after the attack, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it had carried out a combined missile and drone operation targeting United States military positions at the al-Riffa and Awali bases in Bahrain.

The IRGC claimed it destroyed two US Patriot air defence radars at the bases.

The attack was “in response to continued aggression and violations of the airspace of the Islamic Republic of Iran”, the statement said.

“After two US MQ-1 and MQ-9 reconnaissance and combat drones violated Iranian airspace, US military positions at the aforementioned bases were targeted in an operation by the IRGC Aerospace Force,” it added.

Earlier, Iran’s semi-official Fars news agency reported that the IRGC had attacked two military bases used by US forces at Sheikh Isa and Juffair.

However, Iran’s state news agency IRNA reported that an interceptor missile launched from the US Fifth Fleet base in Bahrain had crashed on Sitra Island and started a large fire. It cited an outlet called Bahrain News, which blamed a recurring malfunction in the Patriot air defence system.

Bahrain hosts the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet. It has been attacked repeatedly since the war began, including three drone attacks in recent days after a lull of several weeks.

Gulf Arab states have come under repeated fire from Tehran since the US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28.

Dallas Cowboys owner Jerry Jones said Friday that the team had no record of an alleged fight that resulted in a fan’s death during the team’s game against the San Francisco 49ers, adding that he believed the fan was hospitalized because he "didn’t feel good" at the game—a claim that has raised questions about what happened at AT&T Stadium.

Police say Mario Narro fell during a fight at the stadium. According to reports, he remained at the game but later complained to friends of pain. Paramedics at AT&T Stadium treated Narro before he was transported to a hospital, where he died Wednesday, his family says.

Jones addressed the death during his Nov. 20 appearance on 105.3 The Fan’s "K&C Masterpiece," saying he had only just received information about the situation.

COWBOYS OWNER JERRY JONES UPDATES TIMELINE FOR NFL'S 18-GAME SCHEDULE, FLOATS PRESEASON REDUCTION

"No record of an incident at the game, and I just got that information... so we had no record of an incident, and we'll be obviously looking into that," Jones said, when asked about the Arlington Police Department's report of a fight that allegedly occurred around kick-off time.

Jones added, "My understanding is that the individual went to the game, and didn't feel good at the game, and then left and then had been hospitalized. But we weren't aware of any incident involving a fan at the game."

Dallas Cowboys owner Jerry Jones looks on before the game against the Green Bay Packers at AT&T Stadium on Sept. 28, 2025 in Arlington, Texas. (Kevin Jairaj/Imagn Images)

Jones then pointed to the stadium’s surveillance capabilities, describing them as substantially improved from a decade or more ago. He also cited the roughly 6,000 workers on game days and said an incident escaping the team’s notice would be unusual.

"We have quite a surveillance at every aspect of our game, so it is really a rare if we didn't know of any incident... We have 6,000 workers on game day," Jones said, adding his team would "of course" send any of that footage to the police department.

Asked whether the Cowboys would provide footage to police if needed, Jones replied, "Of course."

Meanwhile, the fan’s family is asking for help bringing their loved one home.

A general view of AT&T Stadium during the NFC Wild Card game between the San Francisco 49ers and the Dallas Cowboys on Jan. 16, 2022, in Arlington, Texas. (Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

COWBOYS GREAT MICHAEL IRVIN OUTLINES FRANCHISE'S TIMELINE TO RETAIN 'AMERICA’S TEAM' STATUS

In a GoFundMe campaign titled "Bringing Mario Home to Rest," organizer Lois DeLara identified herself as Mario’s niece and said he traveled to Texas for a football game before his unexpected death.

The fundraiser seeks assistance with funeral and memorial costs, transporting his remains home and expenses incurred by family members making arrangements in Texas.

DeLara described the family’s struggle to grieve while facing unexpected financial obligations. The campaign does not provide a detailed account of the incident or a medical explanation for his death.

"You will forever be loved and missed," she wrote.

Jackson Thompson is a sports reporter for Fox News Digital covering critical political and cultural issues in sports, with an investigative lens. Jackson's reporting has been cited in federal government actions related to the enforcement of Title IX, and in legacy media outlets including The New York Times, The Los Angeles Times, The Philadelphia Inquirer, The Associated Press and ESPN.com.

articles.title: NBA Hall of Famer and Baltimore native Carmelo Anthony joins the mob in scolding Ravens' Marlon Humphrey
articles.excerpt:
Craig Carton reacts to the Baltimore Ravens deactivating star cornerback Marlon Humphrey after he claimed on his podcast that Baltimore is "best at making criminals".

NBA legend and Baltimore native ...
articles.body_text:
Craig Carton reacts to the Baltimore Ravens deactivating star cornerback Marlon Humphrey after he claimed on his podcast that Baltimore is "best at making criminals".

NBA legend and Baltimore native Carmelo Anthony loves his city. That much is obvious. But, his lengthy Instagram post scolding Ravens' cornerback Marlon Humphrey following the former first-round pick's joke that Baltimore is "best at making criminals" comes across more as virtue signaling than anything.

Anthony grew up in West Baltimore, witnessed the city's struggles firsthand, and understandably takes pride in the place that helped shape him into a basketball superstar, so being defensive of his city shouldn't be surprising. But there's a difference between defending your hometown and pretending its problems don't exist, aren't that bad, or shouldn't be the subject of any jokes, no matter the level of truth to it.

New York Knicks player Carmelo Anthony marches toward city hall in Baltimore, Md., during a demonstration over the death of Freddie Gray on April 30, 2015. Gray, 25, died from a severe spinal cord injury sustained while in police custody following his arrest for possessing a switchblade knife on April 12. (Getty Images)

WHAT IS BALTIMORE BEST AT MAKING? 'CRIMINALS,' SAYS MARLON HUMPHREY WHO THEN FEELS THE HEAT AND CHANGES TUNE

After his comments went viral, Humphrey apologized, was eventually sent home and deactivated by the team for this Sunday's game against the Carolina Panthers.

"I’ve been here my whole career," Humphrey told reporters. "I’ve spent lots of offseasons here, welcomed a son here. I’m an investor in the city, investor in various parts of the state."

Apparently, those comments, his past work, and apology weren't enough for Anthony.

"I’ve been sitting with this one for a couple of days, because Baltimore isn’t a talking point to me. It’s my blood," Anthony wrote on his Instagram post. "I saw what this city can take from you. I lost friends to the streets, and I watched people I loved get swallowed by a system that was built to swallow them. I know the reputation. I’ve heard every joke and every headline my whole life."

But Anthony's own words also reveal the problem with his criticism.

BALTIMORE DC ANTHONY WEAVER ADDRESSES MARLON HUMPHREY 1-GAME BANISHMENT OVER CITY CRIME REMARKS

He acknowledges losing friends to the streets, watching loved ones suffer, and witnessing the consequences of Baltimore's troubled environment. Yet he's upset that Humphrey dared to characterize the city as a place where criminality is a serious problem?

This was a genuinely heartfelt statement from Anthony, who has clearly experienced the uglier side of Baltimore long before becoming a multimillionaire NBA superstar, but it also proves Humphrey's point that criminality has been an issue for the city.

Also, we have to remember this whole post is in response to a side comment, light-hearted joke, rooted in the truth. That's all. Humphrey didn't call all Blacks criminals. He never said that nothing is being done to fix clear problems with crime. He never devalued the hurt and pain Anthony and others have gone through.

Marlon Humphrey of the Baltimore Ravens warms up on the field before a game against the Buffalo Bills at Highmark Stadium on Nov. 1, 2026, in Orchard Park, N.Y. (Getty Images)

According to Security.org's analysis of FBI crime data for 2025, Baltimore ranked fifth in violent crime per capita and sixth in overall reported crime per capita among America's 50 largest cities.

Its violent crime rate was approximately 1,347 offenses per 100,000 residents.

That's not a flattering statistic, but ignoring it doesn't make Baltimore's residents any safer.

And while Baltimore has made measurable progress reducing homicides in recent years, improvement doesn't erase the fact that residents continue to face disproportionately high levels of violent crime. Going along with the liberal narrative that Baltimore is now safe and shouldn't be subject to scrutiny because there's been a decrease in crime, is just a stupid way to deflect and gaslight those who highlight that crime is still clearly an issue in the city.

So why is Humphrey being treated as though he's committed some unforgivable offense for speaking negatively about the very problems Anthony acknowledges experiencing?

Anthony continued saying, "Marlon, I see the apology. I’ll take it, man to man. But Baltimore has been apologized to its whole life. Apologies don’t build anything. Presence does… You don’t get to rep Baltimore on Sundays and talk about it like an outsider on Wednesday."

Anthony is certainly entitled to defend Baltimore's reputation and advocate for its residents, but demanding that Humphrey demonstrate his commitment to the community, after Humphrey specifically cited his investments and personal ties to the city, seems to be more about policing the cornerback's words than addressing the substance of what he said.

Anthony's post, and others like it, makes it seem like Humphrey is being treated as a traitor to his race for making a truthful joke.

Interestingly, Anthony's argument in his Instagram post becomes even more questionable when you examine the people he celebrates as examples of Baltimore's success.

Carmelo Anthony and the Living Classrooms Foundation host the grand opening of the Carmelo Anthony Youth Development Center in Baltimore, Md., on Dec. 14, 2006. (NBAE via Getty Images)

FBI REPORTS LARGEST DROP IN VIOLENT CRIME AND MURDER SINCE 1937 AS HOMICIDES FALL MORE THAN 18%

Anthony also invoked Baltimore-born boxing star Gervonta "Tank" Davis as an example of the talent and success that can emerge from the city.

There's no disputing Davis' accomplishments inside the boxing ring, but outside of the ring, he's committed to the very criminality Humphrey was joking about.

Davis has faced multiple criminal charges and legal controversies throughout his professional career, including domestic violence allegations and a hit-and-run case.

In 2023, Davis was sentenced to probation, home detention and community service after pleading guilty to charges connected to a 2020 hit-and-run crash in Baltimore that injured four people. He subsequently served jail time after violating the terms of his sentence.

That doesn't erase Davis' boxing accomplishments, nor does it mean he cannot serve as an inspiration to young athletes through his athletic ability and hard work, but glamorizing a boxer with a documented criminal history, while chastising Humphrey for discussing Baltimore's crime problem is an awkward choice, to say the least.

Davis' story demonstrates both the extraordinary athletic talent and criminal behavior that Baltimore can produce, which again proves Humphrey's point.

Gervonta "Tank" Davis speaks at news conference about his exhibition match with Jake Paul at Kaseya Center on Sept. 23, 2025 in Miami, Florida. (Leonardo Fernandez/Getty Images)

And while we're discussing uncomfortable truths, Anthony isn't exactly unfamiliar with controversy involving criminal conduct.

In 2004, Anthony was cited on a marijuana possession charge after marijuana was discovered in a backpack associated with him. The charge was later dropped.

That same year, Anthony appeared in the infamous Baltimore-based Stop Snitchin' video, which became associated with an anti-cooperation message toward law enforcement. That controversy was especially troubling because discouraging witnesses from cooperating with police can make it more difficult to prosecute violent offenders and protect communities suffering from crime.

Anthony subsequently distanced himself from the video and its message.

In April 2015, the then-New York Knicks star marched alongside hundreds of protesters through the streets of Baltimore following the death of Freddie Gray, who suffered a fatal spinal injury while in police custody. A year later, he reflected on his complicated relationship with Baltimore police, admitting he used to run from officers and deliberately provoke them as a kid. While acknowledging he had positive relationships with some officers, Anthony declared, "There are good police, and there are f—ed up police. That's the way it is."

To be clear, appearing in that video is not the same as personally threatening witnesses, and a dismissed criminal charge is not proof of guilt, but the episode is relevant when Anthony positions himself as an authority on how Baltimore's crime problem should be discussed.

A city cannot seriously confront violent crime while treating criticism of its reputation as a greater offense than the conditions that created that reputation.

Humphrey's comments are being treated more harshly than the actions of criminals who have wreaked havoc across the city over the years.

Members of Team USA, including LeBron James, Jason Kidd and Kobe Bryant, keep Carmelo Anthony from getting into a scuffle with an Argentina player. (Denver Post via Getty Images)

Humphrey's comments didn't sit well with his Ravens teammates, either.

"I think he was trying to say it in a joking manner. But it’s not a joking matter. That’s not cool. I think he knows that," veteran defensive tackle Calais Campbell said Thursday.

Head coach Jesse Minter deactivated Humphrey for Baltimore's upcoming game against the Carolina Panthers, sending him home for the week.

"When you say something like that, it’s, you know, it’s not a reflection of our team and our organization and how we want to operate," Minter told reporters Thursday.

Anthony, meanwhile, concluded his statement with a declaration that "Baltimore doesn’t make criminals."

Of course, cities don't literally manufacture criminals. Individuals make choices, and millions of law-abiding Americans live in communities struggling with crime, but pretending Baltimore's longstanding struggles with violent crime are merely an unfair stereotype does a disservice to the people living with those consequences.

Anthony's love for his hometown seems sincere. His emotional attachment to the city is understandable, and his desire to see Baltimore portrayed as more than its worst headlines is understandable, but his public lecture of Humphrey risks becoming precisely the kind of performative virtue signaling that substitutes celebrity outrage for meaningful discussion.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Baltimore deserves investment, opportunity, accountability, effective and supported policing, safer neighborhoods, and politicians who actually want to see the problem resolved.

A split image of police responding to riot and Baltimore State Attorney Ivan Bates (Getty Images, Fox News Digital)

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

What Baltimore doesn't need is another famous athlete demanding apologies because someone said something unflattering about a city in which crime statistics remain deeply troubling.

STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW!

Loving Baltimore shouldn't mean refusing to acknowledge what's wrong with Baltimore.

And perhaps the more important question isn't whether Humphrey hurt the city's feelings. It's whether the outrage directed at him is doing anything to help the residents who have to live with the violence Anthony himself remembers so vividly.

Carmelo, we appreciate your heart for your city, but this fell flat.

Jon is a writer and content creator for OutKick

articles.title: Zelenskyy says Russia strikes hometown, criticizes Putin-Trump meeting
articles.excerpt: Steve Yates defends President Donald Trump's meetings with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping following criticism. Yates outlines the strategic value of maintaining communication lines between the three gl...
articles.body_text:
Steve Yates defends President Donald Trump's meetings with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping following criticism. Yates outlines the strategic value of maintaining communication lines between the three global leaders, arguing that dialogue is essential to national security. The discussion follows comments from Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who defended the historic summit.

A Russian strike on Volodymyr Zelenskyy's hometown, Kryvyi Rih, killed two people and wounded 58 others, the Ukrainian leader said Saturday.

A 7-year-old boy and a 20-year-old woman were killed in the attack Friday night in the central Ukraine town, according to Oleksandr Vilkul, the head of the city administration.

Zelenkskyy said in a social media post the woman was an emergency medical worker and the boy was named Tykhon.

PUTIN LAUNCHES UKRAINE BARRAGE HOURS AFTER TRUMP MEETING AMID ALLEGED RUSSIAN MISSILE BREACH OF NATO AIRSPACE

"He was born in 2019, and, sadly, most of his life was lived during a war like this. And the Russians took his life with their strike. My condolences to their families and loved ones," Zelenkskyy said.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky speaks at a press conference following a phone conversation with U.S. President Donald Trump in Kyiv, Ukraine, on May 19, 2025. The two leaders discussed bilateral relations and regional developments. (Photo by Danylo Antoniuk/Anadolu via Getty Images) (Danylo Antoniuk/Anadolu via Getty Images)

On top of the civilian deaths and injuries, the strike sparked four fires and damaged roughly 25 apartment buildings, along with a hospital, schools, an industrial facility, businesses and vehicles.

RUSSIA'S PUTIN VOWS A RESPONSE 'FAR MORE PAINFUL' AFTER UKRAINE ATTACKS PRIZED BRIDGE IN CRIMEA

Zelenkskyy claimed that the Russian strike hit an area of the city with no military targets.

"The strike hit an ordinary civilian area of the city – there are no military facilities nearby, and there never have been," he wrote, adding, "Russia is waging war against life, and there can be NO justification for this."

TRUMP WILL FACE REPORTERS AFTER HISTORIC XI-PUTIN TALKS AS WAR QUESTIONS LINGER

The Ukrainian leader later commented on President Donald Trump's recent trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

President Donald Trump greets Russian President Vladimir Putin as he arrives at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson in Anchorage, Alaska on Aug. 15. Trump has been briefed on a peace plan for ending the Russia-Ukraine war. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

"Putin didn't get his 'Yalta 2,'" Zelenskyy wrote, referring to the famed 1945 Yalta Conference between former U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill, and Soviet Premier Joseph Stalin.

TRUMP’S PROPOSED RUSSIA DEAL RAISES NATO ALARM AS EX-COMMANDER WARNS PUTIN SEEKS INFLUENCE OVER EUROPE

"As far as I understand, he recently commented: 'What's wrong with Yalta? Those were the victories over Nazism, over fascism, and so on, that were sealed there.' First of all, indeed, this was no Yalta. Did Putin want a real Yalta? Yes. In the sense of carving up the world and changing borders. China didn't let itself be drawn into it. I don't know what happened between the United States and Russia in their bilateral, but Ukraine wasn't discussed. Nothing came out publicly. So the redrawing of borders didn't happen," Zelenskyy wrote.

"If there really was an intention to reaffirm the victory over fascism now, then the participants at this summit would have to be the United States, Europe, and Ukraine. Definitely not Russia. I think this trilateral summit turned out very badly for Russia. Not only did Putin fail to get the results he wanted, but we also saw his reaction.

"And, unfortunately, we saw that reaction in Ukraine. There was a massive attack that night – 111 missiles. If Putin wanted to remind the world once again who he is, there was no need – we haven't forgotten that he's a terrorist and a killer," his X post continued.

UKRAINE HITS PUTIN'S PRIZED BRIDGE IN RECORD DRONE BLITZ AS KREMLIN TELLS LAWMAKERS TO PREPARE FOR 'VICTORY'

US President Donald Trump shakes hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China’s President Xi Jinping stands beside, before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, southern China, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa/Pool via Reuters)

The strike on Zelenskyy's hometown is far from uncommon, with periodic Russian attacks targeting the industrial steel town dozens of times since the start of the war in 2022.

The incident also occurred as a Russian ship was struck by drones on Saturday, causing it to catch fire in the Gulf of Finland.

The Russian-flagged Sparta II was struck by a drone shortly before 9 a.m. local time, according to Finnish Coast Guard Commander Mikko Simola.

The damaged Russian cargo ship Sparta II, in a location given as the Gulf of Finland, November 21, 2026. (FINNISH BORDER GUARD/Handout via REUTERS)

"Generally it should be noted that it is known that this Sparta II vessel has been used for transports for the Russian state, including the armed forces," Simola said.

As a result of its damage, the craft entered Finnish territorial waters. Simola also noted that Finland believed a Russian helicopter crossed Finland's sovereign borders as well.

Finnish officials believe that Ukraine was behind the attack.

"It is likely that Ukraine ... is behind (the attack)," Finnish armed forces spokesperson Aki-Mauri Huhtinen said.

James Cirrone is a writer on the Breaking/Trending News team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to james.cirrone@fox.com.

articles.title: JONATHAN TURLEY: Baltimore Raven learns truth is no defense in the NFL
articles.excerpt:
Craig Carton reacts to the Baltimore Ravens deactivating star cornerback Marlon Humphrey after he claimed on his podcast that Baltimore is "best at making criminals".

Baltimore Ravens cornerback Marl...
articles.body_text:
Craig Carton reacts to the Baltimore Ravens deactivating star cornerback Marlon Humphrey after he claimed on his podcast that Baltimore is "best at making criminals".

Baltimore Ravens cornerback Marlon Humphrey will not be playing this Sunday against the Carolina Panthers. He is not on the IL list, but on the FS list. Humphrey was flagged for free speech; uttering four words about the crime problem in Baltimore. The cornerback quipped that the city is "best at making criminals." While Ravens players were allowed to protest the United States at a London game, a player is not allowed to make a political comment on his personal podcast about the crime epidemic in his city. The day Humphrey was suspended, a 30-year-old woman was shot and killed near the M&T Bank Stadium. However, players would be wise not to acknowledge the crime. However, they could presumably condemn the country.

Marlon Humphrey #44 of the Baltimore Ravens looks on before the game against the Jacksonville Jaguars at M&T Bank Stadium on Nov. 5, 2026, in Baltimore, Md. (Getty Images)

Head Coach Jesse Minter announced that Humphrey had been suspended after the 10-year veteran spoke about crime in the city on his podcast, The Marlon Humphrey Show. He was asked what Baltimore is best at making. Notably, Humphrey first offered The Star-Spangled Banner and National Bohemian beer. He then added as a joke that the city is also "best at making criminals."

Crime in Baltimore makes the city one of the most dangerous cities in the United States. Despite a drop in crime levels, it remains in the top five cities for violent crime.

WOMAN KILLED NEAR RAVENS STADIUM SAME DAY MARLON HUMPHREY SENT HOME FOR JOKE ABOUT BALTIMORE CRIMINALITY

Notably, Humphrey's comment was not only tongue-in-cheek, but was not racist or prejudiced toward any group. It was not encouraging violence or other bad conduct. On the contrary, it implied criticism of those who continue to endanger others in the city.

Yet, Minter went public with the virtue-signaling suspension.

WIFE OF RAVENS OFFENSIVE LINEMAN APOLOGIZES MULTIPLE TIMES AFTER BACKLASH FOR CALLING BALTIMORE 'SCARY'

One can only wonder whether the suspension would have happened if the Ravens were not on a dismal five-game losing streak, ranked fourth in the AFC North, and 11th in the AFC playoff rankings.

We have previously discussed how players are not entitled to protest on the field in relation to the kneeling demonstrations. The same rule applies to other employees from Starbucks to Whole Foods. Employers are allowed to limit political expression and protests in the workplace.

COLIN KAEPERNICK IS RIGHT ABOUT THE NFL'S 'PERFORMATIVE' RACISM CAMPAIGN — BUT HE'S ALSO A HYPOCRITE

Companies also may contractually subject employees to discipline for public comments or actions that bring controversy or disrepute to the company.

However, that does not make this right. I was critical of kneeling demonstrations during games, but I fully supported players' right to voice their views outside the game.

Baltimore Ravens coach Jesse Minter attends the NFL Scouting Combine at the Indiana Convention Center in Indianapolis, Ind., on Feb. 24, 2026. (Kirby Lee/Imagn Images)

NFL RESTARTS SOCIAL JUSTICE MESSAGING WHILE BATTLING DOMESTIC ABUSE, DRUNK DRIVING AND PROSTITUTION ARRESTS

The NFL is notorious for hypocrisy and inconsistency in punishing free speech. The Humphrey controversy is reminiscent of the Commanders hammering a coach for expressing a different view of January 6.

The NFL has spent years virtue-signaling with statements on helmets and in the end zones. However, when players or coaches express opposing views, they are silenced or suspended.

NFL TOLD AZEEZ AL-SHAAIR HE'D BE PULLED FROM TEXANS GAME OVER PRO-PALESTINIAN EYEBLACK MESSAGE

The NBA is little better. LeBron James can show disrespect to the National Anthem, but Jaden Ivy was fired for expressing his opposition to Pride Month. Players are expected to engage in mandatory speech while remaining silent on their own views.

Nevertheless, Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott rejected an apology by Humphrey: "While we acknowledge Marlon’s apology, a verbal apology is not enough." He added that Baltimore is "a city full of young Black boys who look to the Ravens as a beacon of light in their lives."

Baltimore Police respond to the scene of a shooting, Tuesday, March 10, 2026, in Baltimore. (KT Kanazawich/AP Photo)

TEXANS' AZEEZ AL-SHAAIR TO BE FINED ONCE AGAIN BY NFL FOR WEARING PRO-PALESTINIAN PERSONAL MESSAGE ON EYEBLACK

That is a curious objection, since Humphrey was highlighting the failure of Scott to make the city safe to protect those lives, given its top-five ranking for criminal violence.

The message is clear. Players are expected to wear and repeat approved views of the team. For the NFL, speech codes reflect whatever values are popular or approved by NFL commissioner Roger Goodell and team owners.

CARDINALS BACKUP CORNERBACK FINED BY NFL FOR WRITING 'GLORY BE 2 GOD' ON HIS EYEBLACK

Now players are on notice that they cannot comment on blue cities being breeding grounds for crime. It is a curious sensitivity for a sport that often sounds like a gangbanger's delight from shotgun and pistol formations.

The NFL and teams should get out of the speech regulation business and focus on football. While they are private companies and not directly subject to First Amendment limits, that does not mean that there are no free speech values at issue in these controversies.

JONATHAN TURLEY: FRANCE'S FREE SPEECH CRACKDOWN SHOWS WHAT HAPPENS WHEN POLITICIANS DEFINE TRUTH

The First Amendment is not the full or exclusive embodiment of free speech. It addresses just one of the dangers to free speech posed by government regulation. Many of us view free speech as a human right. Corporate censorship of social media clearly impacts free speech, and replacing Big Brother with a cadre of Little Brothers actually allows for far greater control of free expression.

Humphrey has now issued the perfunctory apology and is publicly covering himself with sackcloth and ashes. While Baltimore can no longer be called "best at making criminals," the NFL certainly remains the best in coercing silence.

It is fitting that the team was named in reference to Edgar Allan Poe’s poem "The Raven." Any effort by a player to express himself freely in Baltimore will be met by the same answer from Humphrey's attempt at free speech: "Quoth the Raven[s], ‘Nevermore.’"

Jonathan Turley is a Fox News Media contributor and the Shapiro Professor of Public Interest Law at George Washington University.

He is the author of the new book "Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution" (Simon & Schuster, Feb 3, 2026), on the 250th anniversary of the American Revolution.on the 250th anniversary of the American Revolution.

He is a nationally recognized legal scholar who has written extensively in areas ranging from constitutional law to legal history to the Supreme Court. He has written over three dozen academic articles that have appeared in a variety of leading law journals.

Professor Turley also served as counsel in some of the most notable cases in the last two decades including the representation of whistleblowers, military personnel, former cabinet members, judges, members of Congress, and a wide range of other clients.

Professor Turley testified more than 50 times before the House and Senate on constitutional and statutory issues, including the Senate confirmation hearings of cabinet members and jurists such as Justice Neil Gorsuch. He also appeared as an expert witness in both the impeachment hearings of President Bill Clinton and Donald Trump.

Professor Turley received his B.A. at the University of Chicago and his J.D. at Northwestern. In 2008, he was given an honorary Doctorate of Law from John Marshall Law School for his contributions to civil liberties and the public interest.

articles.title: Vance stops short of endorsing Trump’s claim that Iran was close to nuclear weapon
articles.excerpt:
US vice-president says it’s not his place to second-guess the president, but refrains from endorsing Trump’s claim

At a White House news conference on Friday, JD Vance stopped short of endorsing Dona...
articles.body_text:
US vice-president says it’s not his place to second-guess the president, but refrains from endorsing Trump’s claim

At a White House news conference on Friday, JD Vance stopped short of endorsing Donald Trump’s claim that Iran was so close to obtaining a nuclear weapon in February that it was essential for the US to go to war with the Islamic republic.

In the White House briefing room, Trump was asked about reporting this week that he was unhappy with the US vice-president’s statement blaming Republican losses in the midterm elections on the Iran war.

“I didn’t say I was unhappy with it,” Trump said. “I thought the statement was fine, except I would have had one other thing, that if it were asked, I would have said that: ‘Would you do it again?’ And absolutely, the answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”

However, Trump’s claim that Iran was so close to developing a nuclear weapon this year that it was necessary to go to war, which he has made dozens of times in the past nine months, is undermined by public evidence and contradicts his own previous statements on US strikes against Iranian facilities in 2025.

At a campaign rally in Alaska last month, Trump insisted that he had to join Israel in attacking Iran in February because, “they were two weeks away from having a nuclear weapon”.

That claim appears at odds with what his then director of national intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, testified to Congress on 25 March 2025, two months into Trump’s second term: that US intelligence agencies reported that Iran had not tried to make a nuclear weapon for more than two decades. The US intelligence community, Gabbard said, “continues to assess Iran is not building a nuclear weapon and supreme leader Khamenei has not authorized the nuclear weapons program he suspended in 2003”.

Despite that assessment, three months later, on 21 June 2025, Trump ordered the US bombing of Iran’s nuclear enrichment facilities. The strikes, Trump told the public that night, “were a spectacular military success. Iran’s key nuclear enrichment facilities have been completely and totally obliterated.”

Eight months after that, however, when Trump announced the start of a full-scale war on Iran early on 28 February 2026, he said in a video statement from Mar-a-Lago the war was necessary to “ensure that Iran does not obtain a nuclear weapon”.

The morning after this month’s midterm elections, Vance said in a statement posted on social media: “The reason we lost is the war.”

“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so,” he added. “Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost.”

In the White House briefing room on Friday, after Trump said that Vance should have said the war was necessary, a reporter asked the vice-president whether he would argue that the war in Iran was worth it.

In his response, Vance said it was not his place to second-guess the president, but refrained from actually endorsing Trump’s claim that the war was essential to stop Iran from creating a nuclear weapon.

“Look, what I’ve said is the goal of keeping Iran from getting a nuclear weapon is absolutely what we need to be doing. It’s the biggest state sponsor of terrorism. If they had a nuclear weapon, they would use it as leverage or, God forbid, they would attack and kill thousands, hundreds of thousands, of innocent people,” Vance said. “I think the president is the one who makes the decision, and the president has said he would do it again.”

“My view is that my goal is, and my job is, to support the president of the United States,” the vice-president said.

The vice president’s office did not respond to a request to comment.

The strikes hit the central Ukrainian c...
articles.body_text:
A Russian attack on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s hometown of Kryvyi Rih has killed two people and wounded 60 others, according to local officials.

The strikes hit the central Ukrainian city on Friday night, killing a seven-year-old boy and a 20-year-old woman, while six children were among the injured.

About 25 apartment buildings, a hospital, schools and businesses were damaged, according to Oleksandr Vilkul, the head of Kryvyi Rih’s city administration.

Vilkul said on Saturday that Russian forces launched further missiles after emergency workers arrived, hitting rescuers, medical personnel and utility crews.

Footage released by Ukraine’s emergency services appeared to show additional strikes during the rescue operation.

Russian attacks elsewhere in Ukraine killed two people in the southern Zaporizhia region, according to its governor.

Russian authorities also reported six deaths, including a child, from a Ukrainian attack on a residential area in Russian-controlled Luhansk, an eastern Ukrainian region.

The violence followed a separate incident on Friday in which two Russian missiles and a suspected drone landed in southeastern Poland, a member of NATO, the military alliance linking the United States, Canada and European countries.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk described the incident on Friday as a deliberate provocation, questioning its timing alongside military exercises involving European countries preparing for a possible post-war security mission in Ukraine.

NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte condemned the airspace violation on Saturday and pledged that the alliance would defend Polish territory.

The incidents have unfolded as US President Donald Trump seeks progress in negotiations with Moscow and Kyiv.

Trump said on Friday, following talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in China, that the Russian leader wanted to end the war diplomatically.

Zelenskyy, however, told reporters in Kyiv on Saturday that he remained less convinced than Washington that Putin was prepared to compromise.

Moscow continues to demand Ukrainian withdrawal from the entire eastern Donbas region, which Kyiv refuses to surrender.

Zelenskyy also reaffirmed Ukraine’s ambition to join NATO, while Washington has discussed offering Kyiv security guarantees resembling the alliance’s collective-defence commitments.

Such guarantees remain under discussion as negotiations continue over how to end the war and protect Ukraine from future attacks.

articles.title: Could Iran reverse its stated policy of a civil-only nuclear programme?
articles.excerpt: Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said the country’s stockpile of enriched uranium will be used according to its needs, “however they are defined”, as he spoke about possible changes to Iran’...
articles.body_text:
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said the country’s stockpile of enriched uranium will be used according to its needs, “however they are defined”, as he spoke about possible changes to Iran’s longstanding nuclear doctrine.

Araghchi’s comments during an interview with Iranian media on Saturday have increased speculation that Iran may be moving away from its policy of limiting its nuclear programme to civilian purposes amid its conflict with the United States.

The future of Iran’s nuclear programme has become a major sticking point in efforts to end the war, with Washington insisting that it must have guarantees that Iran will never develop a nuclear weapon before it will agree to a full ceasefire.

So, is Iran’s nuclear policy changing, and what could that mean for the conflict?

Iran has consistently maintained that its nuclear programme is for peaceful purposes only, such as for electricity generation, medical research and agriculture.

This policy has been underlined by a decades-old religious decree, or fatwa, issued by the late Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, banning the development of nuclear weapons.

However, Iran has also insisted it has the right to enrich uranium for these purposes under the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), which it joined in 1970. It has called this right “non-negotiable”.

In an interview with Iran’s state-run IRNA news agency on Saturday, Araghchi reiterated that Iran’s stockpile of enriched material would remain inside the country.

The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) estimated in 2025 – before Israel launched strikes on Iran in June that year – that Iran had about 440 kilogrammes (970 pounds) of uranium enriched to about 60 percent. This is short of the 90 percent required for making nuclear weapons, but is the level at which it becomes much quicker to reach 90 percent. It is also far beyond the roughly 3 percent needed for power generation.

This material, Araghchi said during his interview, would “be used according to our needs however those needs are defined”.

Araghchi also made reference to an ongoing debate among lawmakers and officials in Iran about altering its nuclear doctrine, and said people on both sides of that debate have “strong arguments”.

“This is a major strategic debate, and there is nothing wrong with examining it seriously because it directly concerns national interests and security,” Araghchi said, adding that those in favour of reform argue Iran’s current approach of no nuclear weapons has “failed to protect” the country’s nuclear facilities, which have come under attack from US and Israeli forces both last year and this year.

However, Araghchi acknowledged that any official change to the policy would have “far-reaching consequences”.

“For now, our doctrine has not changed, and our official position remains the same,” he said.

Other Iranian officials have also spoken about a potential review of the country’s nuclear doctrine. Earlier this month, security chief Mohsen Rezaei said “there is a discussion on whether we want to continue to follow the previous nuclear doctrine in the event of a new war breaking out”, though he also stressed that Tehran has not yet made any change.

On November 12, Iran’s Assembly of Experts, the body that appoints the supreme leader, said reviewing “the country’s defence doctrine and establishing the necessary deterrence have become unavoidable necessities”.

Ali Fathollah-Nejad, a German-Iranian political scientist who directs the Center for Middle East and Global Order (CMEG), told Al Jazeera the move by the Assembly of Experts “appears to mark the first time a governing institution has endorsed this position”.

Besides being a signatory to the NPT in 1970, Iran also initially complied with a nuclear agreement it struck with the US and other global powers in 2015 – the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), which required it to limit uranium enrichment to very low levels and undergo inspections.

But after Washington pulled out of the deal in 2018 under the first administration of US President Donald Trump, Tehran eventually went back to intensifying its nuclear programme and abandoned restrictions imposed by the deal.

In June 2025, the IAEA’s board of governors declared Iran was no longer complying with its commitment to international nuclear safeguards. Tehran rejected that report and accused the IAEA of giving a pretext for US and Israeli attacks targeting Iranian nuclear facilities, including Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan, just days later during the 12-day war.

In March of this year, IAEA chief Rafael Grossi said at least 200kg (440lbs) of Iran’s enriched material was believed to have survived the US-Israeli attacks and was likely buried underground in or near the Isfahan nuclear facility site.

Grossi has since said the agency cannot verify the amount or location of Iran’s enriched material due to a lack of access.

The IAEA has called Iran’s enrichment level “a matter of serious concern”, while the US has pointed to it as evidence that Iran is pursuing nuclear weapons despite its official policy.

“If you don’t want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60 percent enriched fuel?” US Vice President JD Vance said in an interview with the Reuters news agency last month. “And if you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don’t build highly enriched fuel. That’s a very basic threshold issue.”

President Trump has repeatedly stated that Iran must never be allowed to develop a nuclear weapon.

Officials in Israel, which is widely believed to have its own undeclared nuclear weapons, have also long accused Iran of pursuing nuclear weapons.

“The Iranian regime, which seeks to destroy Israel, is once again working to revive its nuclear programme,” said Israel’s now-caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in an address last week. “We must remove this existential threat once and for all.”

That remains to be seen, but it is “within the realm of possibility”, Rouzbeh Parsi, an Iran analyst and affiliated researcher at Lund University’s Department of History and Human Rights Studies, told Al Jazeera.

He said the US-Israeli war launched against Iran in February this year “has significantly changed all the calculations in Tehran”, with more open discussion about whether to renew the late ayatollah’s ban on nuclear weapons now taking place.

“What used to be a fringe opinion, leaving the NPT and potentially going for a nuclear weapon, is now something that’s within the realm of possibility – even though all the major players are still warning against it,” said Parsi. “It’s not a decision but an indication that deterrence is being rethought in light of the war.”

Simon Mabon, a professor of international politics at Lancaster University, told Al Jazeera that a “broadly rational defensive reason” for potentially shifting Iran’s nuclear policy is emerging within the country, though adding that such a shift would be legally and ethically problematic.

“If you look at the sort of traditional nuclear logic, it says that nuclear weapons play a very strong defensive role in deterring the actions of another state,” Mabon told Al Jazeera. “That would be very sound logic for the Iranians in light of what’s happened.”

“This, of course, is something that’s deeply problematic,” said Mabon. “It goes against the terms of the NPT, it goes against the spirit of the NPT, so it would necessitate withdrawal from that.”

CMEG director Fathollah-Nejad said that there are serious divisions within Iran’s government over the direction of its nuclear programme.

Hardline lawmakers and religious leaders view Iran’s nuclear and missile assets as “indispensable” to “regime security and deterrence”, while a separate camp that includes former Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif argues against the development of nuclear arms, saying it would “almost inevitably” trigger further attacks by the US and Israel, said Fathollah-Nejad.

For now, he added, Iran “plays with the ambiguity” of its nuclear policy.

Fathollah-Nejad said a shift in Iran’s nuclear doctrine would directly counter the US’s “single most important goal” in the conflict: to secure nuclear concessions from Tehran.

The US has insisted Iran must make nuclear commitments at the outset of any negotiations, while Iran wants its own seven stated conditions met, including lifting the blockade, restoring access to its frozen assets and ending hostilities on all fronts, before even beginning discussions about its nuclear programme.

Mabon said a change in Iran’s nuclear policy “would have a dramatic impact on how the Americans and the Israelis read the next phase of this conflict”, with the Israelis likely believing it necessitates a “return to violence”.

“That’s where some of the other dangers start to come in,” Mabon added. “The shift in Iran’s doctrine, even if it’s meant intentionally as a defensive shift, can easily be read in offensive terms.”

“I think it’s a very, very dangerous moment,” he said.

articles.title: Tommy Lee Jones says ‘God loved me’ by putting him in Texas as he opens up about life on his 6,000-acre ranch
articles.excerpt:
Jones moved back to Texas in the early 2000s. (Rick Kern/Getty Images)

Tommy Lee Jones is discussing his decision to live on a ranch in his Texas hometown and one of his hobbies that has carried over...
articles.body_text:
Jones moved back to Texas in the early 2000s. (Rick Kern/Getty Images)

Tommy Lee Jones is discussing his decision to live on a ranch in his Texas hometown and one of his hobbies that has carried over since the '70s.

During a recent interview with The New York Times, the 80-year-old actor shared how he decided to move back to San Saba, Texas in the early 2000s, saying, "I knew that God loved me, because he put me on the ground in Texas."

"There came a time when I became aware that I could live anywhere I wanted to," Jones said. "So, in my wisdom, I went home."

The actor now lives on a 6,000-acre ranch in a two-story home originally built in 1856, and has turned it into the home he always wanted, noting he wanted to live somewhere that didn't have "any fences around the house."

Jones moved back to Texas in the early 2000s. (Rick Kern/Getty Images)

ANTONIO BANDERAS SAYS HE ALWAYS KNEW LOS ANGELES WASN'T WHERE HE BELONGED

When speaking to the outlet, the "No Country for Old Men" star shared that living on the ranch also allowed him to enjoy playing polo. The actor grew up riding horses and began playing polo in the 1970s.

Since moving onto his ranch, Jones has built two polo fields on the property, which now also holds 25 horses, with the actor and his wife, Dawn Laurel-Jones, hosting many polo events throughout the year.

Jones and Dawn Laurel-Jones have been married for 25 years. (Axelle/Bauer-Griffin/FilmMagic)

Although Jones doesn't compete anymore, his wife continues to participate in competitions.

"She’s one of the better female polo players in the United States," Jones said of his wife.

Jones was an avid polo player and now has two polo fields on his ranch. (Chris Weeks/Getty Images)

Jones began playing polo in the 1970s and grew up riding horses. (Chris Weeks/Liaison)

Jones started his acting career in the 1970s, making a name for himself as a cast member on the soap opera "One Life to Live," and appeared in many acclaimed television projects, winning an Emmy Award in 1983 for his work on "The Executioner's Song."

He cemented his status as a leading man and Hollywood heavyweight in the 1990s, earning his first of four Academy Award nominations in 1992 for his role in "JFK." He would go on to win the award for best supporting actor in 1994 for his work in "The Fugitive."

Jones won an Academy Award for his supporting role in "The Fugitive" in 1994. (Ron Galella/Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Despite his prolific acting career, Jones told Esquire in November that he isn't very concerned with the "legacy" he is leaving behind.

"I don’t have long-term thinking, and I don’t even think in a term like legacy," he said. "I think more like a dog. I’m absorbed with what’s in front of me. I might run off and chase a squirrel."

Jones is not concerned with his legacy. (Phillip Faraone/Getty Images)

He is currently starring in the FX show, "The Lowdown," alongside Ethan Hawke, Betty Gilpin and Jeanne Tripplehorn.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

The actor portrays Ethan Hawke's dad, Lee Raybon Sr., who goes by Frog and has recently returned to his son's life following a period of separation.

Jones is currently starring in the second season of "The Lowdown" with Ethan Hawke. (Rick Kern/Getty Images)

"We learn that this character is dying," he said. "That slowly begins to dawn on us, and we see that he’s trying to somehow reconcile life with his son and get to know his granddaughter. But that quest in this character is not advertised. It’s discovered as we watch things unfold in an often amusing way, and always original. That was appealing. I mean, I think that’s the way it works."

Earlier this year, the actor's daughter, Victoria Jones, was found dead in a San Francisco hotel room on Jan. 1. The Office of the Chief Medical Examiner confirmed to Fox News Digital in February that she died because of "toxic effects of cocaine," and that her death was ruled an "accident."

After news of Victoria's sudden death broke, Tommy Lee broke his silence in a statement shared with Fox News Digital.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"We appreciate all of the kind words, thoughts, and prayers. Please respect our privacy during this difficult time. Thank you," the statement, signed by "The Family of Victoria Kafka Jones," said.

Jones' daughter Victoria died earlier this year in January. (Stephane Cardinale - Corbis)

In addition to Victoria, Jones is also a father to his son Austin, whom he shares with his ex-wife, Kimberlea Cloughley.

Lori A. Bashian is an entertainment news writer at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Trump praises 'reasonable guy' Hakeem Jeffries while touting 'ultimate' veto power over Democrats
articles.excerpt:
President Donald Trump joins 'Saturday in America' to discuss the recent FBI hack, bipartisanship and his recent trip to China. Trump says the FBI hack is 'not good.'

President Donald Trump reiterate...
articles.body_text:
President Donald Trump joins 'Saturday in America' to discuss the recent FBI hack, bipartisanship and his recent trip to China. Trump says the FBI hack is 'not good.'

President Donald Trump reiterated his push for bipartisanship Saturday, saying he is confident he can work with Democratic congressional leaders to accomplish "tremendous things" when a divided government convenes in January.

Speaking on "Saturday in America," Trump called House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., a "reasonable guy" and pointed to several issues they may be able to work on together. However, he warned that he is still prepared to use his veto power if Democrats refuse to negotiate.

"There's a chance we could get great healthcare and a lot of other things, and we can do it in a bipartisan way," Trump told host Kayleigh McEnany. "There's a very good chance. Because otherwise, everything gets vetoed."

TRUMP CONGRATULATES DEMOCRATS AFTER DOMINANT MIDTERMS, SAYS HE LOOKS FORWARD TO WORKING WITH THEM

President Donald Trump speaks during a news briefing at the White House on Nov. 20, 2026, in Washington, D.C., after returning from a visit to China, where he met with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. (Mehmet Eser/Anadolu via Getty Images)

"I mean, I could sit there for two years and one month and just veto everything," he added. "Veto everything. And nothing would get done for anyone, and that's not the way to go."

Jeffries ran unchallenged for House speaker on Wednesday, becoming speaker-designate in the internal caucus vote before a full House floor vote in January. In comments after the vote, Jeffries brushed off opposition from the progressive wing of his party and said he expects Democrats will be able to "work together."

HAKEEM JEFFRIES WINS OVERWHELMING SPEAKER-DESIGNATE VOTE AS PROGRESSIVES' REVOLT FALLS FLAT

Only 11 Democrats voted against Jeffries' nomination in the secret-ballot vote. Among those who opposed him — or publicly said they intended to — were Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier, Adam Hamawy, Frederick D. Haynes III, Melat Kiros, Donavan McKinney, Chris Rabb and Claire Valdez.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., speaks during a news conference at the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 17, 2026, in Washington, D.C. House Democrats subsequently nominated Jeffries in a closed-door vote on Nov. 18 to serve as speaker of the House when the new Congress convenes in January, putting him in position to become the first Black speaker of the chamber. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images)

Trump said he looks "forward to working with Hakeem" and congratulated the Democrat on his win.

"What he did was pretty spectacular with getting that position," Trump said. "And it's nice, the first Black person in that position, it's a big deal. It's a big deal, and he should be very proud of himself."

Trump also pushed back on criticism from Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., over his recent trip to China, arguing that he feels the need to maintain relationships and an "open line of communication" with other world leaders.

Still, Trump expressed optimism that he and congressional Democrats can work together, pointing to healthcare, the upcoming debt ceiling and a potential 10% cap on credit card interest rates as areas for compromise.

President Donald Trump attends a multilateral meeting with delegations from Japan, India and Australia at the Solaire Resort Hotel on Nov. 17, 2026, in Manila. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

"I think there's a — and I may be wrong. I may be wrong. But I think there's a real good chance they'll be sending stuff up, and rather than vetoing it — probably we'll start with vetoes just to set the stage," Trump said, adding that "the power of the veto is ultimate."

TRUMP PLEDGES TO VETO 'INSANE' DEM BILLS, PINPOINTS ISSUE PARTIALLY TO BLAME FOR REPUBLICAN LOSSES

"There's a chance that we can do better than we did when we had a very small majority with the Republicans," he continued. "They have some good points on healthcare, and they have some bad points. And we have some good things, and probably they would say we have some bad things. But there's a chance we could get great healthcare and a lot of other things, and we do it in a bipartisan way."

Fox News Digital’s Louis Casiano contributed to this report.

Madison Colombo is a writer for Fox News Digital’s Flash, Media, and Culture team, covering daily breaking news and trending topics with an award-winning background in broadcast and digital journalism.

Tennessee Titans defensive lineman Jaylen Harrell is hospitalized in Tampa, Florida, after being involved in a serious car accident, the team announced.

The team said they have been in constant communication with Harrell's family.

"Yesterday, Jaylen Harrell was involved in a serious car accident that resulted in him being taken to the hospital in his hometown of Tampa, Florida. We have been in constant communication with Jaylen’s family and are still working to gather more information," the Titans said in a statement to OutKick.

"At this time, Jaylen remains in the hospital and continues to receive care. We ask that Jaylen and his family’s privacy be respected at this time. We will provide an update when appropriate."

The 24-year-old hasn't played for the Titans this season after he tore his ACL during the preseason in August and was placed on season-ending injured reserve. The 2026 season would have been his third in the NFL after being drafted in the seventh round of the 2024 NFL Draft out of Michigan.

articles.title: Man charged with attempted murder after councillor stabbed in Bradford
articles.excerpt:
Arfan Ali, 31, has also been charged with assault and possession of an offensive weapon in a public place

A man has been charged with attempted murder after a local councillor was stabbed while worki...
articles.body_text:
Arfan Ali, 31, has also been charged with assault and possession of an offensive weapon in a public place

A man has been charged with attempted murder after a local councillor was stabbed while working in the community in Bradford, police have said.

Arfan Ali, 32, is accused of attacking Ibrar Ali, 52, at about 11am on Thursday in the West Yorkshire city.

The alleged attacker has also been charged with assault and possession of an offensive weapon in a public place, West Yorkshire police said.

He appeared at Leeds magistrates court on Saturday, the Crown Prosecution Service confirmed. He was reportedly remanded in custody ahead of his next appearance, at Bradford crown court on 21 December.

A statement on behalf of Ibrar Ali and his family, shared on Friday, said he had been supporting council wardens with community clean-up activities.

They said: “During the incident, Councillor Ibrar intervened to protect a member of council staff and, in doing so, sustained multiple stab wounds.”

The family said the councillor’s injuries were serious but not life-threatening, and that he was in a stable condition in hospital, adding that he was “grateful for the overwhelming kindness shown and hopes to personally thank everyone once he has recovered”.

Officers were called just after 11am on Thursday to reports the councillor had been found seriously injured on Manse Street.

He is believed to have been injured first in Thornbury Avenue before being driven to Manse Street, according to the force.

Emergency services attended and took him to hospital.

articles.title: Russia-bound ship attacked in Gulf of Finland
articles.excerpt:
The Finnish Border Guard is leading the operations involving the Sparta II

A Russian cargo vessel bound for the country's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad has been hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf...
articles.body_text:
The Finnish Border Guard is leading the operations involving the Sparta II

A Russian cargo vessel bound for the country's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad has been hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland, Russian and Finnish authorities say.

The ship - the Sparta II - caught on fire after the strike on Saturday morning, before drifting into Finnish waters. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.

"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."

Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones had been used, based on preliminary information, and there was "no threat" to the territory's supplies.

The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.

The company says on its website that it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.

Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.

This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.

Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".

A Russian rescue vessel approached the ship and was told by the crew that they did not need to be evacuated, Kaliningrad's governor wrote on Telegram, adding: "The crew is currently carrying out the necessary work and plans to continue on its way."

The Finnish Border Guard later said the crew had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was now already en route to Russia. The Russian rescue vessel had remained at the location of the stricken ship.

It added that no environmental damage had been detected and that there was no danger to maritime traffic or people.

Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.

Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said that the Finnish Border Guard were responsible for the investigation into the attack and were co-operating with other relevant authorities.

Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry said.

The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.

Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland.

articles.title: Maher calls out 'spoiled brats' who left US over Trump presidency, says country ‘self-corrected’ in midterms
articles.excerpt:
Bill Maher mocked celebrities who left the U.S. over President Donald Trump during the season finale of HBO’s "Real Time" on Friday, Nov. 20, 2026. (FilmMagic via Getty Images)

Bill Maher, host of HB...
articles.body_text:
Bill Maher mocked celebrities who left the U.S. over President Donald Trump during the season finale of HBO’s "Real Time" on Friday, Nov. 20, 2026. (FilmMagic via Getty Images)

Bill Maher, host of HBO's "Real Time," took a swipe at liberals who fled the country over President Donald Trump’s administration, calling them "spoiled brats" as he celebrated Democrats’ sweep in this month’s midterm elections.

Speaking to the audience during the show’s season finale Friday night, Maher blasted Democrats who moved abroad following Trump’s election victories in 2016 and 2024.

"But it is also important to remember to mock and ridicule the spoiled brats who fled to England or Ireland because America was so irredeemably ‘Trumpian-Republican,’" Maher said as he flashed a news headline highlighting "21 celebs who fled the U.S. amid Trump’s presidency."

AMERICANS WHO MOVED TO EUROPE AFTER TRUMP WIN NOW SAY THEY REGRET LEAVING

"Real Time" host Bill Maher called Democrats who fled the country after Trump’s election wins "spoiled brats." (Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)

"Only to come back to America now because America did what America does: self-corrected," he added.

Maher went on to question the judgment of those who left their country over election results that they were unhappy with, as he touted Democrats’ historic sweep in the midterm election earlier this month.

NEW YORK TIMES GLEEFUL OVER DEMOCRATS' HUGE MIDTERM VICTORIES, SAYS IT'S TIME TO ‘FEEL PRIDE’

"You left the country you're supposed to love forever because you lost an election or two, and now you look like the husband who leaves his wife because she let herself go for a while," Maher added. "Well, guess what? We got hot again."

Maher began by making fun of conservatives who left blue states: "Let's all allow ourselves a good laugh at the people who uprooted their whole lives in blue states to move to red states that are now blue states."

He praised the results of the midterms, noting, "We should all have a little more faith that democracy can still do its thing. And it's a beautiful thing. The sound of a country turning the page, catching up with its own ideals."

The HBO host's comments come after several high-profile celebrities — including comedians Rosie O’Donnell and Ellen DeGeneres — cited Trump’s election victory as their driving force for moving abroad.

ROSIE O'DONNELL HAMMERS TRUMP REPEATEDLY IN KIMMEL GUEST-HOST GIG AS WHITE HOUSE FIRES BACK

Comedian Rosie O’Donnell moved to Ireland after President Donald Trump’s 2024 election victory. (Photo by Rommel Demano/Getty Images)

"We got here the day before the election and woke up to lots of texts from our friends with crying emojis, and I was like, 'He got in,'" DeGeneres told broadcaster Richard Bacon after she and her wife, Portia de Rossi, decided to relocate to the United Kingdom, according to the BBC in 2025. "And we're like, 'We're staying here.'"

O’Donnell referred to Trump as "Mango Mussolini" on the Aug. 17 episode of "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" during a week-long guest-hosting stint that brought the 64-year-old comic back to the United States from her new home in Ireland.

ART GARFUNKEL JOINS GROWING LIST OF CELEBRITIES CONSIDERING A MOVE ABROAD OVER TRUMP PRESIDENCY

Musician Art Garfunkel told The Guardian earlier this year he was considering leaving the U.S. over President Donald Trump’s policies. (Billboard via Getty Images)

"I read that Project 2025 and said, ‘Got to get myself out of here, you know,’ and I decided to go to Ireland, a place where people are driven to drink regardless of who's running their country," O’Donnell said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Musician Art Garfunkel also weighed the possibility of leaving the United States over Trump’s presidency, telling The Guardian earlier this year that he is unhappy with the administration’s handling of climate change, international affairs and other political issues.

"I don’t like America’s position at all," he told the outlet. "I’m not on board, and I’m thinking of leaving the country, frankly."

Maher's comments were noticed by Democratic strategist Kaivan Shroff, who suggested to Fox News Digital that the comedian could be acting a bit hypocritical in his final monologue of the season.

"This Ireland shot is obviously a Rosie O’Donnell dig, and Maher is flattening 20 years of context to make it work," Shroff said. "Trump has singled her out since 2006 and, after she left, publicly threatened to take away her citizenship."

"You can call her decision dramatic, but it was not some celebrity tantrum over losing an election," he added. "And Maher, who can barely tolerate criticism directed at himself, is an especially funny person to lecture somebody else about having thicker skin."

NewsBusters managing editor Curtis Houck told Fox News Digital: "Bill Maher will sadly be on an island when it comes to calling out people on his own team who fled the country."

"Anyone returning to America as though their tantrums never happened shouldn’t be taken seriously," he added.

Fox News Digital reached out to representatives of DeGeneres and O’Donnell for comment.

Julia Bonavita is a media and culture writer for Fox News Digital, and a Fox Flight Team drone pilot. You can follow her at @juliabonavita13 on all platforms and send story tips to julia.bonavita@fox.com.

articles.title: Voters want to 'move on' from the president, former Trump official claims as reason for GOP's midterm defeat
articles.excerpt:
Former Kansas Republican Sen. Sam Brownback tells Fox News Digital that voters rejected President Trump himself, not his policies, citing inflation and gas prices.

Former Kansas Republican Sen. Sam B...
articles.body_text:
Former Kansas Republican Sen. Sam Brownback tells Fox News Digital that voters rejected President Trump himself, not his policies, citing inflation and gas prices.

Former Kansas Republican Sen. Sam Brownback, who served as an ambassador during Donald Trump's first term, blamed the president's personal leadership style for Republicans' midterm losses.

He claims the outcome of the 2026 elections — where Democrats' sweeping victories in traditional red strongholds helped them reclaim majorities in the House and Senate — was a sign of voters rejecting Trump more than rebuking his policies.

"I think the thing we're missing is that it was really targeted at President Trump. I don't think it was targeted at the policies so much," Brownback told Fox News Digital in an interview. "Pride comes before a fall and a haughty spirit before a stumble."

REPUBLICANS TURN ON TRUMP AFTER DEVASTATING MIDTERM LOSSES HAND DEMOCRATS CONTROL OF CONGRESS

President Donald Trump arrives to speak during a campaign event at the Freeman Coliseum in San Antonio, Texas, on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026. Trump defended his immigration policies during the visit as he sought to boost GOP Senate candidate Ken Paxton ahead of November's midterm elections. (Christopher Lee/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The former Kansas governor argued that Republicans should not write off the midterm results as the typical losses suffered by a president’s party through history during their second term.

Brownback, who represented Kansas in the U.S. Senate from 1996 to 2011 before serving as governor from 2011 to 2018, said economic concerns, including inflation and gas prices, played a role in the election results.

He suggested voters' frustrations extended beyond the economy to Trump's approach to governing.

The Fox News Voter Poll found that 89% of voters considered the cost of living a crucial or major factor in their congressional vote, compared with 74% who said the same about the war in Iran. The findings suggest broader economic frustrations were also a major concern among voters, although the two issues may overlap and the polling does not establish which ultimately drove Republican defections.

DEMS SEIZE ON MIDTERM ROUT TO DEMAND ICE REFORM, BUT POLLS REVEAL A TWIST IN WHO PRIORITIZED IMMIGRATION

The former Kansas senator and Trump ambassador urged Republicans to embrace humility and kindness ahead of 2028 (Sarah Silbiger/Getty Images)

"People just saying I'm ready to move on past President Trump," Brownback said, adding that voters still appreciated the administration's efforts to secure the border but viewed interior immigration enforcement as too aggressive.

The former ambassador-at-large for international religious freedom also urged Republicans to reconsider how they communicate with voters, emphasizing the importance of humility and kindness.

"You just can't be proud. You've got to come forward humbly," Brownback said. "And I think you have to do that with the American public."

Brownback called for a more measured response to voters' concerns ahead of 2028. "We hear you, American public. We're adjusting to the message that we heard," he said.

REPUBLICANS NEED HISTORY LESSON ABOUT THEIR PARTY IF THEY WANT TO MOVE ON FROM DEFEAT

President Donald Trump speaks at a midterm campaign rally at Port of Corpus Christi in Corpus Christi, Texas on October 27. (Photo by Kent NISHIMURA / AFP via Getty Images)

"America is great because it's good. If it ever loses its goodness, it will lose its greatness," he added. "There has to be, as I keep doubling back to, a humility and a kindness about it as well."

Both Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have been floated as potential contenders for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination, with Vance saying he plans to decide whether to launch a White House bid in the spring.

Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.
