The mayor's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

MICHAEL RUIZ: NEW YORK'S GUTTED POLICE UNIT WAS MORE THAN A PROTEST SQUAD

In this still image taken from video, an NYPD member whose uniform reads "Special Response Group" across the back can be seen escorting Zohran Mamdani away from a protest with his wrists bound behind his back. Now the New York City mayor, Mamdani has announced the SRG will be disbanded. (Zohran Mamdani/X)

Mamdani announced that the group will be dissolved at a news briefing early Monday. He had campaigned on the issue in part due to the unit's role in responding to organized protests — and riots — including those that exploded after George Floyd's death in 2020, demonstrations against Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Israel's war with Palestinian Hamas terrorists.

The images were recirculated earlier this week by Crain's New York, a local outlet focused on business, politics and real estate.

A second video, recorded by the local ABC affiliate, appears to show Mamdani arrested again by the unit shortly before he announced his mayoral bid in 2024.

On Monday, Mamdani said he would disband the group and divvy up its responsibilities — which included crowd control at protests and riots, critical incident response and counterterrorism — between three new entities and the NYPD's Intelligence and Counterterrorism Bureau.

One of the new units is the unarmed Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division (CDDD). This civilian team won't have arrest authority.

The back of the officer's uniform can be seen in the video. (Zohran Mamdani/X)

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"His voters won’t care," said Joseph Giacalone, a retired NYPD sergeant and criminal justice professor. "These transplants are all renters using mommy and daddy’s money to live in NYC, and when things go south, and they will, they’ll flee back home."

NYC MAYOR ZOHRAN MAMDANI SAYS HE WON'T FIRE NYPD COMMISSIONER JESSICA TISCH DESPITE SOCIALIST PRESSURE

The NYPD Strategic Response Group (SRG) monitors a crowd outside 26 Federal Plaza on Oct. 21, 2025 in New York City. (Photo by Adam Gray/Getty Images)

Upcoming events like the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade and New Year's ball drop will not be impacted since the changes aren't slated to go into effect until spring 2027.

NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said in a statement that the restructuring would not "diminish the NYPD’s ability to protect New Yorkers, or that put our officers in a position where they lack the resources necessary to confront a serious threat."

articles.title: EU wants ‘closest possible relationship’ with UK after agreeing Brexit reset deal – live
articles.excerpt:
President of European Council says EU ‘remains open to have the closest possible relationship’ with the UK

On the UK’s broader deliberations about its long-term relationship with the EU, Costa says d...
articles.body_text:
President of European Council says EU ‘remains open to have the closest possible relationship’ with the UK

On the UK’s broader deliberations about its long-term relationship with the EU, Costa says diplomatically:

“We respected the sovereign decision taken by the British people in 2016, and I recall the words of the European Council after the referendum: we regret, but we respect. And we will equally respect whatever decision the United Kingdom takes about the future of its long term relationship with the European Union.”

He says the EU “remains open to have the closest possible relationship” with the UK.

But he also pointedly says, “you know our principles well,” including “the indivisibility of all of our four freedoms of the single markets.”

Denmark’s foreign minister on Friday said Moscow’s defence attache in Copenhagen would be expelled after Russia was suspected of being behind an attempted assassination of a Ukrainian rapper.

“We have just summoned the Russian ambassador to the ministry of foreign affairs and notified him of the government’s decision to expel the Russian defence attache from Denmark” within seven days, Lars Lokke Rasmussen told a news conference.

“We are saying this very clearly: we have exposed you”, he said.

He also added Denmark was mulling suspending Schengen visas to Russians.

The UK prime minister called the newly agreed post-Brexit reset deal a “win-win” for the UK and the EU, although the level of tuition fees EU students will pay to study at UK universities remains unresolved.

The prime minister met Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, and António Costa, the European Council president, at the EU-UK summit in Brussels.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage claimed that Andy Burnham’s reset agreements with the EU “was in direct contradiction of the Labour manifesto upon which they were elected in 2024”.

He also said Burnham’s actions “went completely against the pledge that he made to the voters of Makerfield just a few months ago”.

The Reform leader later added: “Burnham’s whole rationale is 73% of the people want to be closer to Europe.

“Well, if you ask me do I want better relations with our European neighbours? Do I think we could have a better trade deal than we’ve got at the moment? I am part of that 73%.

“But what he completely misunderstands is that is not an open ticket to rejoin a significant chunk of the single market today.”

Students and young workers have taken to the streets in more than 20 European countries in coordinated protests over the surging cost of living and housing, deteriorating learning conditions and rising military spending.

Activists from more than 50 groups in countries including Belgium, France, Germany, Greece, Italy, Portugal, Spain and the UK held rallies on Friday, lighting flares, burning cardboard models of tanks and waving placards, many reading “fight for our future”.

Calling it Europe’s biggest coordinated youth protest of recent years, the Youth Strike coalition said demonstrations were planned in about 400 cities under the slogan “fight for our future, not their wars”.

It made five broad demands, including an end to militarisation and conscription; structural investment in education and welfare; solidarity with Palestine; climate and social justice, and a “radical transformation of the system we live in”.

An Italian organiser, Alessandro di Miceli, said the Europe-wide protests were “to claim our right to a better and dignified future”. Specific demands differed from country to country, he said, but were all “deeply connected between each other”.

A Portuguese organiser, Leonor Chicó, said: “As young people, we know that we must organise and fight for our future, because no one else will do it for us.” Governments “show us every day that the needs of our generation are not their priority”, she said.

Shabbir Lakha from the UK-based Stop The War coalition said the mobilisation was “a crucial step towards building a lasting international movement capable of bringing together young people, students and workers around common demands”.

After weeks of demonstrations across several countries sparked by long-running French school protests, governments are struggling to respond to growing calls for affordable housing, functioning public services and greater social equality.

Speaking to British reporters following the leaders’ lunch, Burnham stressed that nothing would happen in the current parliament that went much beyond this deal.

He said: “There is a clear democratic mandate for what has been done today. It’s in the Labour manifesto… There will be nothing beyond the significance of this in this parliament.”

The so-called brainstorming process was, he said, “just looking at options in a new world, and having an open discussion about what those what those might might might be – it will be to inform the next parliament”,

He also challenged political opponents, notably Nigel Farage, who was in Brussels on Friday to hold a retaliatory press conference, to justify why they would reject a deal which, he said, would boost growth and lead to cheaper food and electricity.

“Why would anybody turn their back on that?” he said. “I think it’s for them to justify now [whether] they won’t support the bill that will be presented to parliament next week.”

The campaign group Best for Britain says the UK-EU agreement is an “essential and laudable step” towards Britain rejoining the union.

Commenting on the deal, chief executive Naomi Smith said:

double quotation markToday marks one small step in our economic fortunes but one giant leap for young people’s opportunities, and British businesses who for too long have had their horizons narrowed and wings clipped by needless Brexit red tape.

Having drawn a line under a decade of drift and division, the prime minister must now build on the bold leadership he has shown so far, and take the essential and laudable step towards restoring our EU membership, as the majority of voters the length and breadth of Great Britain now demand.

The joint commitment to open a dialogue on bloc wide touring artists permits (15:20) is a win for the UK.

Brussels always resisted talks on the topic as work permits for singers, actors and other performers are a national competence and not the preserve of Brussels.

This is also the reason behind the length of time it will take to implement the youth mobility programme – the joint statement confirms it will be at least 2028 and latest 2030 when the scheme will be operational.

One EU diplomat this week said of the youth scheme:

“The problem is the UK is negotiating with Brussels but it is the member states that make the decisions.”

However if Brussels can find some way to achieve a “one size fits all” work permit for under 31s in the youth mobility scheme that might apply to touring artists too.

Retailers and manufacturers have welcomed Andy Burnham’s new trade deal with the European Union as a “big win” but warned they need “clear and early” guidance from government to aid the transition, Press Association reported.

The chief executive of the British Retail Consortium (BRC) called the SPS deal a “big win” for UK retailers but warned that businesses need “at least 18 months” to transition to the new arrangements.

“Reducing border friction and simplifying trade will cut costs and support smoother trade in food, drink and plants between the UK and EU, including moving goods to Northern Ireland.

The benefits will be felt across the entire supply chain, from producers and suppliers through to retailers and the millions of consumers they serve.”

The priority now must be to get the detail right and give businesses at least 18 months, alongside clear and early guidance, to transition to the new arrangements without unnecessary cost or disruption.”

But the BRC also told the Press Association that it does not expect to see prices on supermarket shelves fall in response to this deal, even though this is a welcome intervention.

Upward pressures remain heavy and will not be alleviated by the agreement, it said.

The National Farmers Union said they had worked with the Government to secure the deal which “should help” the industry, but warned that it was “only the beginning”.

President of the NFU Tom Bradshaw said that while reducing border friction is welcome, “rebuilding lost exports will take time” as in some cases British products have been replaced by goods from elsewhere.

The managing director of Marks + Spencer Food, Alex Freudmann, said in a blog on Friday that the deal will “remove bureaucracy” from the current regulations.

“How hard can it be to get a spaghetti bolognese from a factory in Lincolnshire onto a shelf in Dublin?

Today, it takes hundreds of extra miles, mountains of paperwork, a vet’s signature and the Latin name of a cow (Bos taurus, if you’re wondering).

This is what food trade looks like after Brexit. And it’s why we need the UK-EU food trade deal announced today.”

To celebrate the EU-UK reset deal Andy Burnham and his cabinet are invited to lunch with the European Commission and European Council.

The menu couldn’t be more fitting: creamy pea and mint soup, battered North Sea cod and chips, followed by Brussels waffle with fruit.

Because everyone in the EU loves a bit of Brussels waffle, in both senses.

For what it’s worth, the EU’s explainer – helpfully written as a Q&A - is here.

The main document from today’s summit is this one: the joint declaration signed by the two sides.

I won’t read it chronologically, but jump a bit, reflecting what I think you are looking for, and not how the document is written.

On “people to people” relations (pages 7-8), the document confirms the Youth Experience Scheme (YES) that will allow “100,000 people from the EU and the UK respectively to reside for up to three years to engage in activities such as work, studies, au-pairing, volunteering or simply travelling.”

On timing, it says the sides “aim to apply this agreement no later than 2028,” and want it to kick in “no later than January 2030.” It will apply to those up to the age of 31, so effectively will help those born in 1999 and later.

The document also confirms the UK’s return to the Erasmus+ programme in 2027, which we already knew about.

On the thorny issue of tuition fees, it says the parties will “work towards a supplementing agreement” to be agreed within six months. It’s very much unfinished business on that point.

In a win for artists and performers, the document also includes a somewhat vague, but promising, commitment to “explore further mutually beneficial solutions” to help touring artists with ridiculous red tape currently in place.

The statement also covers some of the key sectoral deals we mentioned earlier (pages 9-10), on emissions trading systems, sanitary and phytosanitary measures (SPS), and yes – of course – on fish (noting the decision on full reciprocal access to waters to fish until 30 June 2038).

In similarly practical decisions, there is also a note on “the significant progress achieved in discussions on the mutual recognition of professional qualifications for architects” which are set to continue.

The statement also covers important issues on judicial and security matters, noting plans to enhance cooperation between law enforcement agencies and, particularly, on the removal of foreign national offenders and migrant returns (pages 11-12).

The new language on economic resilience and cooperation is on pages 13-14, including commitment to “counter technology leakage in critical sectors, mitigate risks to critical infrastructure, and [to build] resilient supply chains” and so on.

The document, finally, also covers foreign and defence policy, in generally vague language, but across several pages (1-7).

It includes a long list of things the EU and the UK agree on, including on their support for Ukraine, foreign and defence policy priorities related to Africa, Arctic, Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, Nato, Moldova, and the Western Balkans.

It also includes a line on commitment to “effective multilateralism” through the UN, the international criminal court, which continues to attract attacks from the US, and the global rules-based trade system.

Meanwhile, the UK government has published some documents from the reset deal here.

27 pages to go through this beautiful Friday afternoon.

And more to come, no doubt, as there are no legal texts published yet.

Burnham rejects a suggestion that today’s deal is merely “a fig leaf,” saying it is “a little harsh”.

He says today’s developments are “a sign of sensible, constructive collaboration where it is beneficial for both sides.”

“Our experts and European experts, in the same room, dealing with these challenges, together, that is progress. I would say not a fig leaf.”

And then we are back to questions on today’s deal and the tuition fees disagreement – and whether the two EU leaders agree with Burnham that today’s deal marks the high point of what can be done without a broader vision for the EU-UK relationship.

Costa smiles and says that the focus needs to be on building “the closest relationship possible” between the EU and the UK, but how close it can get needs to be defined by the British.

“In the meantime, we need to work very hard to try to solve problems to our companies, to our citizens, to improve the competitiveness of our economies,” he says.

But, somewhat echoing Burnham’s language earlier (14:37), he focuses on younger generations and says “these young people, a large part of them, was not here ten years ago, but they are here today.”

“And this is our duty to open to them new opportunities,” he says.

He says today’s deal on youth mobility for 100,000 people “is the best way to give future to our shared values, our mutual interest, our historic bond and cultural values that we share together.”

Von der Leyen says “we can always work on an incremental improvement to our relationship,” but she agrees that there is a much broader question on “the wider picture, the bigger picture” of how Europe should respond to “dramatic and big changes globally.”

The next question is on something very different – on continuing hybrid attacks about different European countries, asked in the context of airspace violations in Poland.

Two Russian cruise missiles and a jet-powered drone are reported to have crashed in Poland during Russian air attacks on Ukraine that took place amid major western military exercises by allied countries.

EU’s Costa says “it shows that, unfortunately, Russia instead of showing willingness to engage in peace talks continue to spread the threats.”

“This is very dangerous and shows Russia is going in the wrong direction,” he says.

Burnham says the incursion into Polish airspace is “utterly unacceptable,” as he says he wants to send “a strong message of solidarity to prime minister Tusk and the Polish people who we will support, always, in any way that we can.”

He makes a broader point on the back of that, saying “Europe is becoming more coordinated in terms of defence and security,” and today’s agreement helps with that.

He pivots to Ukraine more broadly, saying “if European security is to come into that question, first we must have a ceasefire, and we must have the basis of a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine.”

“We will have to think this through carefully, together, to ensure that we are stronger in the next decade, than we were in the last.

I think some of what we’ve seen in Europe came at us without us being fully prepared. Not just the aggression, but also the disruption within our democracies and other factors that have sought to weaken Europe.

We will come back stronger in this decade, and we collaborate more deeply on security and defence.”

Asked about British people making up their minds, von der Leyen smiles that “I have many British friends and they are very good at making up their minds.”

On today’s deals, she backs Burnham’s line that today’s deal matters.

“We have three major agreements where many people thought we would never be able, to come to the finish line.”

articles.title: Senate Republicans break through Washington gridlock with massive American energy, data center overhaul
articles.excerpt: Oklahoma Sen. Alan Armstrong discusses the critical need for permitting reform to boost American energy independence. He explains that despite abundant U.S. oil and gas resources, outdated processes a...
articles.body_text:
Oklahoma Sen. Alan Armstrong discusses the critical need for permitting reform to boost American energy independence. He explains that despite abundant U.S. oil and gas resources, outdated processes and litigation delay essential infrastructure projects. Armstrong, a former CEO, highlights how legal challenges can halt multi-billion dollar projects, emphasizing the need for robust political action to streamline energy development.

Senate Republicans scored a major win after advancing a massive bill that would overhaul America’s permitting system in a bid to turbocharge infrastructure and energy development in the country.

The Senate advanced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) on a major bipartisan vote Thursday night. The legislation went through fits and starts over the last few months, until a bipartisan coalition, with buy-in from the White House, formed to tinker with the final product.

At the 30,000-foot level, the sweeping package would accelerate environmental review of projects, limit legal challenges, protect approved projects, expand the electric grid and streamline energy development in all fields — like oil, gas and renewables.

AMERICA’S BROKEN PERMITTING SYSTEM IS QUIETLY RAISING YOUR COST OF LIVING

An Amazon Web Services data center is seen on Aug. 26, 2026 in Stone Ridge, Virginia. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

"This is a major step toward making it faster and more efficient and easier to build infrastructure projects, certainly without giving up any of the strong protections for our environment," Chair of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., said when the bill was introduced in September.

The bill also tackles an issue that was front and center for voters across the country: data centers.

Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., the Democratic lead on the legislation, pushed for stronger language in the bill that would shield ratepayers from higher costs that stem from data center development and their usage of electricity.

WHO PAYS FOR US POWER BOOM? BLUE, RED STATES OFFER STARKLY DIFFERENT WAYS TO LOWER UTILITY BILLS AMID AI SURGE

That comes after Republicans tried to ram through similar safeguards before the election with a bill from Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, that Democrats argued lacked real enforcement teeth.

"This process will mean that we develop responsibly. It will mean more jobs. It will mean cheaper energy," Heinrich said. "It will mean that we actually require big load centers, whether that's a factory or a data center, to not pass those costs on to the American consumer by statute, not a suggestion, an actual law."

The provision covers data centers with a demand of at least 20 megawatts of power, and would require them to cover the cost of additional power for them to run, financial guarantees covering costs to build or upgrade facilities, to pay the tab if they leave an area for unpaid infrastructure costs, allow states to charge higher rates to reduce other customers’ bills and tack on power supply conditions.

DEMS KILL REPUBLICAN'S CHANCES OF LOWERING AMERICANS' ELECTRICITY BILLS IN KEY ELECTION FLASHPOINT

Sens. Mike Lee, R-Utah, Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., and Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., hold a news conference on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act in the U.S. Capitol on Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026. (CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Meanwhile, whether the legislation makes it through the House is an open question.

Sen. Alan Armstrong, R-Okla., who was appointed to the position earlier this year to replace Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and has made permitting reform his primary policy issue, told Fox News Digital that there were "a lot of good supporters on both sides of the aisle in the House." But he worried about attendance issues in the lower chamber.

"A lot of the language that's in here came right out of a lot of the House’s work," Armstrong said. "So, I think there'll be some support. I just hope we have people, you know, show up in the numbers that we need to vote for it."

Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

articles.title: FBI arrests Georgia man accused of sending cryptocurrency to ISIS-linked individuals and groups
articles.excerpt: Georgia man faces federal charges after allegedly sending more than $26,000 to ISIS-linked individuals and groups, with FBI agents discovering damaged cellphones and shredded documents submerged in li...
articles.body_text:
Georgia man faces federal charges after allegedly sending more than $26,000 to ISIS-linked individuals and groups, with FBI agents discovering damaged cellphones and shredded documents submerged in liquid during a search of his apartment.

A Georgia man is facing federal charges after allegedly sending more than $26,000 to individuals and groups affiliated with ISIS, the Department of Justice (DOJ) announced.

Younes Moustafa Younes, 34, of Lavonia, Georgia, was charged with one count of international money laundering and one count of destruction of evidence, according to the DOJ.

Younes was arrested Nov. 18 and made his initial appearance Thursday in federal court.

Federal prosecutors allege Younes altered and destroyed evidence leading up to his arrest. During a search of his apartment, FBI agents discovered three cellphones submerged in an unknown solution, including one that had been smashed and another with its identification number removed, according to the criminal complaint.

FBI ARRESTS 3 MEN WHO ALLEGEDLY PLEDGED ALLEGIANCE TO ISIS, FUNDED DRONE ATTACKS TARGETING US TROOPS OVERSEAS

Younes Moustafa Younes, 34, of Lavonia, Georgia, faces federal money laundering and evidence destruction charges after allegedly sending more than $26,000 to ISIS-linked individuals and groups, according to the Justice Department. (FBI Atlanta)

Investigators also found shredded documents submerged in an unknown solution inside a bathtub.

According to the complaint, Younes sent approximately $16,807 through cryptocurrency transactions between December 2025 and June 2026, using multiple phone numbers and accounts allegedly intended to conceal his identity.

Investigators say at least some of the funds were intended to support ISIS operations in Syria.

Prosecutors also allege that Younes sent approximately $9,206 through 11 cryptocurrency transactions between December 2021 and April 2022, using an alias to conceal his involvement.

NAVY VETERAN AMONG TRIO WHO ALLEGEDLY WANTED TO BEHEAD SOLDIER AND FUND ISIS DRONE ATTACKS ON AMERICANS

Federal investigators said they discovered three cellphones submerged in an unknown solution, including one that had been smashed, during a search of Younes Moustafa Younes' apartment. (FBI Atlanta)

The FBI first identified Younes in 2020 after he allegedly accessed ISIS propaganda online, according to the complaint.

During an interview with law enforcement, Younes acknowledged viewing the material but denied supporting extremist ideologies.

Prosecutors allege he later became increasingly radicalized, expressing support for ISIS and other terrorist figures through encrypted communications.

If convicted, Younes faces up to 20 years in federal prison on each charge, according to the Justice Department.

The international money laundering charge also carries a potential fine of up to $500,000, while the destruction of evidence charge carries a potential fine of up to $250,000.

Younes Moustafa Younes was arrested Nov. 18 following an FBI investigation into alleged cryptocurrency transfers to individuals and groups affiliated with ISIS. (FBI Atlanta)

Younes remains in federal custody pending preliminary and detention hearings scheduled for Nov. 23.

Michael Sinkewicz is a writer for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to michael.sinkewicz@fox.com

articles.excerpt:
Exclusive: While PM pushes for EU reset, Tory leader is moving away from ‘divisive’ issue that defined party for years

Kemi Badenoch has been advised by her team to limit the amount of time she spend...
articles.body_text:
Exclusive: While PM pushes for EU reset, Tory leader is moving away from ‘divisive’ issue that defined party for years

Kemi Badenoch has been advised by her team to limit the amount of time she spends discussing Brexit and Europe, the Guardian has been told, moving the Conservatives away from an issue that defined the party for many years.

While the Tory leader still gives views on Brexit – in an opinion piece in the Daily Mail on Thursday she condemned Andy Burnham’s ongoing reset with the EU as a “backwards” move – sources say it is now seen as a second-order subject.

Instead, Badenoch intends to focus on areas the party believes are more fertile electoral ground, in particular the economy, the cost of social security and defence.

One source said Badenoch had been advised to shift the narrative away from Brexit by Stephen Gilbert, a former Conservative official who is now a peer and who joined the Tory leader’s team as a senior political adviser a year ago.

Although another party source said Gilbert’s advice was “more nuanced” than this, Badenoch’s recent run of speeches and interventions appears to demonstrate the change.

In eight sets of prime minister’s questions since Burnham entered No 10 over the summer, Badenoch and her deputy, Alex Burghart, who took one session when Burnham was away, have focused on Europe just once, on 28 October, when she challenged the PM on whether or not he wanted a new Brexit referendum.

Every other outing has focused on various aspects of the welfare state, the cost of living, or defence, also including subjects such as the budget, debt and whether or not the UK should drill for more North Sea oil and gas.

“The way I see it, this is less of a conscious attempt to sideline Europe than it is a way to talk more about the subjects we think are our strong points, like the economy and defence,” one senior Conservative said.

One Tory shadow minister said the wider party was firmly behind the idea: “Europe does still come up from time to time, but as a former remainer even I think we should move on. I’m not sure what is likely to change by us talking about it all the time.”

Another shadow minister said: “We don’t want to be talking about Brexit for multiple reasons – including the simple one that it was so awfully divisive.”

Badenoch does still at times defend Brexit to selected audiences, for example in Thursday’s Daily Mail piece, where she disputed Burnham’s charge that it had hampered the UK’s economic growth, saying the prime minister “wants to reopen arguments from 2016 because he has no answers for the world as it is”.

At other times her language on links with the EU has been more nuanced than the period when the Conservatives liked to disparage the continent as economically moribund and less relevant than more distant economies.

Asked about Burnham’s attempt to renegotiate the post-Brexit trade agreement during a press conference on defence earlier this month, Badenoch said: “They say they want to end red tape on food checks – that’s a good thing”, while then predicting this would not actually happen.

Badenoch also said she accepted that the deal with the EU could and should be updated: “The free trade agreement that we have with the EU, like many others, is one that needs constant negotiating. So I want to see Labour negotiating and improving on deals with all countries. That’s what you do when you have your own trade policy.”

A Conservative spokesperson said: “As Kemi has said, the last thing the country needs is to be dragged back into a debate on Brexit. That absolutely does not mean Kemi and the Conservatives won’t discuss the EU, but we will be very clear that Andy Burnham is only trying to reopen old wounds on Brexit because he doesn’t have anything to say about the challenges facing the country.

“Bringing down the welfare bill, funding defence, cutting taxes to promote growth can all be done outside the EU. Burnham’s reset is one big distraction and we will never shy away from saying so.”

articles.title: Islam set to be the largest religion by 2035: Where will most Muslims live?
articles.excerpt:
Muslims are projected to outnumber Christians worldwide by 2035, according to projections released by the Pew Research Center.

Both religions will keep growing. Between 2020 and 2070, the number of M...
articles.body_text:
Muslims are projected to outnumber Christians worldwide by 2035, according to projections released by the Pew Research Center.

Both religions will keep growing. Between 2020 and 2070, the number of Muslims is expected to rise by 80 percent, from 2.02 billion to 3.64 billion. Christians are projected to grow by 30 percent to 2.96 billion, roughly in step with the world population.

Muslims are projected to grow faster than any other major religious group. Hindus and Jews are expected to grow more slowly than the world population, while the number of Buddhists and people with no religion is projected to shrink.

The main reason is birth rates. Between 2020 and 2025, Muslim women had an average of 3.1 children, compared with 2.5 for Christian women and 1.6 for all other women. A population needs about 2.1 children per woman to replace itself.

Births minus deaths are projected to add 1.6 billion Muslims and 792 million Christians by 2070.

Most of the growth will happen where Muslims are already the majority. The 53 Muslim-majority countries are expected to gain 1.2 billion Muslims by 2070, 74 percent of the global increase.

Indonesia had the world’s largest Muslim population in 2020, at 239 million. Pakistan, just 12 million behind, is projected to take the top spot. Pew’s figures compare 2020 with 2070, so they do not say exactly when, but with Pakistan’s Muslim population set to double to 461 million while Indonesia’s grows 15 percent, the switch is likely to come well before 2070.

By 2070, India’s Muslim population is projected to rise from third to second, growing from 213 million to 334 million. Nigeria jumps from fifth to third, more than doubling to 282 million and pushing Indonesia to fourth.

Four of the top 10 in 2070 are in Africa: Nigeria, Egypt, Ethiopia and Sudan. Ethiopia and Afghanistan join the list, replacing Iran and Algeria, while Sudan’s Muslim population more than doubles to 116 million and climbs above Turkiye.

Pew’s projections cover 201 countries and territories, home to 99.98 percent of the world’s population. They assume current trends in fertility, mortality and religious switching continue, and could change with wars, disasters or economic shifts.

articles.title: Former Secret Service investigator sounds alarm over AI scams as Americans grow increasingly anxious
articles.excerpt: Jason Brown, a former U.S. Secret Service cyberfraud investigator, warns that AI-powered voice cloning and impersonation scams are making it increasingly difficult for Americans to distinguish real co...
articles.body_text:
Jason Brown, a former U.S. Secret Service cyberfraud investigator, warns that AI-powered voice cloning and impersonation scams are making it increasingly difficult for Americans to distinguish real communications from fake ones.

A former Secret Service cyberfraud investigator warned that Americans are increasingly on edge following a wave of major technology disruptions, while artificial intelligence is making scams targeting families and consumers more sophisticated.

Jason Brown, a former U.S. Secret Service cyberfraud investigator and iCounter's director of customer advisory and counter fraud lead, told Fox News Digital on Thursday that Americans have reason to be increasingly cautious about technology.

"There's been a lot of stuff that has happened in the past week in particular that people are concerned about," he continued, citing recent technology outages involving Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and several financial institutions.

TIMELINE: AMERICA HITS A TECH WALL AS OUTAGES CRIPPLE EMAIL, GROUND FLIGHTS AND DISRUPT MAJOR BANKS

The more details a scam includes, the more likely it is built from your publicly available data. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

Brown acknowledged that some incidents involved infrastructure problems while others remained under investigation.

With the holiday season approaching, Brown warned that AI has made it easier for criminals to create convincing fraudulent messages, eliminating many of the warning signs consumers previously relied on.

"AI has just made the criminal a lot more efficient and a little bit more effective," Brown said.

Spelling mistakes, poor grammar and awkward phrasing — once common indicators of fraudulent messages — are becoming less reliable as criminals use AI to generate more convincing communications, he explained.

AI VOICE SCAM TRAPS MOM IN 5-HOUR KIDNAPPING NIGHTMARE

Former U.S. Secret Service cyberfraud investigator Jason Brown warned that artificial intelligence is making scams more sophisticated and increasingly difficult for Americans to recognize. (Fox News Digital)

AI also allows criminals to impersonate familiar voices, potentially tricking victims into believing they are speaking with a family member in distress.

Brown described a scenario in which a scammer uses a short voice recording to impersonate someone's relative and demand thousands of dollars in gift cards.

"AI just makes them a lot more efficient and a lot less prone to errors," he said, warning that Americans must become more skeptical of suspicious messages.

"Unfortunately, we're at a point where everybody needs to have that level of distrust," he said.

As holiday shopping ramps up, Brown said scammers are likely to impersonate major delivery companies, including UPS, FedEx and the U.S. Postal Service.

FAKE E-ZPASS EMAIL THREATENS $100 FINE OVER UNPAID TOLL

Scammers may impersonate major delivery companies during the holiday shopping season, sending fraudulent messages claiming packages cannot be delivered without additional payment. (Ute Grabowsky/Photothek via Getty Images)

He warned that fraudulent messages may claim packages cannot be delivered until additional postage is paid, with scammers demanding payment through cryptocurrency or gift cards.

"If it comes from crypto, especially if it comes from gift cards, that's a red flag for sure," Brown said.

Beyond the emotional toll, Brown warned that increasingly sophisticated scams can result in significant financial losses. He cited FBI reporting that he said identified more than 22,000 AI-related fraud cases in 2025, with losses exceeding $890 million.

Brown noted that businesses are also vulnerable to schemes in which criminals impersonate trusted vendors and redirect legitimate payments into fraudulent accounts.

AGING MEANS LEARNING HOW TO PREVENT COSTLY SCAMS TARGETING OLDER AMERICANS

Former Secret Service investigator Jason Brown warned holiday shoppers to be cautious of suspicious delivery notifications appearing to come from UPS, FedEx or the U.S. Postal Service. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

The holiday season can create additional vulnerabilities as executives travel, employees take time off and temporary workers join company operations, he said.

Brown urged Americans to independently verify suspicious messages and take additional precautions when communicating with family members, including establishing a "safe word" to help confirm someone's identity during an unexpected call.

"Another thing that we always talk about with family members, set up a safe word ahead of time. Have that conversation now," he said, adding that even if a caller provides the correct word, people should still end the call and contact the person independently using a trusted number.

"The biggest safety valve for anybody in a scam when it comes over the internet via your cell phone over the computer is stop, think, and then independently verify," he added.

Michael Sinkewicz is a writer for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to michael.sinkewicz@fox.com

articles.title: Lionel Messi of Inter Miami tops Major League Soccer salaries
articles.excerpt: Lionel Messi remains the highest-paid player in Major League Soccer, with $28.3m in guaranteed compensation, according to a salary release on Thursday by the players’ union, with Chicago’s Robert Lewa...
articles.body_text:
Lionel Messi remains the highest-paid player in Major League Soccer, with $28.3m in guaranteed compensation, according to a salary release on Thursday by the players’ union, with Chicago’s Robert Lewandowski second.

Argentinian legend Messi topped the league list revealed by the MLS Players Association with compensation almost $8m higher than last year, although his figures include only playing compensation, not income from other sources.

Messi signed a contract extension through 2028 last year.

Poland’s Lewandowski, who joined the Chicago Fire earlier this year, was second overall with $19.51m, followed by Orlando’s Antoine Griezmann of France at $13.94m, South Korean star Son Heung-min of Los Angeles FC at $11.15m and Swiss international Breel Embolo of Atlanta United at $10.81m.

Among MLS clubs, Miami topped all teams in total guaranteed compensation at $59.37m, with Chicago second at $41.29m, Atlanta third at $38.35m, the Los Angeles Galaxy fourth at $34.91m and LAFC fifth at $32.91m.

The league’s lowest total team compensation was Philadelphia Union at $12.64m, with Sporting Kansas City second-lowest at $13.30m and DC United third-lowest at $14.55m.

The figures are through October 9 and are annualised for players who arrived in the summer transfer period.

articles.title: UK government borrowing rises less than forecast in surprise boost for chancellor John Healey
articles.excerpt:
UK economy defies City predictions and Iran war fallout, with gap between spending and income about £1bn lower than expected in October, at £17bn

The UK government borrowed less than expected in Octo...
articles.body_text:
UK economy defies City predictions and Iran war fallout, with gap between spending and income about £1bn lower than expected in October, at £17bn

The UK government borrowed less than expected in October despite a rise in debt interest costs, in a boost for chancellor John Healey amid the pressure on Britain’s economy from the Middle East war.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said public sector net borrowing – the difference between government spending and income – was £17bn in October, about £800m higher than the same month a year ago. City economists had forecast borrowing would increase by more, to £18bn.

In the financial year so far, public sector net borrowing was £111.3bn, the ONS said – £7.3bn less than in the same period last year, helped by stronger tax receipts.

Grant Fitzner, the ONS chief economist, said: “Borrowing so far this financial year remained lower than in the same period last year with receipts growing faster than spending. Income-related taxes’ receipts grew particularly strongly.

“However, monthly borrowing was up on last October, partly down to higher debt interest.”

The latest figures showed rising borrowing costs on financial markets drove the UK’s debt interest payments to £11.2bn in October - £2.8bn more than in the same month last year, and the highest figure for any October since monthly records began in 1997.

Some government bonds are directly linked to the retail prices index measure of inflation, with payments rising in line with it. RPI has increased in recent months as the Iran war has pushed up energy costs.

Public sector net debt rose to £3.1tn, equivalent to 95.8% of GDP – 1.9 percentage points higher than last year and at levels last seen in the early 1960s.

Chief secretary to the Treasury, Emma Reynolds, said Britain was showing “standout resilience despite the global impact of the conflict in Iran.

“This year we’ve cut borrowing faster than any other G20 country. Now we’re going to cut waste and bureaucracy by reprioritising spending and making public services more efficient with AI,” Reynolds added.

Britain’s economy has continued to grow at the second-fastest rate in the G7 despite the fallout from the war in the Middle East, bolstered by AI investment and households continuing to spend.

In his budget last month, Healey raised taxes on banks to fund relief for households being squeezed by the energy shock from the Middle East war.

Against a highly uncertain global backdrop, Healey stuck to the government’s fiscal rules with £15bn of headroom – less than the £23.6bn buffer left by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, as the conflict drove up the UK government’s borrowing costs.

After a low-key budget statement designed with febrile bond markets in mind, economists warned the chancellor had set himself up for a “brutal” spending review next year.

Avoiding a return to austerity for unprotected government departments could require a £17bn top-up to the spending plans for 2030-31, according to the Institute for Fiscal Studies. That is before taking into account an additional £11bn needed to fund a commitment to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP.

Official figures on Wednesday showed inflation in the UK rose in October to 3.6% amid the global surge in energy prices triggered by the Iran war. Economic forecasters predict a further rise in inflation, with the Bank of England anticipating a peak of close to 5% next year.

Threadneedle Street raised interest rates from 3.75% to 4% earlier this month and warned further increases might be required to combat inflationary pressures unleashed by the Iran war. Financial markets predict three quarter-point rate increases before the end of next year.

Rob Wood, the chief UK economist at the consultancy Pantheon Macroeconomics, said: “The October budget did little to address the more serious challenges facing the public finances, so we continue to have doubts about the government’s ability to follow through on its fiscal plans, suggesting upside risks to borrowing in the coming years.”

articles.title: The Gambia stood up for the Rohingya, now the world must act
articles.excerpt:
Member of the National Assembly of The Gambia and a Member of Parliamentarians for Global Action. Member of the National Assembly of The Gambia and a Member of Parliamentarians for Global Action.

The...
articles.body_text:
Member of the National Assembly of The Gambia and a Member of Parliamentarians for Global Action. Member of the National Assembly of The Gambia and a Member of Parliamentarians for Global Action.

There are moments in history when a nation is defined not by its size, wealth, military strength or political influence, but by the courage of its conscience.

On Thursday, the International Court of Justice found that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in northern Rakhine State, in breach of its obligations under the Genocide Convention. For the Rohingya, it is a long-overdue recognition. For The Gambia, it concludes a case our country brought to the Court seven years ago.

The Rohingya have lived in Myanmar’s Rakhine State for generations. Their basic human rights have been systematically denied over time, leaving them stateless and subject to dehumanising rhetoric, hate speech and legal persecution. Following the Myanmar military’s “clearance operations” in 2016 and 2017, over 700,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh. The military killed an estimated 10,000 civilians, raped and sexually assaulted women and girls, and burned villages to the ground. There are currently 1.2 million Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh, the majority in the camps of Cox’s Bazar, and 520,000 remain in Myanmar.

When confronted with reports of unimaginable suffering, persecution, displacement and the destruction of communities, The Gambia chose to act. In 2018, our then Minister of Justice, Abubacarr Tambadou, visited the camps in Bangladesh as part of an Organisation of Islamic Cooperation delegation. As a former prosecutor at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, he recognised the signs of genocide in the accounts of the survivors.

With the support of the OIC’s 57 member States, The Gambia brought the case to the International Court of Justice in November 2019. It was the first time in the court’s history that a state with no direct connection to the alleged crimes had filed a case under the 1948 Genocide Convention, which obliges all state parties to prevent and punish genocide wherever it may occur.

Yet, The Gambia’s action before the Court was never only about legal obligations or diplomatic considerations. We asked ourselves one fundamental question: if we remain silent in the face of such suffering, what does our silence make us?

As Gambians, we know the value of dignity. We understand what it means to yearn for justice. We know the pain that comes when our rights are denied, and voices are silenced. Our own history of political struggle taught us that freedom, accountability and human rights are lived realities that shape the lives of us all.

Perhaps that is why this case has resonated deeply with many Gambians: it speaks to our common humanity. In January, Rohingya survivors of the violence testified before the court about what they had lived through. We recognise that the fear of being driven from one’s home knows no nationality, and compassion does not stop at national boundaries.

The years since the case was filed have required patience and perseverance. International justice can often move frustratingly slowly. However, the court’s order in January 2020, the rejection of Myanmar’s objections in 2022, and the interventions from 11 states (Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, the Netherlands, the UK, the Maldives, Slovenia, the DRC, Belgium, and Ireland) on how the Convention should be interpreted have reaffirmed our shared commitment.

The judgement by the world’s highest court today is a reminder that the obligation to prevent genocide applies to every state, large or small, near or far. This is the first time in the history of the court that a state has been found responsible for committing genocide. The court concluded that the widespread rape and sexual violence committed by Myanmar’s security forces were part of the genocide, and that Myanmar failed to prevent genocide and to punish those responsible.

Myanmar is now under a clear obligation to comply fully with the judgement. It is required to investigate and prosecute those responsible, to facilitate the safe, voluntary and dignified return of displaced Rohingya and to protect them from discrimination and persecution. Justice for the Rohingya will also require the restoration of their citizenship and the recognition of their right to be called Rohingya.

Parliamentarians also have a role to play. As the court made clear today, punishing genocide requires laws that explicitly criminalise it. The court has held Myanmar to that standard, and we must hold ourselves to it, too. We must ensure that genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes are fully incorporated into our domestic laws, and that our courts can try them wherever they are committed.

In our National Assembly, we will ask our government about the next steps, monitor Myanmar’s compliance, and ensure that The Gambia continues to press for that compliance at the United Nations and within the OIC. Other states must now step in by ensuring that Myanmar complies, supporting Rohingya refugees and ensuring they will not be sent back into danger.

As Gambians, we have chosen empathy over indifference, principle over convenience, and action over silence. The Rohingya have shown extraordinary courage and determination in their search for justice, and today international law has finally answered them. Our collective responsibility now is to call for compliance and prevent any future acts of genocide.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Vape users hospitalised after losing consciousness, prompting public health warning in New South Wales
articles.excerpt:
Testing confirms presence of etomidate, a strong and fast-acting sedative used as a general anaesthetic overseas but not registered for medical use in Australia

Get our breaking news email, free app ...
articles.body_text:
Testing confirms presence of etomidate, a strong and fast-acting sedative used as a general anaesthetic overseas but not registered for medical use in Australia

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Three people who lost consciousness and were hospitalised in New South Wales after using certain vapes have tested positive for the unregulated anaesthetic agent etomidate, health officials said.

NSW health on Friday issued a public warning about vape liquids containing etomidate, a strong and fast-acting sedative used as a general anaesthetic overseas but not registered for medical use in Australia.

The three people who were hospitalised had used non-nicotine refillable vapes, the state health department said. Testing of their blood and urine confirmed the presence of etomidate.

The department would not confirm how old the three patients were, where they were hospitalised, or their condition on Friday.

The discovery of etomidate in vapes in NSW comes about four months after Victorian health officials announced they had found the powerful anaesthetic agent in an illicit vape sold in Melbourne.

On Friday, NSW health warned vapes sold as space pods, space oil, kpods, piu piu vapes, or zombie vapes may contain etomidate, or other substances, including ketamine, THC and potent opioids.

The medical director of the NSW poisons information centre, Dr Darren Roberts, said etomidate’s effects were unpredictable when used in a vape.

Roberts said etomidate could cause confusion, drowsiness, slow breathing, vomiting, muscle spasms or movements that were hard to control, and people who took it could become unresponsive.

These effects could be life threatening, especially if used with other drugs that could cause sedation, such as alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines, and GHB, Roberts said.

He said etomidate could also cause long-term harm when used regularly, including the disruption of hormones produced by the adrenal gland.

These hormones are important in regulating stress responses and need to be replaced if they aren’t produced naturally, he said.

“The contents found in non-nicotine vapes vary,” Roberts said. “You can’t assume what’s inside.”

He urged anyone considering using a vape to ask themselves what could be in it.

“You won’t get into trouble for seeking medical care,” he said. If you feel unwell, or if your friend feels unwell, after using a vape, do something about it.”

NSW health officials said it recommended people administer Naloxone to anyone who became responsive after using any drug, in case they had ingested opioids.

Naloxone is an opioid overdose treatment, which is free at pharmacies and does not require a prescription.

Naloxone won’t reverse the effects of etomidate, as the sedative does not belong to the opioid class of drugs, but it is still safe to give, health officials said.

The officials said anyone who witnessed someone experiencing unexpected symptoms after using drugs should call triple zero immediately or seek urgent medical attention.

articles.title: UK and EU to agree youth mobility scheme, BBC understands
articles.excerpt:
Watch: Burnham says he wants 'best deal for Britain' at UK-EU summit

Up to 100,000 young people from the EU would be allowed to travel, work and study in the UK per year under a new youth mobility sc...
articles.body_text:
Watch: Burnham says he wants 'best deal for Britain' at UK-EU summit

Up to 100,000 young people from the EU would be allowed to travel, work and study in the UK per year under a new youth mobility scheme set to be agreed on Friday, the BBC understands.

The same number of young Britons would be allowed into Europe under the scheme, expected to be approved at the UK-EU summit in Brussels. Downing Street has not commented on the details, but said talks were "down to the wire" on Thursday.

The prime minister has said a "Channel action plan" on immigration could also be struck, while negotiators are seeking agreements on food trade rules and carbon emissions pricing.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has accused Andy Burnham of "reopening the divisions" of the Brexit referendum.

A new youth mobility scheme would aim to make it easier for young people to work and travel both in the EU and UK.

The UK already has schemes in place with 13 non-EU countries including Australia, Canada and India.

In 2024, the EU proposed allowing 18 to 30 year-olds to work or study in the EU and UK for up to four years.

Labour, which was then in opposition, rejected the deal - arguing it amounted to reinstating freedom of movement.

Since coming to government, the party has suggested it would consider a more restricted scheme with a time limit, a cap on the numbers coming to the UK and a ban on participants from claiming benefits.

The UK's request to limit numbers has proved to be a sticking point in negotiation ahead of the summit, along with the EU's request that EU students should pay the same tuition fees at UK universities as domestic students.

Speaking to broadcasters on Thursday evening, Burnham was asked if there were any circumstances in which the UK would walk away from a deal on Friday.

"There would always be those circumstances because I'm in this to get the best deal for Britain, always," he said.

"But what's in it for us is the possibility of lower food prices and I can't turn my back on that, lower costs for business, cutting red tape, and a really big win potentially of more collaboration on immigration - a Channel action plan - which is a really big deal if we can land that tomorrow.

"So I hope people can understand why I have pushed this because it could be a really good deal for Britain."

Burnham previously said the UK and EU could link up their law enforcement efforts, including sharing more data and criminal records of foreign nationals.

The prime minister's spokesman has said if a deal were secured, the government would introduce legislation to Parliament next week to implement changes.

The Brexit debate is back – and there are nerves about what happens next

Faisal Islam: What's in the Brexit reset food deal and are there trade-offs?

The EU that Burnham is eyeing up is very different to the one Britain left

An agreement on trade could remove checks and paperwork faced by food companies exporting to the EU.

The government argues this could add £5bn to the economy and cut food prices.

However, it could mean the UK will have to follow certain EU rules on products, for example on gene-edited crops or labelling.

Burnham has also said the summit would allow the UK to raise concerns about the Made in Europe scheme, which is designed to protect industries from unfair Chinese competition.

Burnham has previously suggested he could commit Labour to building a closer long-term future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member - however, he has ruled out major changes before the next election.

The party's 2024 manifesto promised not to return to the EU, the single market, customs union or freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa.

Earlier this week, former deputy prime minister David Lammy urged the prime minister to go into the next general election promising to rejoin the EU.

However, the subject has divided his cabinet with one minister warning of the costs that would come with reversing Brexit.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, speaking to The Sun, external, said he does "not believe for a minute" the country would "ever vote to rejoin" the EU.

He added: "I think what Burnham is doing is playing a very cynical political game. He's trying to pick up votes from the Lib Dems, pick up votes from the Greens, and using it as a massive distraction from all the problems that he can't deal with."

Speaking to the BBC's Today programme on Thursday, Badenoch said she wanted to see easier trading with the EU, but "not trade at any cost".

She also said the new deals could see UK companies having to follow EU rules, even those that do not trade with the bloc.

Appearing on BBC Breakfast on Friday, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage described the agreement as a "very, very expensive and costly error" and said Burnham has no "democratic mandate to do any of this".

He added that the Labour party manifesto was clear that the UK would not go back towards the single market and asked: "Where is our democracy?".

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey told BBC Newsnight that while he agreed with Burnham on "the harms of Brexit", he did not think the prime minister was "going to go anywhere near far enough".

"We need to go further and faster," he said, including returning to freedom of movement - which Sir Ed said would help tackle immigration and boost the UK economy.
